Soergel calculus for monodromic Hecke categories
Colton Sandvik

Abstract
. We introduce two 2-categories which categorify the monodromic Hecke algebra. The first is algebraic in nature and generalizes Abe’s theory of Soergel bimodules. The second is a diagrammatic category defined via generators and relations which generalizes the Elias–Williamson diagrammatic calculus. As our first main result, we prove that these algebraic and diagrammatic categorifications are equivalent, extending an earlier theorem of Abe. Furthermore, we relate these new categorifications to a third categorification via parity sheaves which was previously studied by the author. More precisely, we provide a monodromic analogue of a theorem of Riche and Williamson to show that the diagrammatic category is equivalent to the monodromic Hecke category of parity sheaves associated to a reductive group. Finally, we show that these monodromic Hecke categories can be described by unipotent Hecke categories associated to endoscopic Coxeter groups.



1.
Introduction

1.1.
Hecke Algebras

Let
G
be a connected reductive group over
\mathbb{F}=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}
. Pick a prime
\ell\neq p
and a power
q=p^{n}
.
Let
B\subset G
be a Borel subgroup with split maximal torus
T\subset B
.
The Hecke algebra

\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\coloneq\Fun_{B(\mathbb{F}_{q})\times B(\mathbb{F}_{q})}(G(\mathbb{F}_{q}),\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell})

is the algebra of
B(\mathbb{F}_{q})
-biinvariant
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
-valued functions on
G(\mathbb{F}_{q})
with multiplication given by convolution.
The Hecke algebra was originally introduced to study unipotent
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
-representations of
G(\mathbb{F}_{q})
; however, since their introduction, Hecke algebras have become ubiquitous throughout many areas of representation theory.

In the study of the non-unipotent representation theory of
G(\mathbb{F}_{q})
, Lusztig
[
Lus19
]
introduced a generalization of the Hecke algebra which is now called the
monodromic Hecke algebra
.
Let
\chi,\chi^{\prime}:T(\mathbb{F}_{q})\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}^{\times}
be two characters of the maximal torus.
We can regard
\chi
and
\chi^{\prime}
as characters
B(\mathbb{F}_{q})\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}^{\times}
by the projection
B\to T
.
We can then consider the
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
-vector space of
(B(\mathbb{F}_{q})\times B(\mathbb{F}_{q}),\chi\times\chi^{\prime})
-invariant
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
-valued functions on
G(\mathbb{F}_{q})
,

\displaystyle{}_{\chi}\mathcal{H}_{\chi^{\prime}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})

\displaystyle\coloneq\Fun_{(B(\mathbb{F}_{q})\times B(\mathbb{F}_{q}),\chi\times\chi^{\prime})}(G(\mathbb{F}_{q}),\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell})

\displaystyle=\{f:G(\mathbb{F}_{q})\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}^{\times}\mid f(b_{1}gb_{2})=\chi(b_{1})f(g)\chi^{\prime}(b_{2})\text{ for }b_{1},b_{2}\in B,g\in G\}.

When
\chi=\chi^{\prime}
,
{}_{\chi}\mathcal{H}_{\chi}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
is also an algebra under convolution. When
\chi\neq\chi^{\prime}
,
{}_{\chi}\mathcal{H}_{\chi^{\prime}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
is no longer an algebra.
Instead, convolution gives suitably associative maps

{}_{\chi}\mathcal{H}_{\chi^{\prime}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\times{}_{\chi^{\prime}}\mathcal{H}_{\chi^{\prime\prime}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\to{}_{\chi}\mathcal{H}_{\chi^{\prime\prime}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q}).

If we fix a
W
-orbit
\mathfrak{o}
of characters
T(\mathbb{F}_{q})\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
, we can define the
monodromic Hecke algebra
as the direct sum of these vector spaces

\underline{\mathcal{H}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})=\bigoplus_{\chi,\chi^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}}{}_{\chi}\mathcal{H}_{\chi^{\prime}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})

which becomes an algebra under convolution and the relation
{}_{\chi}\mathcal{H}_{\chi^{\prime}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\cdot{}_{\chi^{\prime\prime}}\mathcal{H}_{\chi^{\prime\prime\prime}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})=0
if
\chi^{\prime}\neq\chi^{\prime\prime}
.

Iwahori gave a presentation of the Hecke algebra which is independent of
\mathbb{F}_{q}
and only depends on the Weyl group
W

[
Iwa64
]
.
In particular, Iwahori defined a
\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}]
-algebra
\mathcal{H}
such that
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\cong\mathcal{H}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}]}\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
along the specialization
v^{-1}\mapsto\sqrt{q}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
.
This presentation allowed for the generalization of the Hecke algebra to any Coxeter group and not just the crystallographic ones.
We write
\mathcal{H}(W)
for the (non-specialized) Hecke algebra with Coxeter group
W
.

Lusztig has given a presentation of the monodromic Hecke algebra closely inspired by Iwahori’s presentation
[
Lus16
]
.
In particular, Lusztig defined a
\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}]
-algebra
\underline{\mathcal{H}}^{\mon}(\mathfrak{o})
which specializes to
\underline{\mathcal{H}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
along
v^{-1}\mapsto\sqrt{q}
.
Note that this presentation still depends on
q
since
\mathfrak{o}
depends on
q
; however, this presentation is still favorable for the purposes of categorification.
To remove the restriction to a fixed
W
-orbit
\mathfrak{o}
of characters, we instead define the
monodromic Hecke algebroid
.
Instead of an algebra, the monodromic Hecke algebroid
\mathcal{H}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
is a category whose objects are characters
T(\mathbb{F}_{q})\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}^{\times}
and whose morphisms are the vector spaces
{}_{\chi}\mathcal{H}_{\chi^{\prime}}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
.
The composition in
\mathcal{H}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
is given by convolution.
We give a presentation of this algebroid in §
3.3
by means of generators and relations.
This presentation allows us to define the monodromic Hecke algebroid over an arbitrary Coxeter group
W
and allows us to replace the set of characters
T(\mathbb{F}_{q})\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}^{\times}
by any
W
-set
\mathfrak{o}
.

Lusztig has shown that the monodromic Hecke algebra is closely related to the ordinary Hecke algebra
[
Lus19
]
.
For simplicity, assume that
G
has connected center.
For each character
\chi
of
T(\mathbb{F}_{q})
, one can associate a reductive group
H_{\chi}^{\circ}
, called the
endoscopic group
. We denote its Weyl group by
W_{\chi}^{\circ}
.
In
loc. cit.
, it is then proved that there is an isomorphism of algebras

{}_{\chi}\mathcal{H}_{\chi}^{\mon}(\mathbb{F}_{q},W)\cong\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{F}_{q},W_{\chi}^{\circ}).

This isomorphism is called the
monodromic-endoscopic equivalence
.
Moreover, a similar description of all of
\mathcal{H}^{\mon}
can be given in terms of ordinary Hecke algebras for the Weyl groups of endoscopic groups.
This is closely related with Lusztig’s classification of
G(\mathbb{F}_{q})
-representations where the non-unipotent representations are parameterized by unipotent representations of the endoscopic groups.

1.2.
Motivation from Geometry

In their foundational work
[
KL79
]
, Kazhdan and Lusztig categorified the Hecke algebra
\mathcal{H}
via the sheaf-function correspondence.
In particular, one can define the geometric Hecke category as the category
\Semis(B\backslash G/B,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell})

of semisimple étale constructible sheaves on the stack
B\backslash G/B
.
The geometric Hecke category is a monoidal category under convolution.
The split Grothendieck group
[\Semis(B\backslash G/B,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell})]_{\oplus}
is then an algebra. In
loc. cit.
, it is then shown that there is an isomorphism of algebras

[\Semis(B\backslash G/B,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell})]_{\oplus}\cong\mathcal{H}.

Moreover, this isomorphism takes the simple IC-sheaves to the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis.

The geometric Hecke category is closely related with the category of unipotent
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
-representations of finite groups of Lie type (cf.,
[
BZN09
,
BFO12
,
Lus05
]
).
This poses the question: if one replaces
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
-coefficients with
\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}
-coefficients, does the geometric Hecke category give information about unipotent
\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}
-representations?
The answer is yes, but with some degree of caution.
Namely, with
\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}
-coefficients, the decomposition theorem fails and the category of semisimple complexes is no longer the correct object of study.
There are two common replacements in the literature:

(1)

One can instead work with the derived category of constructible sheaves on
B\backslash G/B
instead of just the semisimple complexes.
This category has many nice formal properties and in
[
Zhu16
]
it is shown that its categorical center is closely related with unipotent
\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}
-representations of finite groups of Lie type.
However, the category is hard to compute with. Moreover, it no longer categorifies
\mathcal{H}
, but instead just the group algebra
\mathbb{Z}[W]
.

(2)

Another option is to work with the category of parity sheaves
\textnormal{Par}(B\backslash G/B,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell})
introduced in
[
JMW14
]
.
While it is less clear what applications this category has to representations of finite groups of Lie type, it does provide a novel categorification of
\mathcal{H}
.
Moreover, the indecomposable parity sheaves get sent to the “
p
-Kazhdan–Lusztig basis” which has found numerous applications throughout modular representation theory.

One can ask how much of this story transfers over to the monodromic setting.
In
[
LY20
]
, Lusztig and Yun gave a geometric categorification of the monodromic Hecke algebra.
In this setup, a character
\chi:T(\mathbb{F}_{q})\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}^{\times}
get associated to a character sheaf
\mathcal{L}_{\chi}\in\Loc(T,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell})
.
One can then define the geometric
(\mathcal{L}_{\chi},\mathcal{L}_{\chi^{\prime}})
-monodromic Hecke category as the category

\Semis_{(T\times T,\mathcal{L}_{\chi}\boxtimes\mathcal{L}_{\chi^{\prime}}^{-1})}(U\backslash G/U,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell})

of
(T\times T,\mathcal{L}_{\chi}\boxtimes\mathcal{L}_{\chi^{\prime}}^{-1})
-equivariant semisimple complexes on the stack
U\backslash G/U
.
This is a monoidal category under convolution of sheaves.

For simplicity, we again assume that
G
has connected center.
The main result of
loc. cit.
upgrades the description of the monodromic-endoscopic equivalence of Hecke algebras to Hecke categories.
Note that
H_{\chi}^{\circ}
is defined so that
T
is a maximal torus for
H_{\chi}^{\circ}
. A Borel subgroup
B
of
G
containing
T
determines a Borel subgroup
B_{\chi}
of
H_{\chi}^{\circ}
containing
T
as well.
Lusztig and Yun
[
LY20
]
proved that there is an equivalence of monoidal categories

\Semis_{(T\times T,\mathcal{L}_{\chi}\boxtimes\mathcal{L}_{\chi})}(U\backslash G/U,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell})\cong\Semis(B_{\chi}\backslash H_{\chi}^{\circ}/B_{\chi},\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}).

This equivalence can also be extended to the case of unequal parameters
\chi,\chi^{\prime}
and
G
having a disconnected center.

In
[
San25
]
, we extended the result of
[
LY20
]
to positive characteristic coefficients.
We defined categories of parity sheaves

\textnormal{Par}_{(T\times T,\mathcal{L}_{\chi}\boxtimes\mathcal{L}_{\chi^{\prime}}^{-1})}(U\backslash G/U,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}).

We then showed that there is an equivalence of monoidal categories

\textnormal{Par}_{(T\times T,\mathcal{L}_{\chi}\boxtimes\mathcal{L}_{\chi}^{-1})}(U\backslash G/U,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell})\cong\textnormal{Par}(B_{\chi}\backslash H_{\chi}^{\circ}/B_{\chi},\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}).

These categories of parity sheaves can be assembled into a 2-category denoted by

\>{}_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}(G,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell})

We further showed in
[
San25
, Theorem 3.8.4]
that the split Grothendieck algebroid of
\>{}_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}(G,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell})
is isomorphic to the monodromic Hecke algebroid.
More generally, the
\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}
-coefficients appearing here can be replaced by
\mathbbm{k}
-coefficients where
\mathbbm{k}
is a field or a complete local ring.

1.3.
Soergel Bimodules

In
[
Soe90
,
Soe92
,
Soe00
]
, Soergel constructed another categorification of the Hecke algebra using bimodules over the equivariant cohomology ring

R=H_{T}^{\bullet}(\pt;\mathbb{C})\cong\Sym(\mathfrak{h}^{*})

where
\mathfrak{h}
is the Lie algebra of
T
. Note that
R
is a graded algebra over
\mathbbm{k}
with
\mathfrak{h}^{*}
in degree 2.
The Weyl group
W
acts on
R
, and from this, one considers the subalgebra of
s
-invariants, denoted
R^{s}
, for
s\in S
.
Soergel bimodules are then generated by taking direct sums and direct summands from graded
R
-bimodules of the form

R\otimes_{R^{s_{1}}}R\otimes_{R^{s_{2}}}\ldots\otimes_{R^{s_{k}}}R(n)

where
s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}\in S
and
(n)
denotes a shift in grading by
n\in\mathbb{Z}
.
The resulting category of Soergel bimodules, denoted
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathfrak{h},W)
, again categorifies the Hecke algebra.

The key advantage with using Soergel bimodules is that they can be easily generalized to non-crystallographic Coxeter groups.
In
[
Soe07
]
, Soergel extends the eponymous theory to arbitrary Coxeter systems
W
and “reflection faithful” representations
\mathfrak{h}
of
W
.
This affords a categorification of Hecke algebras for non-crystallographic Coxeter groups.

Unfortunately, Soergel bimodules starts to become ill-behaved whenever
W
is infinite or
\mathbbm{k}
has small characteristic (in which case, reflection faithful representations are hard to find).
More recently, Abe
[
Abe21
]
was able to rectify this undesirable behavior by enhancing the category of Soergel bimodules.
Roughly speaking, in Abe’s incarnation of Soergel bimodules, one also keeps track of the various localization data associated to a given bimodule.
This localization data helps to shrink the Hom spaces and ensures that Soergel bimodules associated to distinct elements of
W
stay distinct in the Grothendieck group.
As a consequence, Abe’s enhancement of Soergel bimodules, denoted
\mathcal{A}(\mathfrak{h},W)
, again categorifies the Hecke algebra.

Building off of work in
[
LY20
]
, we will develop an analogous theory for the monodromic Hecke algebroid associated to a Coxeter group
W
with a
W
-set
\mathfrak{o}
and a
W
-realization
\mathfrak{h}
.
In the monodromic theory, one considers two types of building blocks for Soergel bimodules associated to a simple reflection
s\in S
.
The first is the non-monodromic Soergel bimodule
C_{s}\coloneq R\otimes_{R^{s}}R(1)
associated to
s
which we use whenever
s
stabilizes the monodromy parameter
\mathcal{L}
.
The second is the
s
-twisted standard bimodule
R_{s}
which we use whenever
s
does not stabilize
\mathcal{L}
.
The two different types of building blocks can then be used together to produce a 2-category of monodromic Soergel bimodules over
\mathfrak{o}
, denoted
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

Monodromic Soergel bimodules have a convenient feature compared to parity sheaves.
Since the category of monodromic Soergel bimodules is a subcategory of
R
-bimodules, it is quite straightforward to prove a categorified version of the monodromic-endoscopic equivalence.
For
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
, write
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
for the endomorphism category of
\mathcal{L}
viewed as an object of
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
There is a decomposition of
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
into a direct sum of full subcategories called blocks. We write
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
for the block containing the monoidal unit
R
.
There is a normal subgroup
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
of the stabilizer of
\mathcal{L}
in
W
called the
endoscopic Coxeter group
. This recovers the Weyl group of the endoscopic group when we are in the setting from before.

Proposition 1.3.1

(Proposition
3.5.7
)
.

There is an equivalence of monoidal categories

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\cong\mathcal{A}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}).

This can also be extended to an equivalence of the 2-category
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
with a 2-category of Abe–Soergel bimodules constructed by gluing the categories
\mathcal{A}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ})
together as
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
varies (see Theorem
3.5.10
).

1.4.
Diagrammatic Hecke Category

There is one final categorification of the Hecke algebra we will consider. Elias and Williamson asked, and answered, the following question: is it possible to present the category of Soergel bimodules by means of generators and relations
[
EW16
]
?
The morphisms of the Elias–Williamson diagrammatic Hecke category
\mathcal{D}(\mathfrak{h},W)
are defined using certain isotopy classes of decorated planar graphs.
We will not review these generators and relations at this time, and instead defer the construction to later on.

One key result from
[
EW16
]
is that the Grothendieck group of the diagrammatic Hecke category is isomorphic to the Hecke algebra.
The strategy for proving this result is rather involved. Namely, they define a basis for the Hom spaces
\mathcal{D}(\mathfrak{h},W)
called the double leaves basis which is closely based on Libedinsky’s light leaves basis
[
Lib08
]
for Soergel bimodules.
The hard part is showing that a given (potentially massive) diagram can be simplified via the defining relations into a linear combination of double leaves.

We will perform an analogous construction in the monodromic setting. Namely, we will give a presentation of monodromic Soergel bimodules in terms of generators and relations.
Since the categories involved are 2-categories, the resulting generators turn out to be planar graphs with faces labeled by monodromy parameters.
We also construct a double leaves basis for the monodromic diagrammatic Hecke category following ideas of
[
EW16
]
.
The cellular structure of the double leaves basis along with a mixed-sheaf formalism allows us to deduce that the monodromic diagrammatic Hecke category categorifies the monodromic Hecke algebroid regardless of the base ring of the realization.

1.5.
Main Results

We have at this point reviewed three different incarnations of the Hecke category.
Since they all have isomorphic Grothendieck groups (when they are all properly defined), one can ask whether the categories themselves are equivalent.
Two key theorems give answers in the affirmative. First, Abe
[
Abe21
]
has shown that his incarnation of Soergel bimodules is equivalent to the Elias–Williamson diagrammatic category.
Abe’s result extends a similar result by
[
EW16
]
when
\mathfrak{h}
is reflection faithful.
Second, Riche and Williamson
[
RW18
]
have shown that the parity sheaf incarnation of the Hecke category is equivalent to the Elias–Williamson diagrammatic category.

We are now ready to state our main results which are monodromic variants of the Abe and the Riche–Williamson theorems.

Theorem 1.5.1

(Monodromic Abe)
.

There is an equivalence of 2-categories

\Upsilon_{\textnormal{A}}:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}).

Theorem 1.5.2

(Monodromic Riche–Williamson)
.

Assume that
\mathbbm{k}
is either a finite extension of
\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}
, the residue field of such an extension, or the field of fractions of such an extension.
Let
G
be a connected complex reductive group with Weyl group
W
and denote by
\mathfrak{h}
the Kac–Moody realization for
G
.
Let
\mathfrak{o}
be the
W
-orbit of a torsion character sheaf
\mathcal{L}
on the maximal torus
T
.
There is an equivalence of 2-categories

\Upsilon_{\RW}:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\>_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}(G,\mathbbm{k}).

Remark 1.5.3
.

These theorems along with the monodromic-endoscopic equivalence for Soergel bimodules gives rise to monodromic-endoscopic equivalences for the diagrammatic category.

Remark 1.5.4
.

One may hope to extend the monodromic Riche–Williamson theorem to arbitrary Kac–Moody groups or for more general rings
\mathbbm{k}
.
The only obstruction is in defining the image under
\Upsilon_{\RW}
of a simple reflection in
s\in S
when
\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}
.
In this case, the minimal IC sheaf associated to
\mathcal{L}
and
s
is only well-defined up to a choice of scalar.
It is hard to check whether these choices can be made in a sufficiently coherent manner to ensure the functor is well-defined.

1.6.
Organization

In §
2
, we will study systems of monodromy parameters for arbitrary Coxeter groups. Associated to a monodromy parameter, we will construct the endoscopic Coxeter group.
We will further discuss realizations of Coxeter groups and the necessary 2-colored quantum combinatorics needed to have well-behaved theories of monodromic Abe–Bott–Samelson bimodules.

In §
3
, we introduce the 2-category of monodromic Abe–Bott–Samelson bimodules. As part of their study, we will establish an algebraic version of the monodromic-endoscopic equivalence. We continue the study of the algebraic category in §
4
where we develop a version of the double leaves basis for monodromic Abe–Bott–Samelson bimodules.

In §
5
, we introduce the main character of the paper– the diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category. We will then define a functor from the diagrammatic category to the algebraic category.
Finally, we will provide a diagrammatic incarnation of the double leaves basis, and deduce an equivalence between the diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category and the category of Abe–Bott–Samelson bimodules (Theorem
1.5.1
).
We delay the proof that double leaves span until §
6
.

In §
7
, we recall that geometric monodromic Hecke category of
[
San25
]
. We then construct a functor from the geometric category to the diagrammatic category and show that this functor is an equivalence (Theorem
1.5.2
).

The paper includes two appendices. In §
A
, we prove that the functor from the diagrammatic Hecke category to the category of Bott–Samelson bimodules is invariant under 3-color relations.
This effort is largely computational and depends on an exhaustive search of the possible systems of monodromy parameters. In §
B
, we develop a general theory of “mixed derived categories” for object-adapted cellular categories closely based on
[
ARV20
]
.

2.
Monodromic Coxeter Systems

2.1.
Endoscopic Coxeter Group

2.1.1.
Notation

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter system and let
e\in W
denote the identity.
By definition
W
is the group generated by the set of simple reflections
S
subject to the relations:

(2.1.1)

s^{2}=e\text{ for all }s\in S,

(2.1.2)

\underbrace{sts\ldots}_{m_{s,t}}=\underbrace{tst\ldots}_{m_{s,t}}\text{ for all }s\neq t\in S.

The numbers
m_{s,t}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}
associated to each pair of distinct simple reflections determine
W
.
The group
W
is equipped with the Bruhat order
\leq
and the length function
\ell:W\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
.
If
W
is finite, then it admits the longest element
w_{0}
under the Bruhat order.
The rank of
W
is the cardinality of
S
which we allow to be (countably) infinite.

For any subset
I\subset S
, the corresponding parabolic subgroup
W_{I}
of
W
is the subgroup generated by
s\in I
.
It follows that
(W_{I},I)
is also Coxeter system.

We write
\Exp(W)
for the set of expressions in
W
. These consist of sequences
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
of simple reflections.
We write
\overline{\underline{w}}=(s_{k},\ldots,s_{1})
for the reversed expression of
\underline{w}
.
The length of
\underline{w}
is
\ell(\underline{w})\coloneq k
. Note that
\ell(\underline{w})\geq\ell(w)
where
w=s_{1}\ldots s_{k}
is the product, and equality holds if and only if
\underline{w}
is a reduced expression.
We adopt the convention of
[
EW16
]
and shorten “reduced expression” to
rex
with the plural form being
rexes
.

A subexpression
\underline{e}
of an expression
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
is a tuple
(e_{1},\ldots,e_{k})
where
e_{i}\in\{0,1\}
for all
i=1,\ldots,k
.
Given such a subexpression, we can consider the evaluation of
\underline{w}
at
\underline{e}
which is the element
\underline{w}^{\underline{e}}\coloneq s_{1}^{e_{1}}\ldots s_{k}^{e_{k}}\in W
.
The
Bruhat stroll
associated to
\underline{e}
is the sequence
w_{0},\ldots,w_{k}
in
W
defined by
w_{i}=s_{1}^{e_{1}}\ldots s_{i}^{e_{i}}
.
We denote the set of all subexpressions of
\underline{w}
by
\Subexp(\underline{w})
.

Suppose we have a pair of distinct simple reflections
s,t
.
For
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1}
, we denote the expressions given by alternating sequences starting with
s
(resp.
t
) by

{}_{s}\underline{k}\coloneq\underbrace{(s,t,s,\ldots)}_{k\text{ terms}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{}_{t}\underline{k}\coloneq\underbrace{(t,s,t,\ldots)}_{k\text{ terms}}.

We write
{}_{s}k
and
{}_{t}k
for the elements in
W
obtained by evaluating
{}_{s}\underline{k}
and
{}_{t}\underline{k}
respectively.
We could also consider alternating expressions ending in
s
or
t
, denoted
\underline{k}_{s}=\overline{{}_{s}\underline{k}}
and
\underline{k}_{t}=\overline{{}_{t}\underline{k}}
. Their evaluations will similarly be denoted by
k_{s}
and
k_{t}
respectively.

A
reflection
in
W
is an element of the form
wsw^{-1}
for
w\in W
and
s\in S
. Every reflection is clearly an involution. We denote the set of reflections in
W
by
\mathscr{R}(W)
.

2.1.2.
Basic Definitions

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter system.

Definition 2.1.3
.

A set of
monodromy parameters
is a set
\mathfrak{o}
equipped with a right
W
-action on
\mathfrak{o}
.
Given monodromy parameters
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
, we define

{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}\coloneq\{w\in W\mid\mathcal{L}w=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\}.

If
\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
, we will often write
W_{\mathcal{L}}\coloneq{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}}
.

From
\mathfrak{o}
, we can construct a groupoid
M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W)
whose object set is
\mathfrak{o}
and whose set of morphisms from
\mathcal{L}
to
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
is given by
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.
Composition in
M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W)
is given by multiplication in
W
.

Example 2.1.4
.

(1)

Let
\mathfrak{o}
be a set with a single object. Then
W
acts trivially on
\mathfrak{o}
. In this case,
M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W)
is isomorphic as a groupoid to
W
. We often call this example the
non-monodromic
or
unipotent
case.
We will sometimes write
\mathfrak{o}=1
to refer to
\mathfrak{o}
having only one object which we also denote by
1
.

(2)

Let
\mathfrak{o}=W
and have
W
act on
\mathfrak{o}
by right multiplication. In this case,
M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W)
is equivalent as a groupoid to the trivial group.

(3)

The running example for a set of monodromy parameters comes from geometry. Namely, let
G
be a connected reductive group (or more generally a Kac–Moody group) over
\mathbb{C}
with maximal torus
T
and Weyl group
W
.
Let
\mathbbm{k}
be a commutative ring. We can then consider
T_{\mathbbm{k}}^{\vee}
, the Langland’s dual torus of
T
.
In this case,
\mathfrak{o}
is the
\mathbbm{k}
-points of
T_{\mathbbm{k}}^{\vee}
.

(4)

Let
I\subset S
and consider
W_{I}\subseteq W
the parabolic subgroup generated by
I
. We define
\mathfrak{o}=W_{I}\backslash W
and have
W
act via right multiplication.
Let
e
denote the identity coset in
\mathfrak{o}
. Then
W_{e}=W_{I}
. More generally, for
x,y\in W_{I}\backslash W
, then
{}_{x}W_{y}=xW_{I}y^{-1}
.

(5)

Example
2.1.4
(4) admits a mild generalization. Let
W^{\prime}\subseteq W
be a subgroup. Define
\mathfrak{o}=W^{\prime}\backslash W
and have
W
act via right multiplication.
Let
e
denote the identity coset. Then
W_{e}=W^{\prime}
.

The set
W_{\mathcal{L}}
is a subgroup of
W
, but it need not be a parabolic subgroup. In fact,
W_{\mathcal{L}}
need not admit a Coxeter structure whatsoever.
However, we will show that there is a normal subgroup
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
of
W_{\mathcal{L}}
which (naturally) can be endowed with a Coxeter structure.

Note that
\Exp(W)
is a monoid under concatenation with identity
\varnothing
– the empty expression.
There is an antiinvolution of
\Exp(W)
taking
\underline{w}\in\Exp(W)
to the reversed expression
\overline{\underline{w}}
.
Moreover, there is a map of monoids
\ev:\Exp(W)\to W
given by evaluating an expression in
W
.
If
\mathfrak{o}
is a set of monodromy parameters for
W
, then there is a monoid action of
\Exp(W)
on
\mathfrak{o}
via the evaluation map
\ev
.

Let
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})\in\Exp(W)
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
. For each
0\leq i\leq k
, we write
\underline{w}_{\leq i}
for the expression given by the first
i
terms of
\underline{w}
.
By definition
\underline{w}_{\leq 0}=\varnothing
. We then define

K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L})\coloneq\{1\leq i\leq k\mid\mathcal{L}\underline{w}_{\leq i}=\mathcal{L}\underline{w}_{\leq i-1}\}.

Associated to each
\underline{w}
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
is a certain subexpression
\underline{e}=(e_{1},\ldots,e_{k})
defined as follows:

e_{i}=\begin{cases}1&i\notin K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L}),\\
0&i\in K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L}).\end{cases}

This procedure defines a map
\underline{b}_{\mathcal{L}}:\Exp(W)\to\Exp(W)
taking
\underline{w}
to
\underline{w}^{\underline{e}}
. We also define
b_{\mathcal{L}}\coloneq\ev\circ\underline{b}_{\mathcal{L}}
.

Lemma 2.1.5
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
.

(1)

b_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x}\underline{y})=b_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x})b_{\mathcal{L}\underline{x}}(\underline{y})
;

(2)

b_{\mathcal{L}}(\overline{\underline{x}})=b_{\mathcal{L}\overline{\underline{x}}}(\underline{x})^{-1}
;

(3)

b_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x})=b_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{y})
if
\underline{x},\underline{y}
are both expressions for some
w\in W
.

In particular, the maps
b_{\mathcal{L}}
factor through a morphism of groupoids

\Bl^{\min}:M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W)\to M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W).

Proof.

Statements (1) and (2) are clear from definitions.
We will now prove (3).
In general, if
\underline{x}
and
\underline{y}
are both expressions for some
w\in W
, then
\underline{x}
and
\underline{y}
differ by a series of relations of the form

{}_{s}\underline{m}=\underbrace{(s,t,\ldots)}_{m_{s,t}\text{ terms}}\leftrightarrow\underbrace{(t,s,\ldots)}_{m_{s,t}\text{ terms}}={}_{t}\underline{m}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(s,s)\leftrightarrow\varnothing.

By (1), it suffices to show that
b_{\mathcal{L}}
is invariant under these relations. It is clear from definitions that
b_{\mathcal{L}}((s,s))=e=b_{\mathcal{L}}(\varnothing)
.

We will now show that
b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{s}\underline{m})=b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{t}\underline{m})
.
Suppose that
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
.
Then we have that

\mathcal{L}{}_{t}\underline{m}=\mathcal{L}{}_{s}\underline{m}=\mathcal{L}{}_{t}\underline{m-1}.

We can then compute that

b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{s}\underline{m})=b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{t}\underline{m-1})=b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{t}\underline{m}).

The same argument shows that if
\mathcal{L}t=\mathcal{L}
, then
b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{s}\underline{m})=b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{t}\underline{m})
.

If
\#K({}_{s}\underline{m},\mathcal{L})=0
, then one can easily check that
b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{s}\underline{m})=w_{0}
where
w_{0}
is the longest element of
\langle s,t\rangle
.
Likewise, we have that
b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{t}\underline{m})=w_{0}
.
As a result, we may assume that
\mathcal{L}{}_{s}\underline{k}=\mathcal{L}{}_{s}\underline{k-1}
for some
1\leq k\leq m
.
Write
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}{}_{s}\underline{k}
and set
u=s
if
m
is even and
u=t
if
m
is odd.
By the previous case, we have that
b_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}({}_{s}\underline{m})=b_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}({}_{t}\underline{m})
.
We can then multiply on the left by
b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{s}\underline{k})
and on the right by
b_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}{}_{s}\underline{m}}({}_{u}\underline{k-1})^{-1}
.
By iterated applications of (1) and (2), we can conclude that
b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{s}\underline{m})=b_{\mathcal{L}}({}_{t}\underline{m})
.
∎

Lemma
2.1.5
gives a groupoid morphism
\Bl^{\min}:M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W)\to M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W)
. In particular, this restricts to a map
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}:{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}\to{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
for
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
.
We define the set of
blocks

{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
as the set of nonempty fibers of
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.
Associated to each block
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
is an element
w^{\beta}={}_{\mathcal{L}}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}w}(w)
for any
w\in\beta
.

There is a monodromic length function on
\Exp(W)
defined by

\ell_{\mathcal{L}}:\Exp(W)\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\qquad\underline{w}\mapsto\#K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L}).

We also define
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}:W\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
by
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)=\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w})
where
\underline{w}
is any reduced expression of
w
.
It is easy to check for any expression
\underline{x}
that
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x})=\ell(\underline{x})-\ell(b_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x}))
.
By Lemma
2.1.5
, it then follows that
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}
is independent of the choice of reduced expression.

If
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
is a block, then
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w^{\beta})=0
and
w^{\beta}
is the unique element in
\beta
with monodromic length 0.
We also note that
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}
does not necessarily agree with the length in
W
.
However, we always have that
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)\leq\ell(w)
.

One of the most important examples of blocks are the
neutral blocks
which have minimal element
e\in W
.
We define the neutral block
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}\coloneq({}_{\mathcal{L}}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}})^{-1}(\{e\})
.
By Lemma
2.1.5
, the neutral block
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is a normal subgroup of
W_{\mathcal{L}}
.

Proposition 2.1.6
.

Let
S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}=\ell_{\mathcal{L}}^{-1}(1)\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
. Then
(W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ})
is a Coxeter group with length function
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}
.

Proof.

We first claim that
S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
generates
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
.
Let
w\in W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
. We will argue by induction on
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)
that
w\in\langle S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}\rangle
.
If
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)=1
, the claim is obvious. Suppose
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)>1
. We can then write
w=xsy
such that
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(x)=\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)-1
,
s\in S_{\mathcal{L}x}^{\circ}
, and
\ell_{\mathcal{L}x}(y)=0
.
Write
w=(xy)(y^{-1}sy)
and observe that
xy\in W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
and
y^{-1}sy\in S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
. Note that
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(xy)=\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)-1
. The claim then follows via induction.

Next, we will show that the elements of
S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
are reflections.
Let
s\in S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
. We can then find blocks
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and
\gamma\in{}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}}
and a simple reflection
t\in S
such that
s=w^{\beta}tw^{\gamma}
and
t\in S_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\circ}
.
By definition of
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
, we must have that
w^{\beta}w^{\gamma}=e
; therefore,
s=w^{\beta}tw^{\beta,-1}
.

We have now shown that
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is a reflection subgroup. By a classical theorem of Dyer
[
Dye90
]
and Deodhar
[
Deo89
]
,
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is a Coxeter group with a canonical set of generators
T_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
.
We can describe
T_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
as follows.
For each
x\in W
, define
N(x)\coloneq\{r\in\mathscr{R}(W)\mid\ell(xr)<\ell(x)\}
. Then
T_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}=\{t\in\mathscr{R}(W)\mid N(t)\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}=\{t\}\}
.

We claim that
T_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}=S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
.
First, let
x\in W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
. Let
(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
be a reduced expression of
x
. If
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(x)>1
, we can find some index
1\leq i\leq k
such that
\mathcal{L}s_{1}\ldots s_{i}=\mathcal{L}s_{1}\ldots s_{i+1}
and that
i
is minimal with respect to this property.
Let
r=s_{1}\ldots s_{i-1}s_{i}s_{i-1}\ldots s_{1}\in\mathscr{R}(W)\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
. By construction,
\ell(rx)<\ell(x)
; therefore,
x\notin T_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
.
As a result,
T_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}\subseteq S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
.
For the other inclusion, let
s\in S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
and
r\in\mathscr{R}(W)\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
such that
\ell(sr)<\ell(s)
. Since
s\in S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
, we have that
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(sr)\leq\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(s)=1
.
If
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(sr)=1
, then
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(r)=0
and hence
r=e
which is a contradiction. Therefore,
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(sr)=0
.
As a result,
sr=e
, and hence,
N(s)\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}=\{s\}
.
∎

In light of Proposition
2.1.6
, the group
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is also called the
endoscopic Coxeter group
for
\mathcal{L}
.
We refer to the elements in
S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
as the
endosimple reflections
.

The following lemma gives an easy way to calculate the endoscopic Coxeter group.

Lemma 2.1.7
.

For all
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
, one has that
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}=\langle\mathscr{R}(W)\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}\rangle
.

Proof.

Proposition
2.1.6
implies that
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}\subseteq\langle\mathscr{R}(W)\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}\rangle
since
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is a reflection subgroup.
It remains to check the opposite inclusion. Let
r\in\mathcal{R}(W)\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}
and write
r=wsw^{-1}
for some
w\in W
and
s\in S
.
Note that
s\in W_{\mathcal{L}w}^{\circ}
.
By Lemma
2.1.5
, we have that

{}_{\mathcal{L}}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}}(r)=\left({}_{\mathcal{L}}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}w}(w)\right)\left({}_{\mathcal{L}w}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}w}(s)\right)\left({}_{\mathcal{L}w}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}}(w^{-1})\right)=\left({}_{\mathcal{L}}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}w}(w)\right)\left({}_{\mathcal{L}}\Bl^{\min}_{\mathcal{L}}(w)^{-1}\right)=e.

Therefore,
r\in W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
which completes the proof.
∎

Example 2.1.8
.

(1)

Let
\mathfrak{o}=1
. Then
W_{1}^{\circ}=W
.

(2)

Let
\mathfrak{o}=W
and have
W
act on
\mathfrak{o}
by right multiplication. Then for all
x\in W
,
W_{x}^{\circ}=\{e\}
.

(3)

Let
G
be a connected reductive group with maximal torus
T
and Weyl group
W
and set
\mathfrak{o}=T_{\mathbbm{k}}^{\vee}
.
Let
\Phi
denote the root system of
G
with respect to
T
and
\Phi^{\vee}
the set of coroots.
Each coroot in
\Phi^{\vee}
defines a character of
T_{\mathbbm{k}}^{\vee}
. We can then set

\Phi_{t}^{\vee}\coloneq\{\alpha^{\vee}\in\Phi^{\vee}\mid\alpha^{\vee}(t)=1\}.

Let
\Phi_{t}
denote the subset of
\Phi
dual to
\Phi_{t}^{\vee}
. The subset
\Phi_{t}
is a sub-root system of
\Phi
with positive roots
\Phi_{t}\cap\Phi^{+}
.
It follows from
[
LY20
, §4]
that the Weyl group of
\Phi_{t}
with respect to
\Phi_{t}^{+}
is equal to
W_{t}^{\circ}
.

(4)

Let
J\subset S
and
\mathfrak{o}=W_{I}\backslash W
. Then
W_{e}^{\circ}=W_{I}
. More generally, for all cosets
x\in W_{I}\backslash W
with representative
\dot{x}\in W
,
W_{x}^{\circ}=\dot{x}W_{I}\dot{x}^{-1}
.

(5)

Let
W^{\prime}\subseteq W
be a reflection subgroup. Let
\mathfrak{o}=W^{\prime}\backslash W
. As in Example
2.1.4
, we have that
W_{e}=W^{\prime}
.
It then follows from Lemma
2.1.7
that
W_{e}^{\circ}=W^{\prime}
. In particular, every reflection subgroup may arise as an endoscopic Coxeter group.

Example 2.1.9
.

(1)

Endoscopic Coxeter subgroups need not be parabolic subgroups of
W
.
Let
W
be the Coxeter group of type
B_{2}
, with generators
s
and
t
. Let
W^{\prime}
be the reflection subgroup generated by the reflections
s
and
tst
.
Note that
W^{\prime}
is of type
A_{1}\times A_{1}
and clearly is not a parabolic subgroup of
W
. We can then take
\mathfrak{o}=W^{\prime}\backslash W
.
By Example
2.1.8
(5), we have that
W_{e}^{\circ}=W^{\prime}
.

(2)

Endoscopic Coxeter subgroups need not be finite rank Coxeter groups even when
W
has finite rank.
Let
W
be the universal Coxeter group on three generators
s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}
.
Consider the element
x=s_{1}s_{2}
, which has infinite order. Define an infinite sequence of reflections
r_{n}=x^{n}s_{3}x^{-n}
for all
n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
.
Let
W^{\prime}
be the reflection subgroup of
W
generated by
\{r_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}
.
Here we have that
W^{\prime}
is isomorphic to the free product of countably infinitely many copies of
\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}
. It can then be easily verified that
W^{\prime}
is not isomorphic to a Coxeter group with finitely many simple reflections.
Again, we can take
\mathfrak{o}=W^{\prime}\backslash W
and Example
2.1.8
(5) shows that
W_{e}^{\circ}=W^{\prime}
.

Definition 2.1.10
.

An expression
\underline{w}\in\Exp(W)
of
w\in W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is said to be
endo-reduced
if
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w})=\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)
.

Definition 2.1.11
.

An
endosimple expansion datum
for
\mathcal{L}
is a function

\iota:S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}\to\Exp(W)

such that
\iota(s)
is an endo-reduced expression for
s\in W
.

Given an endosimple expansion datum
\iota
for
\mathcal{L}
, then
\iota
can be extended uniquely to all
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
-expressions,

\iota:\Exp(W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ})\to\Exp(W).

Moreover,
\iota
satisfies that if
\underline{x}
is a reduced expression for some
x\in W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
, then
\iota(\underline{x})
is an endo-reduced expression in
W
.

2.2.
Realizations

For both Bott–Samelson bimodules and the diagrammatic category, the starting point will be the data of a realization of a Coxeter system.
In order for the resulting categories to be well-defined, one has to impose some rather technical combinatorial constraints.
We will cover the necessary combinatorics in this section.

2.2.1.
Two-Colored Quantum Numbers

Let
A=\mathbb{Z}[x,y]
be the integral polynomial ring in two variables.
We define a collection of elements of
A
called the
two-colored quantum numbers
as follows.
First set
[0]_{x}=0
,
[0]_{y}=0
,
[1]_{x}=1
,
[1]_{y}=1
,
[2]_{x}=x
, and
[2]_{y}=y
.
Define the remaining quantum numbers recursively by the formulas

(2.2.1)

[n+1]_{x}=[2]_{x}[n]_{y}-[n-1]_{x}\qquad\text{and}\qquad[n+1]_{y}=[2]_{y}[n]_{x}-[n-1]_{y}.

One can use the same formulas to define
[n]_{x}
and
[n]_{y}
for
n\leq 0
. It is easy to check that
[-n]_{x}=-[n]_{x}
and
[-n]_{y}=-[n]_{y}
.
For all
d\in\mathbb{Z}
, we define the
d
-twisted variables
,

x(d)=[d+1]_{x}-[d-1]_{x}\qquad\text{and}\qquad y(d)=[d+1]_{y}-[d-1]_{y}.

For all
n\in\mathbb{Z}
, we will write
[n]_{x(d)}
(resp.
[n]_{y(d)}
) for the element of
A
obtained by substituting
x
with
x(d)
and
y
with
y(d)
in
[n]_{x}
(resp.
[n]_{y}
).

We now recall some standard facts about two-colored quantum numbers (cf.,
[
Eli16
,
EW16
,
EW23
]
).

Lemma 2.2.2
.

Let
n,m\in\mathbb{Z}
.

(1)

If
n
is odd, then
[n]_{x}=[n]_{y}
. As a result, if
d
is even, then
x(d)=y(d)
.

(2)

If either
n
is even or both
n,m
are odd, then

[n]_{x}[m]_{y}=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}[n+m-1-2k]_{x}.

(3)

If
n
divides
m
, then
[n]_{x}
divides
[m]_{x}
.

(4)

We have that
[2n]_{x}=[n]_{x}([n+1]_{x}-[n-1]_{x})
.

It will be useful to give a recursive formula for computing the
d
-twisted variables similar to the two-colored quantum numbers.
We write
x^{\prime}(0)=2
,
y^{\prime}(0)=2
,
x^{\prime}(1)=x
, and
y^{\prime}(1)=y
. We can then define inductively for
d\geq 2
,

x^{\prime}(d)=\begin{cases}-x^{\prime}(d-2)+x\cdot x^{\prime}(d-1)&\text{if }d\text{ odd},\\
-x^{\prime}(d-2)+y\cdot x^{\prime}(d-1)&\text{if }d\text{ even},\end{cases}

y^{\prime}(d)=\begin{cases}-y^{\prime}(d-2)+y\cdot y^{\prime}(d-1)&\text{if }d\text{ odd},\\
-y^{\prime}(d-2)+x\cdot y^{\prime}(d-1)&\text{if }d\text{ even}.\end{cases}

Lemma 2.2.3
.

For all
d\geq 0
, we have that
x^{\prime}(d)=x(d)
and
y^{\prime}(d)=y(d)
.

Proof.

We will just prove that
x^{\prime}(d)=x(d)
. The other statements follow from an entirely symmetric argument. We will argue by induction on
d
.
If
d=0
, then
x(0)=1-(-1)=2
. If
d=1
, then
x(1)=[2]_{x}=x
.
Assume that
x^{\prime}(k)=x(k)
for
k<d
and
d\geq 2
.
If
d
is even, then

\displaystyle x^{\prime}(d)

\displaystyle=-x^{\prime}(d-2)+y\cdot x^{\prime}(d-1)

\displaystyle=-x(d-2)+y\cdot x(d-1)

\displaystyle=-[d-1]_{x}-[d-3]_{x}+y[d]_{x}-y[d-2]_{x}

\displaystyle=(y[d]_{x}-[d-1]_{y})-(y[d-2]_{x}-[d-3]_{y})

\displaystyle=[d+1]_{y}-[d-1]_{y}

\displaystyle=[d+1]_{x}-[d-1]_{x}.

The case of
d
odd is similar, and thus omitted.
∎

The twisted variables are intimately related with quotients of two-colored polynomials as explained by the following proposition.

Proposition 2.2.4
.

Let
n,v\in\mathbb{Z}
such that
v\mid n
and
v\neq 0
. Write
d=n/v
.

(2.2.2)

[v]_{x(d)}=\frac{[n]_{x}}{[d]_{x}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad[v]_{y(d)}=\frac{[n]_{y}}{[d]_{y}}.

Proof.

We will argue by induction on
v
. If
v=0
or
v=1
, there is nothing to show.
The case of
v=2
follows immediately from Lemma
2.2.2
(4).
Suppose
v>2
. We will just consider the case when
v
is even and
d
is odd. The other cases are entirely similar.
Then we can compute via induction and Lemma
2.2.2
(2),

\displaystyle[v]_{x(d)}[d]_{x}

\displaystyle=([v-1]_{y(d)}[2]_{x(d)}-[v-2]_{x(d)})[d]_{x}

\displaystyle=[v-1]_{y(d)}[2d]_{x}-[dv-2d]_{x}

\displaystyle=\frac{[d(v-1)]_{y}[2d]_{x}-[dv-2d]_{x}[d]_{y}}{[d]_{y}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{[d]_{y}}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{2d-1}[dv+d-1-2k]_{x}-\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}[dv-d-1-2k]_{x}\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{[d]_{y}}\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}[dv+d-1-2k]_{x}

\displaystyle=\frac{[dv]_{x}[d]_{y}}{[d]_{y}}

\displaystyle=[dv]_{x}.

∎

Definition 2.2.5
.

Let
n,d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
and
0\leq k\leq n
. Define the
two-colored quantum binomial coefficients
as

(2.2.3)

\begin{bmatrix}n\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x}\coloneq\frac{[n]_{x}[n-1]_{x}\ldots[n-k+1]_{x}}{[1]_{x}[2]_{x}\ldots[k]_{x}}.

We also define the
d
-twisted two-colored quantum binomial coefficients
as

(2.2.4)

\begin{bmatrix}n\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x(d)}\coloneq\frac{[n]_{x(d)}[n-1]_{x(d)}\ldots[n-k+1]_{x(d)}}{[1]_{x(d)}[2]_{x(d)}\ldots[k]_{x(d)}}.

We can also define
\begin{bmatrix}n\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x}
(resp.
\begin{bmatrix}n\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x(d)}
) by switching all occurrences of
x
(resp.
x(d)
) by
y
(resp.
y(d)
) in the above formulas.

Note that
A
is a UFD, and one can use standard arguments to prove that the (
d
-twisted) quantum binomial coefficients are elements of
A
.
In light of Proposition
2.2.4
, the
d
-twisted coefficients are also given by the following equation,

(2.2.5)

\begin{bmatrix}n\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x(d)}=\frac{[d(n)]_{x}[d(n-1)]_{x}\ldots[d(n-k+1)]_{x}}{[d]_{x}[2d]_{x}\ldots[kd]_{x}}.

2.2.6.
Rank 2 Reflection Subgroups of Dihedral Groups

Let
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\cup\{\infty\}
.
Let
W_{m}
denote the dihedral group of order
2m
. If
m\geq 2
, we regard
W_{m}
as a Coxeter group via the presentation
\langle s,t\mid s^{2}=t^{2}=(st)^{m}\rangle
.
More generally, we interpret
W_{0}
as the trivial group and
W_{1}
as the type
A_{1}
Coxeter group.

The following lemma is well-known and can be proved using basic group theory.

Lemma 2.2.7
.

Assume
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\cup\{\infty\}
.
Let
W^{\prime}
be a rank
\leq 2
reflection subgroup of
W_{m}
. If
m<\infty
, then
W^{\prime}
is isomorphic as a Coxeter group to
W_{v}
for some
v
dividing
m
or
v=0
.
If
m=\infty
, then
W^{\prime}
is an infinite dihedral group.

If
\mathfrak{o}
is a
W_{m}
-set and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
, the endoscopic subgroup
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is a reflection subgroup.
We define
v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\cup\{\infty\}
where
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is of type
I_{2}(v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}})
(where
I_{2}(0)
is defined to be trivial and
I_{2}(1)
is defined to be
A_{1}
). We call
v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
the
endoscopic order
of
st
.

2.2.8.
Abe Realizations

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be an integral domain. Let
a,b\in\mathbbm{k}
. Consider the ring homomorphism
A\to\mathbbm{k}[x,y]/(x-a,y-b)\cong\mathbbm{k}
defined by the canonical map
\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbbm{k}
.
Given
p\in A
, we will write
p(a,b)
for the element of
\mathbbm{k}
obtained via this homomorphism.
At times, when the choice of
a,b
are obvious, we will simply refer to
p
as an element of
\mathbbm{k}
.

Definition 2.2.9
.

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be an integral domain. A
pre-realization
of a Coxeter group
(W,S)
over
\mathbbm{k}
consists of a free, finite rank
\mathbbm{k}
-module
\mathfrak{h}
along with subsets

\{\alpha_{s}^{\vee}:s\in S\}\subset\mathfrak{h}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\{\alpha_{s}:s\in S\}\subset\mathfrak{h}^{*},

called the simple coroots and simple roots respectively, such that

(1)

\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\alpha_{s}\rangle=2
for all
s\in S
;

(2)

the assignment

s(v)=v-\langle v,\alpha_{s}\rangle\alpha_{s}^{\vee}

for all
s\in S
and
v\in\mathfrak{h}
defines a representation of
W
on
\mathfrak{h}
;

(3)

\alpha_{s}:\mathfrak{h}\to\mathbbm{k}
is surjective for all
s\in S
.

Here we are writing
\langle-,-\rangle:\mathfrak{h}\times\mathfrak{h}^{*}\to\mathbbm{k}
for the canonical pairing. The third condition is called
Demazure surjectivity
.

To every pre-realization
\mathfrak{h}
, there is a
Cartan matrix

(a_{s,t})_{s,t\in S}
where
a_{s,t}\coloneq\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\alpha_{t}\rangle
.
We will further call a pre-realization
\mathfrak{h}
an
Abe realization
if for all distinct
s,t\in S
such that
st
has order
m_{s,t}<\infty
, we have

\begin{bmatrix}m_{s,t}\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=\begin{bmatrix}m_{s,t}\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{y}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=0

for all integers
1\leq k\leq m_{s,t}-1
.

Hazi has shown that in the absence of parabolic subgroups of type
H_{3}
, the diagrammatic Hecke category is well-defined if and only if the underlying realization is an Abe realization
[
Haz24
]
.
We will later see that the diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category may not be well-defined, even if the underlying realization is an Abe realization.
To resolve this, we introduce a collection of modified versions of the Abe realization condition.

Definition 2.2.10
.

Let
\mathfrak{h}
be a pre-realization over
\mathbbm{k}
of a Coxeter group
(W,S)
. Let
\mathfrak{o}
be a right
W
-set.
We call
\mathfrak{h}
an
endoscopic Abe realization
if
\mathfrak{h}
is an Abe realization of
(W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ})
for all
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
.

Definition 2.2.11
.

Let
\mathfrak{h}
be a pre-realization over
\mathbbm{k}
of a Coxeter group
(W,S)
. Let
\mathfrak{o}
be a right
W
-set.
We call
\mathfrak{h}
a
reflection-stable Abe realization
if for all distinct
s,t\in S
with
m_{s,t}<\infty
and
v\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1}
dividing
m_{s,t}
, we have that

\begin{bmatrix}v\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x(m_{s,t}/v)}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=\begin{bmatrix}v\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{y(m_{s,t}/v)}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=0

for all integers
1\leq k\leq v-1
.

Definition 2.2.12
.

Let
\mathfrak{h}
be a pre-realization over
\mathbbm{k}
of a Coxeter group
(W,S)
. Let
\mathfrak{o}
be a right
W
-set.
We call
\mathfrak{h}
a
monodromic Abe realization
if for all distinct
s,t\in S
with
m_{s,t}<\infty
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
such that
0<v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}<\infty
, we have that

\begin{bmatrix}v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x(m_{s,t}/v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}})}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=\begin{bmatrix}v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{y(m_{s,t}/v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}})}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=0

for all integers
1\leq k\leq v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}-1
.

The notion of a monodromic Abe realization is sufficient to have a well-behaved category of monodromic Abe–Soergel bimodules.
The author suspects that any monodromic Abe realization is also an endoscopic Abe realization; however, the author does not currently know a way to prove this.
It is clear from their definitions that any reflection-stable Abe realization is also a monodromic Abe realization.
We will show in Corollary
2.2.22
that reflection-stable Abe realizations are also endoscopic Abe realizations.
As a result, they are a sufficiently restrictive to give well-behaved monodromic Hecke categories and endoscopic Hecke categories.
We summarize the above in the following diagram:

reflection stable
endoscopic
monodromic
Cor
2.2.22
Definitions
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces???}

Fortunately, asking that a pre-realization
\mathfrak{h}
be a reflection-stable Abe realization is not too restrictive.
For example, we show in Proposition
2.2.25
that if
\mathfrak{h}
arises via a root system of a Kac–Moody group, then it is automatically reflection-stable.

Remark 2.2.13
.

Let
r\in W
be a reflection. We can then write
r=wsw^{-1}
for some
s\in S
and
w\in W
.
We can then define elements
\alpha_{r}^{\vee}=w\alpha_{s}^{\vee}\in\mathfrak{h}
and
\alpha_{r}=w\alpha_{s}\in\mathfrak{h}^{*}
.
Unfortunately,
\alpha_{r}^{\vee}
and
\alpha_{r}
are not actually well-defined. Namely, they depend on the choice of
w
and
s
.
However, by
[
Abe21
, Lemma 2.1]
,
\alpha_{r}
and
\alpha_{r}^{\vee}
is independent of the choice of
w
and
s
up to a scalar in
\mathbbm{k}^{\times}
.
Let
r=xtx^{-1}
for some other
t\in S
and
x\in W
.
We now have that
w\alpha_{s}=\lambda x\alpha_{t}
for some
\lambda\in\mathbbm{k}^{\times}
. It can be easily checked that the constraint from Definition
2.2.9
(1) ensures that
w\alpha_{s}^{\vee}=\lambda^{-1}x\alpha_{t}
.
As a consequence, for two reflections
r,r^{\prime}\in W
, we have that
a_{r,r^{\prime}}a_{r^{\prime},r}\coloneq\langle\alpha_{r}^{\vee},\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\rangle\langle\alpha_{r^{\prime}}^{\vee},\alpha_{r}\rangle
is well-defined and independent of all choices.

Definition 2.2.14
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter group and
(W^{\prime},S^{\prime})
be a reflection subgroup.
A
reflection datum
for
W^{\prime}
consists of a pair of functions
w_{-}:S^{\prime}\to W
and
r_{-}:S^{\prime}\to S
such that for all
s^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}
, we have that
s^{\prime}=w_{s^{\prime}}r_{s^{\prime}}w_{s^{\prime}}^{-1}
and
w_{s^{\prime}}r_{s^{\prime}}>w_{s^{\prime}}
.

Lemma 2.2.15
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter group and
W^{\prime}
is a reflection subgroup of
W
with canonical generators
S^{\prime}
.
Let
\mathfrak{h}
be a pre-realization for
W
.

(1)

Let
w_{-}:S^{\prime}\to W
and
r_{-}:S^{\prime}\to S
be a reflection datum for
W^{\prime}
. Then

(\mathfrak{h},\{w_{s^{\prime}}\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}\}_{s^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}},\{w_{s^{\prime}}\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}^{\vee}\}_{s^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}})

is a pre-realization for
W^{\prime}
.

(2)

The condition that
\mathfrak{h}
be an Abe realization for
W^{\prime}
is independent of the choice of reflection datum for
W^{\prime}
.

Proof.

Let
w_{-}:S^{\prime}\to W
and
r_{-}:S^{\prime}\to S
be a reflection datum for
W^{\prime}
. Let
s^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}
.
We define
\alpha_{s^{\prime}}=w_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}
and
\alpha_{s^{\prime}}^{\vee}=w_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}^{\vee}
.
It then follows that

\langle\alpha_{s^{\prime}}^{\vee},\alpha_{s^{\prime}}\rangle=\langle w_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}^{\vee},w_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}\rangle=\langle\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}^{\vee},\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}\rangle=2.

Let
v\in\mathfrak{h}
.

\displaystyle v-\langle v,w_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}\rangle w_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}^{\vee}

\displaystyle=v-\langle w_{s^{\prime}}^{-1}v,\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}\rangle w_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}^{\vee}

\displaystyle=w_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\left(w_{s^{\prime}}^{-1}v-\langle w_{s^{\prime}}^{-1}v,\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}\rangle\alpha_{r_{s^{\prime}}}^{\vee}\right)

\displaystyle=w_{s^{\prime}}(r_{s^{\prime}}(w_{s^{\prime}}^{-1}v))

\displaystyle=s^{\prime}(v).

As a result, the
W^{\prime}
action on
\mathfrak{h}
given by restricting the
W
action coincides on
S^{\prime}
with the formula from Definition
2.2.9
(2).
Finally, Demazure surjectivity for
\mathfrak{h}
follows from
\langle-,-\rangle
being
W
-invariant.

It remains to check that whether
\mathfrak{h}
is an Abe realization for
W^{\prime}
is independent of the choice of reflection datum.
Let
y_{-}:S^{\prime}\to W
and
u_{-}:S^{\prime}\to S
be another reflection datum for
W^{\prime}
.
We define
\alpha_{s^{\prime}}^{\prime}=y_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\alpha_{u_{s^{\prime}}}
and
(\alpha_{s^{\prime}}^{\prime})^{\vee}=y_{s^{\prime}}\cdot\alpha_{u_{s^{\prime}}}^{\vee}
. Denote by
a_{\bullet,\bullet}
(resp.
a_{\bullet,\bullet}^{\prime}
) the Cartan matrix for the restriction of
\mathfrak{h}
to
W^{\prime}
with respect to the reflection datum
(w_{-},r_{-})
(resp.
(y_{-},u_{-})
).
By Remark
2.2.13
, we have that

(2.2.6)

a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}\coloneq\langle\alpha_{s^{\prime}}^{\vee},\alpha_{t^{\prime}}\rangle\langle\alpha_{t^{\prime}}^{\vee},\alpha_{s^{\prime}}\rangle=\langle(\alpha_{s^{\prime}}^{\prime})^{\vee},\alpha_{t^{\prime}}^{\prime}\rangle\langle(\alpha_{t^{\prime}}^{\prime})^{\vee},\alpha_{s^{\prime}}^{\prime}\rangle\eqcolon a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}^{\prime}a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}^{\prime}.

Let
n\in\mathbb{Z}
be odd. Then
[n]\in\mathbb{Z}[xy]
. As a result, evaluating
[n]
at
x=a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}
and
y=a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}
is the same as evaluating
[n]
at
x=a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}^{\prime}
and
y=a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}^{\prime}
.
If
n\in\mathbb{Z}
is even, then
[n]_{x}\in x\mathbb{Z}[xy]
and
[n]_{y}\in y\mathbb{Z}[xy]
.
As a result,

[n]_{x}(a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}})=\lambda[n]_{x}(a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}^{\prime},a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}^{\prime})

for some
\lambda\in\mathbbm{k}^{\times}
and similarly for
[n]_{y}
.
As a result, the vanishing of the quantum binomial coefficients is independent of the choice of reflection datum.
∎

Since we are primarily concerned with knowing when the realization
\mathfrak{h}
for
W
restricts to an Abe realization for a reflection subgroup
W^{\prime}
, we do not particularly care what choice of simple roots and coroots is needed.
This in addition with Lemma
2.2.15
(2) empowers us to suppress the reflection datum when discussing restricted pre-realizations to
W^{\prime}
.
In particular, we will call any of the pre-realizations arising via Lemma
2.2.15
(1)
the
restricted pre-realization even though it does depend on a choice.
This abuse of terminology will be fully rectified in Lemma
2.2.29
.

The following two lemmas easily follow from the definitions.

Lemma 2.2.16
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter system and let
\mathfrak{h}
be a pre-realization for
W
.
Let
P
be one of the following properties of a (pre-)realization: monodromic Abe, reflection-stable Abe, or Abe.
The following are equivalent

(1)

\mathfrak{h}
is a
P
realization for
W_{\{s,t\}}
for distinct
s,t\in S
;

(2)

\mathfrak{h}
is a
P
realization for
W
;

(3)

\mathfrak{h}
is a
P
realization for
W_{I}
for all
I\subseteq S
;

(4)

\mathfrak{h}
is a
P
realization for
{}^{x}W_{I}\coloneq xW_{I}x^{-1}
for all
x\in W
and
I\subseteq S
.

Lemma 2.2.17
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter system and let
\mathfrak{h}
be a pre-realization for
W
.
Let
(W^{\prime},S^{\prime})
be a reflection subgroup of
W
and let
x\in W
.
Then
\mathfrak{h}
is an Abe realization for
(W^{\prime},S^{\prime})
if and only if
\mathfrak{h}
is an Abe realization for
(xW^{\prime}x^{-1},xS^{\prime}x^{-1})
.

Lemma 2.2.18
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter group and
W^{\prime}
is a reflection subgroup of
W
with canonical generators
S^{\prime}
.
Assume that
W^{\prime}
is a finite Coxeter group of rank
r
. Then there exists a rank
r
parabolic subgroup
{}^{w}W_{I}
of
W
such that
W^{\prime}\subseteq{}^{w}W_{I}
.

Proof.

It is a classical result that
W^{\prime}
is contained in some finite parabolic subgroup of
W
(see
[
Bou68
, Page 130]
).
As a result, without loss of generality, we may assume that
W
itself is finite.
The result then follows from
[
DPR13
, Lemma 2.1]
.
∎

Lemma 2.2.19
.

Let
W=W_{m}=\langle s,t\rangle
be a finite dihedral group.
For each
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1}
, define

\alpha_{k}\coloneq\begin{cases}({}_{t}(k-1))\cdot\alpha_{t}&\text{if }k\text{ odd},\\
({}_{t}(k-1))\cdot\alpha_{s}&\text{if }k\text{ even},\end{cases}\qquad\qquad\alpha_{k}^{\vee}\coloneq\begin{cases}({}_{t}(k-1))\cdot\alpha_{t}^{\vee}&\text{if }k\text{ odd},\\
({}_{t}(k-1))\cdot\alpha_{s}^{\vee}&\text{if }k\text{ even}.\end{cases}

We also set
\alpha_{0}=-\alpha_{s}
and
\alpha_{0}^{\vee}=-\alpha_{s}^{\vee}
.
We then have that

\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\alpha_{k}\rangle=(-1)^{k+1}\left(x(k)\right)(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\langle\alpha_{k}^{\vee},\alpha_{s}\rangle=(-1)^{k+1}\left(x(k)\right)(a_{s,t},a_{t,s}).

Proof.

We will prove the lemma by induction on
k
.
The base cases when
k=0
and
k=1
are obvious. We will just show the first equality and the case when
k
is even. The other cases are similar.

\displaystyle\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\alpha_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},{}_{t}(k-2)\alpha_{s}\rangle-\langle\alpha_{t}^{\vee},\alpha_{s}\rangle\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},{}_{t}(k-2)\alpha_{s}\rangle

\displaystyle=-\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},{}_{t}(k-3)\alpha_{s}\rangle-\langle\alpha_{t}^{\vee},\alpha_{s}\rangle\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},{}_{t}(k-2)\alpha_{s}\rangle

\displaystyle=(x(k-2))(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})-a_{t,s}(x(k-1))(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})

\displaystyle=-(x(k))(a_{s,t},a_{t,s}).

The first equality is the definition of
t\cdot\alpha_{s}
, the third equality is the inductive hypothesis, and the last equality is Lemma
2.2.3
.
∎

Lemma 2.2.20
.

Let
W=W_{m}=\langle s,t\rangle
be a finite dihedral group and let
W^{\prime}\cong W_{v}
be a rank-2 reflection subgroup of
W
.
Let
\mathfrak{h}
be a pre-realization of
W
.
Suppose that

(2.2.7)

\begin{bmatrix}v\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x(m/v)}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=\begin{bmatrix}v\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{y(m/v)}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=0

for all
1\leq k\leq v-1
. Then
\mathfrak{h}
is an Abe realization for
W^{\prime}
.

Proof.

By Lemma
2.2.17
and possibly relabelling
s
and
t
, we may replace
W^{\prime}
by a conjugate subgroup with
S^{\prime}=\{s,(ts)^{k}t\}
for some
k
.
Note that
v=m/(k+1)
. Write
t^{\prime}=(ts)^{k}t
and define the simple root and coroot associated to
t^{\prime}
by

\alpha_{t^{\prime}}=\begin{cases}({}_{t}k)\cdot\alpha_{t}&k\text{ even},\\
({}_{t}k)\cdot\alpha_{s}&k\text{ odd},\end{cases}\qquad\qquad\alpha_{t^{\prime}}^{\vee}=\begin{cases}({}_{t}k)\cdot\alpha_{t}^{\vee}&k\text{ even},\\
({}_{t}k)\cdot\alpha_{s}^{\vee}&k\text{ odd}.\end{cases}

By Lemma
2.2.19
, we have that

(x(k+1))(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=(-1)^{k}\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\alpha_{t^{\prime}}\rangle\text{ and }(y(k+1))(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=(-1)^{k}\langle\alpha_{t^{\prime}}^{\vee},\alpha_{s}\rangle.

Since
[n]_{x}\in x\mathbb{Z}[xy]
and
[n]_{y}\in y\mathbb{Z}[xy]
when
n
is even and
[n]_{x},[n]_{y}\in\mathbb{Z}[xy]
when
n
is odd, it is easy to conclude that

[n]_{x(k+1)}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=\pm[n]_{x}(\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\alpha_{t^{\prime}}\rangle,\langle\alpha_{t^{\prime}}^{\vee},\alpha_{s}\rangle),

[n]_{y(k+1)}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=\pm[n]_{y}(\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\alpha_{t^{\prime}}\rangle,\langle\alpha_{t^{\prime}}^{\vee},\alpha_{s}\rangle),

for all
n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
.
Therefore, (
2.2.7
) is equivalent to the defining condition for an Abe realization.
∎

Proposition 2.2.21
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter group and
W^{\prime}
be a reflection subgroup of
W
with canonical generators
S^{\prime}
.
Let
\mathfrak{h}
be a reflection-stable Abe realization. Then
\mathfrak{h}
is an Abe realization for
W^{\prime}
.

Proof.

By Lemma
2.2.15
,
\mathfrak{h}
is a pre-realization for
W^{\prime}
.
Let
s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}
such that
s^{\prime}t^{\prime}
has finite order (greater than 1). Write
W_{\{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\}}^{\prime}
for the parabolic subgroup of
W^{\prime}
generated by
s^{\prime},t^{\prime}
.
By Lemma
2.2.16
, it suffices to show that
\mathfrak{h}
is an Abe realization for
W_{\{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\}}^{\prime}
.
Note that
W_{\{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\}}^{\prime}
is a rank-2 reflection subgroup of
W
.
By Lemma
2.2.18
, we can find some
w\in W
and
s,t\in S
such that
W_{\{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\}}^{\prime}\subseteq{}^{w}W_{\{s,t\}}
.
By another application of Lemma
2.2.16
, we have that
\mathfrak{h}
is a reflection-stable Abe realization for
{}^{w}W_{\{s,t\}}
.
Then
\mathfrak{h}
is an Abe realization for
W_{\{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\}}^{\prime}
by Lemma
2.2.20
.
∎

Corollary 2.2.22
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter system and
\mathfrak{o}
be a
W
-set.
Any reflection-stable Abe realization of
W
is also an endoscopic Abe realization.

Proof.

The claim follows from Proposition
2.2.21
after the observation that every endoscopic Coxeter group is a reflection subgroup (see Proposition
2.1.6
).
∎

Remark 2.2.23
.

Proposition
2.2.21
implies that
\mathfrak{h}
being reflection-stable is sometimes a necessary condition for
\mathfrak{h}
to be endoscopic.
Indeed, by Example
2.1.8
(5), every reflection subgroup can arise as an endoscopic Coxeter group. As a result, we can pick
\mathfrak{o}
such that every reflection subgroup of
W
is of the form
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
for some
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
.
On the other extreme, we can always consider the non-monodromic case where
\mathfrak{o}=1
. Here, being reflection-stable is substantially stronger than being endoscopic.

Proposition 2.2.24
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter system and
\mathfrak{o}
be a
W
-set.
Let
\mathfrak{h}
be a monodromic Abe realization of
W
.
Fix some
s,t\in S
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
.
Define
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}\coloneq W_{\{s,t\}}\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
.
Then
\mathfrak{h}
is an Abe realization for
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

Proof.

If
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
is of rank 0 or 1, then
\mathfrak{h}
is trivially an Abe realization for
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
If
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
is of rank 2, then we are done by Lemma
2.2.20
.
∎

2.2.26.
Balanced Realizations

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter group.
We saw in the previous section that the restriction of a realization
\mathfrak{h}
of
W
to a reflection subgroup
W^{\prime}\subseteq W
is not strictly well-defined.
In particular, it depends on the choice of a reflection datum.
In practice, keeping track of this additional data becomes quite tedious. As a result, we will usually restrict our attention to
balanced
realizations.
This ensures that the restriction to a reflection subgroup does not depend on the reflection datum.
However, it is not clear whether the restricted realization is also balanced. To compensate, we will impose a further condition that ensures all restricted realizations are also balanced.

The constraint that our realizations are balanced is not strictly necessary. For the theory of Soergel bimodules, we will not use it at all.
For the diagrammatic theory, using balanced realizations will greatly simplify our constructions.

Definition 2.2.27
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter group with pre-realization
\mathfrak{h}
.
We say that
\mathfrak{h}
is
balanced
if

[m_{s,t}-1]_{x}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=1=[m_{s,t}-1]_{y}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})

for all
s,t\in S
.

We further say that
\mathfrak{h}
is
reflection-balanced
if

[m_{s,t}/d-1]_{x}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=1=[m_{s,t}/d-1]_{y}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})

for all non-trivial divisors
d
of
m_{s,t}
.

Remark 2.2.28
.

If
\mathfrak{h}
is balanced, then
[m_{s,t}-k]_{x}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=[k]_{x}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})
for all
k
.
Using Proposition
2.2.4
, we can then see that a sufficient but not necessary constraint for
\mathfrak{h}
to be reflection-balanced is if
[d]_{x}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})\neq 0
for all proper divisors
d
of
m_{s,t}
.

Lemma 2.2.29

(
[
Pat25
, Lemma 1.2]
)
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter group with a balanced pre-realization
\mathfrak{h}
.
Let
r
be a reflection in
W
.
Assume that
r=xsx^{-1}=yty^{-1}
for some
x,y\in W
,
s,t\in S
such that
xs>x
and
yt>y
. Then
x\alpha_{s}=y\alpha_{t}
.

It immediately follows from Lemma
2.2.29
that if
\mathfrak{h}
is balanced, that the restriction of
\mathfrak{h}
to any reflection subgroup is independent of the choice of reflection datum.

Proposition 2.2.30
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter group with a reflection-balanced reflection-stable Abe realization
\mathfrak{h}
.
Let
(W^{\prime},S^{\prime})
be a reflection subgroup of
W
. Then
\mathfrak{h}
is a balanced Abe realization for
(W^{\prime},S^{\prime})
.

Proof.

Let
s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}
such that
s^{\prime}t^{\prime}
has order
v<\infty
. By Lemma
2.2.18
, there exists some
s,t\in S
and
x\in W
such that

\langle s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle\subset{}^{x}W_{s,t}
.
Note that
\mathfrak{h}
is a balanced realization for
{}^{x}W_{s,t}
.
By conjugation, we may assume that
s^{\prime}=xsx^{-1}
and
t^{\prime}=x(ts)^{d-1}tx^{-1}
for some
d\geq 1
with
m=dv
.
By Lemma
2.2.29
,
\alpha_{s^{\prime}}=x\alpha_{s}
and
\alpha_{t^{\prime}}=x({}_{t}(d-1))\alpha_{u}
where
u=t
if
d
is odd and
u=s
if
d
is even.
From this description, we have that
a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}=\langle\alpha_{s^{\prime}}^{\vee},\alpha_{t^{\prime}}\rangle=\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},{}_{t}(d-1)\alpha_{u}\rangle
and
a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}=\langle\alpha_{t^{\prime}}^{\vee},\alpha_{s^{\prime}}\rangle=\langle{}_{t}(d-1)\alpha_{u}^{\vee},\alpha_{s}\rangle
.
We will now prove that

[v-1]_{x}(a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}})=1=[v-1]_{y}(a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}})

using a case-by-case analysis on
v
and
d
. The second equality follows from the same equality as the first.

If
v
is even, then
[v-1]_{x}\in\mathbb{Z}[xy]
. Since
[v-1]_{x}
is concentrated in even degrees, by Lemma
2.2.19
, we have equalities
[v-1]_{x}(a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}})=[v-1]_{x(d)}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=1
.

If
v
is odd, then
d
must also be odd divisor. By Lemma
2.2.19
, we have equalities
(x(d))(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}
and
(y(d))(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}
.
Therefore,
[v-1]_{x}(a_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}})=[v-1]_{x(d)}(a_{s,t},a_{t,s})=1
.
∎
