\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta_{\underline{w}_{i-1,s_{i}}^{\prime},\underline{w}_{i}}}

4.3.
Linear Independence

For each
s\in S
, fix
\delta_{s}\in\mathfrak{h}^{*}
such that
\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\delta_{s}\rangle=1
as in §
3.4
.
Let
\underline{x}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})\in\Exp(W)
,
w\in W
, and
\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)
.
Define
b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}\in B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
by
b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}=b_{1}\otimes\ldots\otimes b_{k}
where
b_{i}\in B_{s_{i}}^{\mathcal{L}s_{1}\ldots s_{i-1}}
is defined by

b_{i}=\begin{cases}1\otimes 1\in C_{s_{i}}&\text{if }\lab_{i}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=U,i\in K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L}),\\
\delta_{s_{i}}\otimes 1\in C_{s_{i}}&\text{if }\lab_{i}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=D,i\in K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L}),\\
1\in R_{s_{i}}&\text{if }i\notin K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L}).\end{cases}

Let
\LL_{\underline{x},w}^{\mathcal{L}}\coloneq\{\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}\colon\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w\}
.

Lemma 4.3.1
.

Let
w\in W
,
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
, and
\underline{e},\underline{f}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)
. Write
\underline{w}=\rex(w)
.
Then

\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x},\underline{f}})=\begin{cases}u_{\underline{w}}&\text{if }\underline{f}=\underline{e},\\
0&\text{if }\underline{f}<\underline{e}.\end{cases}

In particular,
\LL_{\underline{x},w}^{\mathcal{L}}
is linearly independent over
R
.

Proof.

We claim that if
\lab_{i}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=\lab_{i}(\underline{x},\underline{f})
for all
i\leq j
, then
\LL_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}})=u_{\underline{w}_{j}}
by induction on
j
.

Assume
\dec_{j}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=U0
and
j\in K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
. In this case,
b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}}=b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}}\otimes(1\otimes 1)
.
Then we have

\displaystyle\LL_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}})

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1},\underline{w}_{j}}\left(\LL_{j-1}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}})\otimes\epsilon^{s_{j}}(1\otimes 1)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1},\underline{w}_{j}}(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1}})

\displaystyle=u_{\underline{w}_{j}}.

Assume
\dec_{j}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=U1
and
j\in K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
. In this case,
b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}}=b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}}\otimes(1\otimes 1)
.
Then we have

\displaystyle\LL_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}})

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1}s_{j},\underline{w}_{j}}\left(\LL_{j-1}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}})\otimes 1\otimes 1\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1}s_{j},\underline{w}_{j}}(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1}}\otimes 1\otimes 1)

\displaystyle=u_{\underline{w}_{j}}.

Assume
\dec_{j}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=U1
and
j\notin K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
. In this case,
b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}}=b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}}\otimes 1
.
Then we have

\displaystyle\LL_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}})

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1}s_{j},\underline{w}_{j}}\left(\LL_{j-1}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}})\otimes 1\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1}s_{j},\underline{w}_{j}}(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1}}\otimes 1)

\displaystyle=u_{\underline{w}_{j}}.

Assume
\dec_{j}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=D0
and
j\in K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
. In this case,
b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}}=b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}}\otimes(\delta_{s_{j}}\otimes 1)
.
Then we have

\displaystyle\LL_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}})

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes m^{s_{j}})\left(\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1},\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\left(\LL_{j-1}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}})\right)\otimes(\delta_{s_{j}}\otimes 1)\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes m^{s_{j}})\left(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\otimes\delta_{s_{j}}\otimes 1\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}},\underline{w}_{j}}\left(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\right)

\displaystyle=u_{\underline{w}_{j}}.

Assume
\dec_{j}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=D1
and
j\in K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
. In this case,
b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}}=b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}}\otimes(\delta_{s_{j}}\otimes 1)
.
Then we have

\displaystyle\LL_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}})

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes\cap^{s_{j}})\left(\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1},\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\left(\LL_{j-1}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}})\right)\otimes(\delta_{s_{j}}\otimes 1)\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}^{\prime},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes\cap^{s_{j}})\left(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\otimes\delta_{s_{j}}\otimes 1\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}^{\prime},\underline{w}_{j}}\left(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}^{\prime}}\right)

\displaystyle=u_{\underline{w}_{j}}.

Assume
\dec_{j}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=D1
and
j\notin K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
. In this case,
b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}}=b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}}\otimes 1
.
Then we have

\displaystyle\LL_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}})

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes\cap^{s_{j}})\left(\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1},\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\left(\LL_{j-1}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}})\right)\otimes 1\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}^{\prime},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes\cap^{s_{j}})\left(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\otimes 1\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}^{\prime},\underline{w}_{j}}\left(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}^{\prime}}\right)

\displaystyle=u_{\underline{w}_{j}}.

By induction, we can then conclude that
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}})=u_{\underline{w}}
.

Assume that
\underline{f}<\underline{e}
. Take
j
such that for all
i<j
,
\lab_{i}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=\lab_{i}(\underline{x},\underline{f})
and
\lab_{j}(\underline{x},\underline{e})=D
and
\lab_{j}(\underline{x},\underline{f})=U
.
Since
\underline{e}
and
\underline{f}
are
\mathcal{L}
-monodromic, we must have that
j\in K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
. As a result,
b_{\underline{w}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}}=b_{\underline{w}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}}\otimes(1\otimes 1)
.

If
e_{j}=0
, we have

\displaystyle\LL_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}})

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes m^{s_{j}})\left(\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1},\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\left(\LL_{j-1}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}})\right)\otimes(1\otimes 1)\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes m^{s_{j}})\left(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\otimes 1\otimes 1\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}},\underline{w}_{j}}\left(0\right)

\displaystyle=0.

If
e_{j}=1
, we have

\displaystyle\LL_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j},\underline{f}_{\leq j}})

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes\cap^{s_{j}})\left(\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1},\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\left(\LL_{j-1}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x}_{\leq j-1},\underline{f}_{\leq j-1}})\right)\otimes(1\otimes 1)\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}^{\prime},\underline{w}_{j}}\left((\id\otimes\cap^{s_{j}})\left(u_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}}\otimes 1\otimes 1\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\beta_{\underline{w}_{j-1,s_{j}}^{\prime},\underline{w}_{j}}\left(0\right)

\displaystyle=0.

Therefore,
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x},\underline{f}})=0
if
\underline{f}<\underline{e}
.
∎

4.4.
Support Theory

Let
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
,
w\in W
,
\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)
, and
\underline{w}=\rex(w)
.
Recall the map
\pi_{\underline{x}}^{w}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\subseteq B_{\underline{x},Q}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
defined in §
3.1.5
.
Define
b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{w}\coloneq\pi_{\underline{x}}^{w}(b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}})\in B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
.

Write
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
. We define a degree
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)
morphism
\varphi_{\underline{w}}:B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to R_{w}
in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{/\mathcal{L}w}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
inductively on
k
.
Let
w_{i}\in W
be the evaluation of
\underline{w}_{\leq i}
for each
1\leq i\leq k
.
First, we define
\varphi_{\varnothing}:R\to R
as the identity map.
Assume that
\varphi_{\underline{w}_{\leq i-1}}:B_{\underline{w}_{\leq i-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to R_{w_{i-1}}
is already defined.
If
\mathcal{L}w_{i-1}s_{i}=\mathcal{L}w_{i-1}
, we define
\varphi_{\underline{w}_{\leq i}}
by the composition

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{\underline{w}_{\leq i}}:B_{\underline{w}_{\leq i-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\otimes_{R}C_{s_{i}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{w_{i-1}}\otimes_{R}R_{s_{i}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{w_{i}},}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{\underline{w}_{\leq i-1}}\otimes a_{s_{i}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}

where
a_{s_{i}}:C_{s_{i}}=R\otimes_{R^{s_{i}}}R\to R_{s_{i}}
is defined by
a_{s_{i}}(f\otimes g)=fs(g)
.
If
\mathcal{L}w_{i-1}s_{i}\neq\mathcal{L}w_{i-1}
, we define
\varphi_{\underline{w}_{\leq i}}
by the composition

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{\underline{w}_{\leq i}}:B_{\underline{w}_{\leq i-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\otimes_{R}R_{s_{i}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{w_{i-1}}\otimes_{R}R_{s_{i}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{w_{i}}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{\underline{w}_{\leq i-1}}\otimes\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}

Proposition 4.4.1
.

Let
\underline{x}
,
\underline{w}
, and
w
be as above.

(1)

The left
R
-module
B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
has a basis
\{b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{w}\}_{\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)}
.

(2)

The left
R
-module
B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
is graded free with graded rank

\textnormal{rank}^{\mathbb{Z}}_{R}(B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}})=\sum_{\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)}v^{d(\underline{x},\underline{e})+\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)}=v^{\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)}p_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}(v).

(3)

The set
\{\varphi_{\underline{w}}\circ\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}\}_{\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)}
is a left
R
-basis of
\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{/\mathcal{L}w}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},R_{w})
.

Proof.

By Lemma
4.3.1
, we have

\varphi_{\underline{w}}\left(\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x},\underline{f}})\right)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\underline{f}=\underline{e},\\
0&\text{if }\underline{f}<\underline{e}.\end{cases}

By Lemma
3.1.6
, we get a homomorphism of
R
-bimodules
\psi_{\underline{e}}:B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\to R_{x}
corresponding to
\varphi_{\underline{x}}\circ\LL_{\underline{w},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
We then have

\psi_{\underline{e}}(b_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}^{x})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\underline{f}=\underline{e},\\
0&\text{if }\underline{f}<\underline{e}.\end{cases}

Via backwards induction on
\underline{e}
, we construct a map
\psi_{\underline{e}}^{\prime}:B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\to R_{x}
such that
\psi_{\underline{e}}^{\prime}\in\psi_{\underline{e}}+\sum_{\underline{e}^{\prime}>\underline{e}}R\psi_{\underline{e}^{\prime}}
and
\psi_{\underline{e}}^{\prime}(b_{\underline{x},\underline{f}}^{x})=\delta_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}
for all
\underline{f}
.
If
\underline{e}
is the maximum subexpression, then
\psi_{\underline{e}}^{\prime}=\psi_{\underline{e}}
.
Assume that
\psi_{\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\prime}
has been defined for all
\underline{e}^{\prime}>\underline{e}
. We define

\psi_{\underline{e}}^{\prime}=\psi_{\underline{e}}-\sum_{\underline{e}^{\prime}>\underline{e}}\psi_{\underline{e}}(b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{x})\psi_{\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\prime}.

It can be easily checked that
\psi_{\underline{e}}^{\prime}
satisfies the desired constraints.

We can then construct a map
\psi:B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\to\bigoplus_{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w}Rb_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{w}
by
\psi(m)=\sum_{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w}\psi_{\underline{e}}^{\prime}(m)b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{w}
.
By construction,
\psi
is a section of the inclusion map
\bigoplus_{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w}Rb_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{w}\hookrightarrow B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
.
Therefore, we can find some
N\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
such that
B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}=\bigoplus_{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w}Rb_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{w}\oplus N
.
We then have an isomorphism
B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\otimes_{R}Q=\bigoplus_{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w}Qb_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{w}\oplus(N\otimes_{R}Q)
.
On the one hand, by Lemma
3.3.5
,
\dim_{Q}(B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\otimes_{R}Q)=p_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}(1)
.
On the other hand, by Lemma
4.1.2
,
\dim_{Q}\left(\bigoplus_{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w}Qb_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{w}\right)=p_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}(1)
.
As a result,
N\otimes_{R}Q=0
. However, since
N\subset B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\subset B_{\underline{x},Q}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
, we know that
N
has no
Q
-torsion. Therefore,
N=0
.

Statement (2) follows immediately from Lemma
4.1.2
.

Finally, we will prove (3). By construction
\{\psi_{\underline{e}}^{\prime}\}
is a basis of
\Hom_{R\textnormal{-mod}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}},R)
which is dual to
\{b_{\underline{w},\underline{e}}\}
.
As a result,
\{\psi_{\underline{e}}\}
is also a basis. Under the isomorphism from Lemma
3.1.6
(2),

\Hom_{R\textnormal{-mod}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}},R)\cong\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{/\mathcal{L}w}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}},R_{w})\cong\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{/\mathcal{L}w}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},R_{w}),

the map
\psi_{\underline{e}}
corresponds to
\varphi_{\underline{w}}\circ\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
∎

Corollary 4.4.2

(
[
Abe21
, Corollary 3.13]
)
.

Let
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
and
w\in W
.
The left
R
-module
B_{\underline{x},w}^{\mathcal{L}}
is graded free and
\textnormal{rank}^{\mathbb{Z}}(B_{\underline{x},w}^{\mathcal{L}})=v^{-\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)}p_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}(v^{-1})
.

We can regard
W
as a topological space with the order topology for the Bruhat order.
In particular, a subset
I\subseteq W
is
closed
if for all
x\in I
,
y\in W
, then
y\leq x
implies that
y\in I
.

Lemma 4.4.3

(
[
Abe21
, Lemma 3.16]
)
.

Let
I\subseteq W
be a closed finite subset and
w\in I
a maximal element under the Bruhat order.
Then there exists an enumeration
w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{\#I}
of the elements in
I
such that
\{w_{1},\ldots,w_{i}\}
is closed for all
i
and
w_{\#I}=w
.

Let
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
,
w\in W
, and
\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)
. Since
D(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}})=B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
(Lemma
3.2.5
), we can define

\overline{\LL}_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}\coloneq D(\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}):B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
which has degree
d(\underline{x},\underline{e})
.

Let
I\subseteq W
and
w\in I
.
Note that
B_{\underline{x},I\setminus\{w\}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is kernel of the composition
B_{\underline{x},I}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
.
As a result,
\pi_{\underline{x}}^{w}
factors through a map
B_{\underline{x},I}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{x},I}^{\mathcal{L}}/B_{\underline{x},I\setminus\{w\}}^{\mathcal{L}}
which we will also denote by
\pi_{\underline{x}}^{w}
.

Proposition 4.4.4
.

Let
I
be a closed subset and
w
a maximal element in
I
.
Let
\underline{w}=\rex(w)
and
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
.
Then
\{\pi_{\underline{x}}^{w}(\overline{\LL}_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}})(u_{\underline{w}})\}_{\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)}
is a left
R
-module basis of
B_{\underline{x},I}^{\mathcal{L}}/B_{\underline{x},I\setminus\{w\}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

Proof.

The proposition follows from the same argument give for
[
Abe21
, Theorem 3.17]
after the results on the polynomials
p_{\underline{x}}^{w}
are replaced by their monodromic counterparts (see Lemma
3.2.1
and Lemma
3.3.4
).
∎

Corollary 4.4.5

(
[
Abe21
, Corollary 3.18]
)
.

Let
M\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

(1)

Let
I\subset W
be a closed subset with maximal element
w\in I
. Then there is an isomorphism
M_{\leq w}/M_{<w}\cong M_{I}/M_{I\setminus\{w\}}
.

(2)

Let
\underline{w}=\rex(w)
for
w\in W
. Then the map
\Hom(B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}},M)\to\Hom(B_{\underline{w}}^{w,\mathcal{L}},M_{\leq w}/M_{<w})
is surjective.

4.5.
Soergel Hom Formula

Proposition 4.5.1
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
.
Then the graded left
R
-module
\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
is graded free of finite rank. Moreover, its graded rank can be computed by

\textnormal{rank}^{\mathbb{Z}}_{R}\Hom(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})=\langle H_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}},H_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}\rangle.

Proof.

By Lemma
3.2.3
and (
3.3.2
), we may assume that
\underline{x}=\varnothing
and
\mathcal{L}\underline{y}=\mathcal{L}
.
There is an isomorphism of left graded
R
-modules,

\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{/\mathcal{L}}}(R_{e},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})\cong B_{\underline{y},e}^{\mathcal{L}}.

This left
R
-module is graded free and of graded rank
p_{\underline{y}}^{e,\mathcal{L}}(v^{-1})
by Corollary
4.4.2
.
On the other hand, a straightforward computation (cf., the proof of
[
Abe21
, Theorem 4.6]
) using
\overline{\underline{H}_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}}=\underline{H}_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
shows that

\langle\underline{H}_{e}^{\mathcal{L}},\underline{H}_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}\rangle=p_{\underline{y}}^{e,\mathcal{L}}(v^{-1})
.
∎

Corollary 4.5.2
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
.
Then

\textnormal{rank}^{\mathbb{Z}}_{R}\Hom(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})=\sum_{w\in W}p_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}(v^{-1})p_{\underline{y}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}(v^{-1}).

Corollary 4.5.3
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
.
Then

\textnormal{rank}^{\mathbb{Z}}_{R}\Hom(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})=\sum_{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}}v^{d(\underline{x},\underline{e})+d(\underline{y},\underline{f})}.

4.6.
Double Leaves

Definition 4.6.1
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
.
Let
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
,
\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)
, and
\underline{f}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{y},w)
.
A
double leaf
is a degree
d(\underline{x},\underline{e})+d(\underline{y},\underline{f})
map given by a composition of the form

\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\coloneq\overline{\LL}_{\underline{y},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}\circ\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}.

Theorem 4.6.2
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
.
Let
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
denote the set containing one double leaf
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
for each
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and each pair of monodromic subsequences
(\underline{x},\underline{e})
and
(\underline{y},\underline{f})
expressing
w
.
Then
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is a left graded
R
-module basis for
\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
.

Proof.

Let
w\in W
,
\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x},w)
,
\underline{f}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{y},w)
.
The degree of
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
is
d(\underline{x},\underline{e})+d(\underline{y},\underline{f})
.
We can then compute using Corollary
4.5.2
,

\displaystyle\sum_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle w\in W}}{{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w=\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}}}}v^{-\deg(\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}})}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle w\in W}}{{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w}}}v^{-d(\underline{x},\underline{e})}\sum_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle w\in W}}{{\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}=w}}}v^{-d(\underline{y},\underline{f})}

\displaystyle=\sum_{w\in W}p_{\underline{x}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}(v^{-1})p_{\underline{y}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}(v^{-1})

\displaystyle=\textnormal{rank}^{\mathbb{Z}}_{R}\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}).

As a result, it suffices to prove that the
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is linearly independent over
R
.

Suppose that
\sum c_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w}\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}=0
.
Define
I=\{w\in W\mid\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=\underline{y}^{\underline{f}},c_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w}\neq 0\}
. We will argue by contradiction that
I
must be empty.
Let
x\in I
be an element with maximal length in
W
.
We can then consider the closure
\overline{I}
of
I
.
Note that
x
also has maximal length in
\overline{I}
.
For all
\underline{e}
,
\underline{f}
, and
w\in W
such that
\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w=\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}
, the image of
c_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w}\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
is supported on
\overline{I}
.
As a result, we have that
c_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w}\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
factors through
B_{\underline{y},\overline{I}}^{\mathcal{L}}\hookrightarrow B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
Moreover, since
I\subset\overline{I}
, we have that
\pi_{\underline{y}}^{x}\circ\left(c_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w}\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\right)=0
unless
w=x
.

Define
E=\{\underline{e}\mid c_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{x}\neq 0\}
. Let
\underline{e}^{\prime}\in E
denote the minimal element under the label-lexicographic order.
By Lemma
4.3.1
, for all
\underline{e}\in E
, we have that
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}^{\prime}})=0
unless
\underline{e}=\underline{e}^{\prime}
.
Therefore, by Lemma
4.3.1
again, we have

\sum_{\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}=x}c_{\underline{e}^{\prime},\underline{f}}^{x}\pi_{\underline{y}}^{x}(\overline{\LL}_{\underline{y},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}(u_{\underline{w}}))=\sum_{\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}=x}c_{\underline{e}^{\prime},\underline{f}}^{x}\pi_{\underline{y}}^{x}(\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e}^{\prime},\underline{f}}^{x,\mathcal{L}}(b_{\underline{x},\underline{e}^{\prime}}))=0.

By Proposition
4.4.1
, we then must have that
c_{\underline{e}^{\prime},\underline{f}}^{x}=0
for all
\underline{f}
such that
\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}=x
.
This contradicts our assumption that
I
was not empty. Therefore,
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is linearly independent.
∎

Let
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})\in\Exp(W)
and take
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}\underline{w}}
to be the block containing the evaluation of
\underline{w}
.
We will define a morphism of degree
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w})

\epsilon^{\underline{w}}:B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to R_{w^{\beta}}

inductively on
\ell(\underline{w})
. When
\underline{w}=\varnothing
, we set
\epsilon^{\varnothing}:R\to R
to be the identity map.
Suppose
\epsilon^{\underline{w}_{\leq k-1}}
is defined. If
\mathcal{L}\underline{w}=\mathcal{L}\underline{w}_{\leq k-1}
, we define
\epsilon^{\underline{w}}
as the composition

B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}=B_{\underline{w}_{\leq k-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\otimes_{R}C_{s_{k}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\epsilon^{\underline{w}_{\leq k-1}}\otimes\epsilon^{s_{k}}}}{{\longrightarrow}}R_{w^{\beta}}\otimes_{R}R\cong R_{w^{\beta}}.

If
\mathcal{L}\underline{w}\neq\mathcal{L}\underline{w}_{\leq k-1}
, we define
\epsilon^{\underline{w}}
as the composition

B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}=B_{\underline{w}_{\leq k-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\otimes_{R}R_{s_{k}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\epsilon^{\underline{w}_{\leq k-1}}\otimes\id}}{{\longrightarrow}}R_{w^{\beta}s_{k}}\otimes_{R}R_{s_{k}}\cong R_{w^{\beta}}.

Note that from the definition of
\epsilon^{\underline{w}}
we have that
\epsilon^{\underline{w}}(u_{\underline{w}})=1
.

We can use Theorem
4.6.2
to get a few uniqueness criterions for
\beta_{s,t}
.

Lemma 4.6.3
.

Let
s,t\in S
be distinct simple reflections with
m=m_{s,t}<\infty
. The map
\beta_{s,t}:B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is the unique map satisfying either of the following criterion:

(1)

\beta_{s,t}(u_{{}_{s}\underline{m}})=u_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}
;

(2)

\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}(\epsilon^{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ\beta_{s,t})=\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}\epsilon^{{}_{s}\underline{m}}:\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\mathbbm{k}
.

Proof.

(1): It is clear from its defining condition that
\beta_{s,t}
takes the 1-tensor to the 1-tensor. Moreover, we can compute from Theorem
4.6.2
that the space of degree 0 morphisms
B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is a rank 1
\mathbbm{k}
-module generated by
\beta_{s,t}
.
This then uniquely determines
\beta_{s,t}
.

(2): Using the same argument as in (1), the uniqueness claim will be clear after proving that
\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}(\epsilon^{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ\beta_{s,t})=\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}\epsilon^{{}_{s}\underline{m}}
.
By Theorem
4.6.2
, we can write

\epsilon^{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ\beta_{s,t}=\sum_{\underline{e}\in\Exp^{\mathcal{L}}({}_{s}\underline{m}),e}c_{\underline{e}}\LL_{{}_{s}\underline{m},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}

for some
c_{\underline{e}}\in R
. Let
\underline{f}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})
denote the maximally 0 monodromic subexpression, i.e.,
f_{i}=0
for
i\in K({}_{s}\underline{m},\mathcal{L})
.
Now the degree of
\LL_{{}_{s}\underline{m},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is
d({}_{s}\underline{m},\underline{e})
and the degree of
\epsilon^{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ\beta_{s,t}
is
m
.
In particular, we have that
\deg\left(\LL_{{}_{s}\underline{m},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}\right)\leq m
with equality if and only if
\underline{e}=\underline{f}
.
As a consequence the constant
c_{\underline{e}}
has no component in degree
0
unless
\underline{e}=\underline{f}
. Moreover,
\LL_{{}_{s}\underline{m},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}=\epsilon^{{}_{s}\underline{m}}
.
These facts imply that

\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}(\epsilon^{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ\beta_{s,t})=\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}c_{\underline{f}}\epsilon^{{}_{s}\underline{m}}.

It remains to check that
c_{\underline{f}}=1
. To check this, we evaluate both sides at the 1-tensor,

(\epsilon^{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ\beta_{s,t})(u_{{}_{s}\underline{m}})=\epsilon^{{}_{t}\underline{m}}(u_{{}_{t}\underline{m}})=1=\epsilon^{{}_{s}\underline{m}}(u_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}).

Therefore,
c_{\underline{f}}=1
.
∎

Proposition 4.6.4
.

Let
s\in S
. Recall that
D(M)=M
for all
M\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

(1)

If
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
, then we have

D(\nu^{s})=\mu^{s},\qquad D(\epsilon^{s})=\eta^{s},\qquad D(\cup^{s})=\cap^{s},

D(\mu^{s})=\nu^{s},\qquad D(\eta^{s})=\epsilon^{s},\qquad D(\cap^{s})=\cup^{s}.

(2)

If
\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}
, then we have

D(\cup^{s})=\cap^{s}\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(\cap^{s})=\cup^{s}.

(3)

If
t\in S
, then we have

D(\beta_{s,t})=\beta_{t,s}.

Proof.

One can check (1) from definitions using the proof of
[
Abe21
, Lemma 2.20]
. Likewise, (2) can be similarly computed from definitions.
We will now prove (3). Let
m=m_{s,t}
. By Lemma
4.6.3
that
\beta_{t,s}:B_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\to B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}
is the unique degree 0 morphism taking the 1-tensor to the 1-tensor.
One can then check from definitions that
D(\beta_{s,t})
also takes the 1-tensor to the 1-tensor. As a result, we may conclude that
\beta_{t,s}=D(\beta_{s,t})
.
∎

Remark 4.6.5
.

From Proposition
4.6.4
, we can see that every upside down light leaf
\overline{\LL}_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is generated under tensors and compositions by
\id_{B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}},\eta^{s},\nu^{s},\cap^{s}
, or the rex moves
\beta_{s,t}
.

4.7.
Localization and Cellular Structure

In this section, we will discuss some techniques for studying Bott–Samelson bimodules via localization.
We will then use localization to further study light leaves and double leaves. Our main result will be a generalization of Theorem
4.6.2
for the “ideal of lower terms” which gives a cellular structure on the category of Bott–Samelson bimodules.

4.7.1.
The Localization Functor

For each
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
, we define a 1-category
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
whose objects consist of tuples
(P^{w})_{w\in W}
such that

(1)

P^{w}
is a graded
Q
-bimodule;

(2)

m\cdot q=w(q)\cdot m
for any
m\in P^{w}
and
q\in Q
;

(3)

P^{w}=0
if
w\notin{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and is only nonzero for finitely many
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.

A morphism in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
from
(P_{1}^{w})_{w\in W}
to
(P_{2}^{w})_{w\in W}
consists of a tuple
(\varphi_{w})_{w\in W}
where each
\varphi_{w}:P_{1}^{w}\to P_{2}^{w}
is a
Q
-bimodule homomorphism.

There are bifunctors

(-)\otimes_{Q}(-):\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\times\>_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

induced from the tensor product of graded
Q
-bimodules. More precisely,
(P_{1}\otimes_{Q}P_{2})^{w}=\bigoplus_{xy=w}P_{1}^{x}\otimes_{Q}P_{2}^{y}
.
These bifunctors are suitably associative and there is a unit object
Q_{e}
given by
(Q_{e})^{e}=Q
and
(Q_{e})^{w}=0
if
w\neq e
.
The tensor product allows us to assemble a 2-category
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
with object set
\mathfrak{o}
and whose morphism categories are given by
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
We sometimes omit the tuple
(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
from the notation for
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
and
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

The assignment
(M,(M_{Q}^{w})_{w\in W},\xi_{M})\mapsto(M_{Q}^{w})_{w\in W}
defines a 2-functor

(-)_{Q}:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

called the
localization functor
.
Since
M\to M\otimes_{R}Q
is injective (
M
is free over
R
), the localization functor is faithful on morphism categories.

4.7.2.
Localizing Bott–Samelson Bimodules

For
w\in W
, we define
Q_{w}\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/\mathcal{L}w}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
by

•

(Q_{w})^{w}=Q
as a left
Q
-module and the right action of
q\in Q
is given by
m\cdot q=w(q)\cdot m
;

•

(Q_{w})^{x}=0
if
x\neq w
.

Any object in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{C}_{Q/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
is isomorphic to a direct sum of
Q_{w}(n)
’s where
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and
n\in\mathbb{Z}
. Moreover, there is a canonical isomorphism
Q_{x}\otimes_{Q}Q_{y}\cong Q_{xy}
via
f\otimes g\mapsto fx(g)
characterized as the unique
Q
-bimodule morphism taking
1\otimes 1
to
1
.

By (
3.2.1
), we have isomorphisms of graded
Q
-bimodules

(4.7.1)

B_{s,Q}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\begin{cases}Q_{e}\oplus Q_{s}(1)&\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L},\\
Q_{s}&\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}.\end{cases}

Let
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})\in\Exp(W)
and
\underline{e}=(e_{1},\ldots,e_{k})\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w})
. Define the
relative length
of
\underline{w}
with respect to
\underline{e}
by

\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w},\underline{e})=\#\{i\mid e_{i}=1\}+\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w})-\ell(\underline{w}).

We can define the
\underline{e}
-component
of
B_{\underline{w},Q}^{\mathcal{L}}
, denoted
B_{\underline{w},Q}^{\underline{e},\mathcal{L}}
, as the direct summand corresponding to the bimodule

Q_{s_{1}^{e_{1}}}\otimes_{Q}Q_{s_{2}^{e_{2}}}\otimes_{Q}\ldots\otimes_{Q}Q_{s_{k}^{e_{k}}}(\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w},\underline{e}))\cong Q_{\underline{w}^{\underline{e}}}(\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w},\underline{e}))
under the isomorphisms afforded by (
4.7.1
).
The following lemma then follows via induction on the length of an expression along with (
4.7.1
).

Lemma 4.7.3
.

Let
\underline{w}\in\Exp(W)
. There is a decomposition of graded
Q
-bimodules,

B_{\underline{w},Q}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\bigoplus_{\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w})}B_{\underline{w},Q}^{\underline{e},\mathcal{L}}\cong\bigoplus_{\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w})}Q_{\underline{w}^{\underline{e}}}(\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w},\underline{e})).

Let
\varphi:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be a morphism of Bott–Samelson bimodules.
For
\mathcal{L}
-monodromic subexpressions
\underline{e}
of
\underline{x}
and
\underline{f}
of
\underline{y}
, we can consider the map

(\varphi_{Q})_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{f}}:B_{\underline{x},Q}^{\underline{e},\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y},Q}^{\underline{f},\mathcal{L}}

given by the composition

B_{\underline{x},Q}^{\underline{e},\mathcal{L}}\hookrightarrow B_{\underline{x},Q}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\varphi_{Q}}}{{\to}}B_{\underline{y},Q}^{\mathcal{L}}\twoheadrightarrow B_{\underline{y},Q}^{\underline{f},\mathcal{L}}.

Since both the source and target of this map are 1-dimensional
Q
-vector spaces, it is determined by a scalar
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{f}}(\varphi)\in Q
.
Note that if
\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}\neq\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}
, then
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{f}}(\varphi)=0
. We call these scalars the
localization coefficients
of
\varphi
.
Since
(-)_{Q}
is faithful, it follows that
\varphi
is uniquely determined by its matrix of localization coefficients
\left(c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{f}}(\varphi)\right)_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}
.

Remark 4.7.5
.

The localization coefficients for
\beta_{s,t}:B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}
are known for being rather difficult to compute.
In the non-monodromic case a formula is given in
[
Abe24
]
and
[
EW23
]
.
By applying the monodromic-endoscopic equivalence, one can deduce a similar formula in the monodromic case.
We only need the following corollary of this formula
[
EW23
, (2.31)]
: if
\underline{e}
and
\underline{f}
are the all 1’s subexpressions, then
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{f}}(\beta_{s,t})=1
.

4.7.6.
Localizing Light Leaves

We will now study the localization coefficients for light leaves and double leaves.
Let
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be a light leaf.
We write
c_{\underline{e},\underline{e}^{\prime}}
for the localization coefficient
c_{\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\underline{f}^{\prime}}(\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}})
where
\underline{f}^{\prime}
is the all 1’s subexpression of
\underline{w}
.
The following is a monodromic variation of what is called “path dominance upper triangularity” in
[
EW16
]
.

Proposition 4.7.7
.

Let
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
and
\underline{e},\underline{e}^{\prime}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x})
.
If
c_{\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\underline{e}}\neq 0
, then
\underline{e}^{\prime}\prec\underline{e}
. Moreover,
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{e}}
is nonzero.

The argument for Proposition
4.7.7
will follow the proof of
[
EW16
, Proposition 6.6]
closely.
Before we can prove the proposition, we need the following lemma.

Lemma 4.7.8
.

Let
\phi:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be a morphism of Bott–Samelson bimodules consisting solely of compositions and tensors of morphisms of the form
\id_{B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}}
,
\cap^{s}
, and
\beta_{s,t}
.
Let
\underline{e}
and
\underline{f}
denote the all 1’s subexpressions of
\underline{x}
and
\underline{y}
respectively.
Then
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{f}}(\phi)\neq 0
.

Proof.

Write
\phi=\phi_{1}\circ\phi_{2}\circ\ldots\circ\phi_{n}
such that
\phi_{1}
is an identity morphism and each
\phi_{i}
for
i>1
is either a morphism of the form
\cap^{s}
or
\beta_{s,t}
with identity morphisms tensored on either side.
We will argue by induction on
n
. The claim is obvious when
n=1
.
Write
\phi^{\prime}=\phi_{1}\circ\ldots\circ\phi_{n-1}:B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
\phi_{n}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
Let
\underline{e}^{\prime}
be the all 1’s subexpression for
\underline{w}
.

We claim that the following diagram commutes:

(4.7.2)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{\underline{x},Q}^{\underline{e},\mathcal{L}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{\underline{x},Q}^{\mathcal{L}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{\underline{w},Q}^{\mathcal{L}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{\underline{x},Q}^{\mathcal{L}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{\underline{w},Q}^{\mathcal{L}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{\underline{w},Q}^{\underline{e}^{\prime},\mathcal{L}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\phi_{n})_{Q}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\phi_{n})_{Q}}

We will check (
4.7.2
) case by case.
The claim is equivalent to showing that
(\phi_{n})_{Q}\left(B_{\underline{x},Q}^{\underline{e},\mathcal{L}}\right)\subseteq B_{\underline{w},Q}^{\underline{e}^{\prime},\mathcal{L}}
. By 2-functorality of localization, we can check this when
\phi_{n}
is of the form
\id_{B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}}
,
\cap^{s}
, and
\beta_{s,t}
.
This is obvious when
\phi_{n}=\id_{B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}}
or
\phi_{n}=\cap^{s}
(with either
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
or
\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}
).
When
\phi_{n}=\beta_{s,t}
, the only subexpression of
{}_{t}\underline{m}
whose evaluation is
w_{s,t}
is the all 1’s subexpression (since
{}_{t}\underline{m}
is reduced).
As a result, there are no nonzero maps between
B_{{}_{s}\underline{m},Q}^{\underline{e},\mathcal{L}}
and
B_{{}_{t}\underline{m},Q}^{\underline{f}^{\prime},\mathcal{L}}
unless
\underline{f}^{\prime}
is the all 1’s subexpression.
Therefore, (
4.7.2
) commutes.

By induction, it then suffices to show that
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{e}^{\prime}}(\phi_{n})\neq 0
. This can be checked case by case using the tables in Example
4.7.4
and the comments in Remark
4.7.5
.
∎

Proof of Proposition
4.7.7
.

We will first show upper-triangularity.
Write
w_{k}
for the element expressing
(\underline{w}_{\leq k},\underline{e}_{\leq k})
and
v_{k}
for the element expressing
(\underline{w}_{\leq k},\underline{e}_{\leq k}^{\prime})
.
Write
\LL_{k}
for the light leaf constructed after
k
-steps.
Since the target of
\LL_{k}
is a reduced expression
\underline{w}_{k}
for
w_{k}
, we have that
c_{\underline{e}_{\leq k}}^{\underline{e}_{\leq k}^{\prime}}(\LL_{k})=0
unless
v_{k}\leq w_{k}
.
Therefore,
c_{\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\underline{e}}=0
unless
v_{k}\leq w_{k}
for every
k
. This is the precise condition for
\underline{e}^{\prime}\prec\underline{e}
.

It remains to show that
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{e}}\neq 0
. We first claim that
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{e}}=q\cdot c_{\underline{f}^{\prime}}^{\underline{f}}(\phi)
where
q\in Q^{\times}
and
\phi
is some morphism of Bott–Samelson bimodules consisting solely of compositions and tensors of morphisms of the form
\id_{B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}}
,
\cap^{s}
, and
\beta_{s,t}
, and
\underline{f},\underline{f}^{\prime}
are all 1’s subexpressions.
Let
\underline{x}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
. We will argue inductively on
k
.
Suppose
e_{k}
is decorated by
U0
, then by Example
4.7.4
, we have that

c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{e}}=\alpha_{s_{k}}c_{\underline{e}_{\leq k-1}}^{\underline{e}_{\leq k-1}}.

If
e_{k}
is decorated by
D0
, then one can check using Example
4.7.4
and from definitions that

c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{e}}=c_{\underline{e}_{\leq k}}^{(1,\ldots,1)}\left(\beta_{\underline{w}_{k-1,s_{k}},\underline{w}_{k}}\circ\beta_{\underline{x}_{\leq k-1},\underline{w}_{\leq k-1,s_{k}}}\circ\LL_{k-1}\right).

Note that the right-hand side of the above equation is still
c_{\underline{e}_{\leq k-1}}^{\underline{e}_{\leq k-1}}
but for a different choice of
\LL
-datum in defining the light leaf.
As a result, by induction we can reduce to checking that
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{e}}\neq 0
when
\underline{e}
is the all 1’s subexpression.
The proposition then follows from Lemma
4.7.8
.

\square

Let
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be a double leaf. We write
c_{\underline{e},\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\underline{f},\underline{f}^{\prime}}
for the localization coefficient
c_{\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\underline{f}^{\prime}}(\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}})
.

Corollary 4.7.9
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
,
\underline{e},\underline{e}^{\prime}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x})
, and
\underline{f},\underline{f}^{\prime}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{y})
.

(1)

c_{\underline{e},\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\underline{f},\underline{f}^{\prime}}=0
unless both
\underline{e}^{\prime}\prec\underline{e}
and
\underline{f}^{\prime}\prec\underline{f}
. In particular, if
c_{\underline{e},\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\underline{f},\underline{f}^{\prime}}\neq 0
, then
\underline{x}^{\underline{e}^{\prime}}\leq\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}
.

(2)

c_{\underline{e},\underline{e}^{\prime}}^{\underline{f},\underline{f}^{\prime}}\neq 0
.

Let
I\subseteq W
be a closed subset, and
M,N\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
We define a subset
\Hom_{I}(M,N)\subseteq\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\oplus}}(M,N)
consisting of maps
f:M\to N
such that
f(M_{Q}^{w})=0
whenever
w\notin I
.

The following lemma readily follows from Lemma
4.7.3
.

Lemma 4.7.10
.

Let
I\subseteq W
be a closed subset.
A map
f:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}(d)
is in
\Hom_{I}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
if and only if
c_{\underline{e}}^{\underline{f}}(f)=0
for all
\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x})
,
\underline{f}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{y})
such that
\underline{x}^{\underline{e}},\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}\notin I
.

Regard
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
as a topological space under the order topology for the restricted Bruhat order.

Proposition 4.7.11
.

Let
I\subseteq{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
be a closed subset.
Let
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{I,\mathcal{L}}
denote the set containing one double leaf
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
for each
w\in I
and each pair of monodromic subsequences
(\underline{x},\underline{e})
and
(\underline{y},\underline{f})
expressing
w
.
Then
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{I,\mathcal{L}}
is a left graded
R
-module basis for
\Hom_{I}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
.

Proof.

The fact that
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}\in\Hom_{I}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
follows from Corollary
4.7.9
.
Moreover,
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{I,\mathcal{L}}
is linearly independent by Theorem
4.6.2
.
It remains to show that any morphism
f\in\Hom_{I}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
is spanned by double leaves in
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{I,\mathcal{L}}
.

Write
f
as a linear combination of double leaves. Unless
f
is zero, some
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
has a nonzero coefficient.
Choose
w,\underline{e},
and
\underline{f}
successively such that each is maximal in the Bruhat/path dominance order relative to the constraint that, with the previous choices, there is a nonzero coefficient
\gamma
for
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}
.
By Corollary
4.7.9
,
c_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}(f)=\gamma c_{\underline{e},\underline{e}}^{\underline{e},\underline{e}}\neq 0
.
We can then conclude by Lemma
4.7.10
that
w\in I
.
Since this is true for each maximal choice of
w
, we must have that
f
is in the
R
-span of
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{I,\mathcal{L}}
.
∎

Remark 4.7.12
.

Proposition
4.7.11
essentially states that
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
is an object-adapted cellular category (see Proposition
5.7.2
).

5.
Monodromic Hecke Category

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter system and
\mathfrak{o}
a set of monodromy parameters for
W
.
We will fix a reflection-balanced reflection-stable Abe realization
\mathfrak{h}
of
W
.
By Corollary
2.2.22
and Proposition
2.2.30
, we have that
\mathfrak{h}
is a balanced Abe realization of
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
for all
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
as well.

We will define numerous 2-categories in this section.
To keep notation consistent, unless otherwise stated,
\circ
will refer to the vertical composition and
\star
will refer to the horizontal composition in a 2-category.

5.1.
Face Colorings of Elias–Williamson Graphs

Definition 5.1.1
.

An
Elias–Williamson graph
is a planar graph
\Gamma
embedded on the planar strip
\mathbb{R}\times[0,1]
with the following data:

(1)

the edges of
\Gamma
are colored by elements of
S
;

(2)

the faces of
\Gamma
are decorated by boxes labelled by homogenous
f\in R
;

(3)

the vertices of
\Gamma
are of 3 types:

(a)

univalent vertices,

(b)

trivalent vertices, where all three adjoining edges have the same color,

(c)

2m_{s,t}
-valent vertices, where the adjoining edges alternate in color between two elements
s\neq t\in S
.

Given an Elias–Williamson graph, we define its
degree
as the sum of the degrees of each vertex, and the degrees of each polynomial. The degrees on vertices and boxes are given as follows:

(5.1.1)

f
1
-1
0
\textnormal{deg}(f)
Degree:

Definition 5.1.2
.

A
monodromic Elias–Williamson graph
is an Elias–Williamson graph with an additional coloring of the faces by elements of
\mathfrak{o}
such that if two faces colored
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
and
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
are adjacent along an edge colored by
s\in S
, then
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}s
.

We can define the
degree
of a monodromic Elias–Williamson graph as the degree of its underlying Elias–Williamson graph.

Example 5.1.3
.

Let
W=S_{3}\times S_{2}
with simple reflections
S=\{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}s},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t},{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}u}\}
where
({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}s}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t})^{3}=1
.
Define a right
W
-set
\mathfrak{o}=\{{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}2},{\color[rgb]{1,1,0}3}\}
by

{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}1}\cdot{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}s}={\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}1},\qquad{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}2}\cdot{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}s}={\color[rgb]{1,1,0}3},\qquad{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}1}\cdot{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}={\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}2},\qquad{\color[rgb]{1,1,0}3}\cdot{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}={\color[rgb]{1,1,0}3},\qquad{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}1}\cdot{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}u}={\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}1},\qquad{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}2}\cdot{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}u}={\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}2},\qquad{\color[rgb]{1,1,0}3}\cdot{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}u}={\color[rgb]{1,1,0}3}.

An example of a monodromic Elias–Williamson graph for
(W,\mathfrak{o})
is given below.

\alpha_{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}s}}

Convention 5.1.4
.

The face coloring of a monodromic Elias–Williamson graph is uniquely determined by the coloring of any face in the underlying Elias–Williamson graph.
As a result, we will not always color every face of a monodromic Elias–Williamson graph. If the left most color is clear from context, we often will only draw the underlying Elias–Williamson graph.
At times, we will color only key parts of a monodromic Elias–Williamson graph to highlight important behavior.

We denote the set of isotopy classes of Elias–Williamson graphs by
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}
and the set of isotopy classes of monodromic Elias–Williamson graphs by
\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}
.
If
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
, we will write
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
for the subset of
\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}
consisting of graphs whose most left face is colored by
\mathcal{L}
and whose right most face is colored by
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
.
We can consider the subset
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}(\underline{x},\underline{y})
of
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}
consisting of Elias–Williamson graphs with bottom boundary
\underline{x}
and top boundary
\underline{y}
.
We similarly define a subset
\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}(\underline{x},\underline{y})
of
\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}
consisting of monodromic Elias–Williamson graphs whose underlying Elias–Williamson graph is in
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}(\underline{x},\underline{y})
.
Likewise, we denote
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\underline{x},\underline{y})\coloneq\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}(\underline{x},\underline{y})\cap{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.

5.1.5.
Endosimple Expansion

Let
I\subseteq S
. Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that the simple reflections constituting
\underline{x}
and
\underline{y}
are in
I
.
We will write
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}^{I,1}(\underline{x},\underline{y})
for the subset of
(I,1)
-colored
Elias–Williamson graphs of
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}(\underline{x},\underline{y})
which consists of Elias–Williamson graphs with no
2m_{s,t}
-valent vertices and all strands are colored by elements of
I
.
We also define
\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}^{I,1}(\underline{x},\underline{y})
consisting of monodromic Elias–Williamson graphs whose underlying Elias–Williamson graph is
(
I
,1)-colored
. Likewise, we define
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{I,1}(\underline{x},\underline{y})=\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}^{I,1}(\underline{x},\underline{y})\cap{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.
If
S=I
, we will usually drop the
I
from the notation in all the previously defined collections of graphs.

Fix
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
.
Let
s^{\prime}\in S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
and
\underline{s}^{\prime}\in\Exp(W,s^{\prime})
be a reduced expression. Since
s^{\prime}
is a reflection,
\underline{s}^{\prime}
is of the form
(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k},s,s_{k},\ldots,s_{1})
where
\mathcal{L}s_{1}\ldots s_{k}s=\mathcal{L}s_{1}\ldots s_{k}
.
For each
n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, we define
s^{\star n}
as the expression
(s,s,\ldots,s)
of length
n
.
Define a map, called
endosimple expansion
,

\textnormal{endo}_{\underline{s}}:\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}^{\{s\},1}(s^{\star n},s^{\star m})\to{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}}^{1}((\underline{s}^{\prime})^{\star n},(\underline{s}^{\prime})^{\star m}),

which on generating vertices is defined by

We can generalize the endosimple expansion to multiple simple reflections as follows.
Let
I\subseteq S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
. Write
W_{\mathcal{L},I}^{\circ}
for the standard parabolic subgroup of
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
generated by
I
.
Let
\iota:I\to\Exp(W)
be an endosimple expansion datum for
W_{\mathcal{L},I}^{\circ}
.

\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W_{\mathcal{L},I}^{\circ})
.

\textnormal{endo}_{\underline{s}}
maps, we obtain a function

\textnormal{endo}_{\iota}:\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}^{I,1}(\underline{x},\underline{y})\to{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}}^{1}(\iota(\underline{x}),\iota(\underline{y})).

\displaystyle\coloneq\cup^{s}.

Proof.

Almost all the relations can be derived from their non-monodromic counterparts (cf.,
[
EW16
, Claim 5.13]
).
It remains to check that
\Upsilon_{s}
is invariant under the polynomial forcing relation when
\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}
and the block minimality relations.
The polynomial forcing relation is the defining property of the
R
-bimodule structure on
R_{s}=B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
Similarly, block minimality follows from
\cup^{s}
and
\cap^{s}
being inverse, i.e., they define the canonical isomorphism
R_{s}\otimes_{R}R_{s}\cong R
.
∎

It turns out that
\Upsilon_{s}
is actually fully faithful on morphism categories. However, we will need to develop much more technology before proving this.

5.2.4.
The Universal Calculus

In the non-monodromic setting, one usually goes straight from the 1-color diagrammatics to 2-colors diagrammatics when defining Hecke categories.
However, in the monodromic setting, it is useful to introduce an intermediary where we allow for arbitrary 1-morphisms, but only consider 2-morphisms corresponding to rank 1 parabolic subgroups.
This has the advantage of allowing for monodromy parameters to play a more central role– giving way to glimpses of endoscopy.

Definition 5.2.5
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter system. Let
\mathfrak{o}
be a
W
-set and
\mathfrak{h}
be a pre-realization for
W
.
The
universal diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category
, denoted
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S,\mathfrak{o})
, is the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear strict 2-category defined as follows.
The object set is
\mathfrak{o}
. The 1-morphisms are tensor generated by 1-morphisms
B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}:\mathcal{L}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle s}}{{\to}}\mathcal{L}s
for all
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
and
s\in S
.
In particular, a general 1-morphism is of the form
B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}:\mathcal{L}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\underline{w}}}{{\to}}\mathcal{L}\underline{w}
where
\underline{w}\in\Exp(W)
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
.
The 2-morphisms
2\textnormal{-}\Hom_{\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
is the free
\mathbbm{k}
-module with basis
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{1}(\underline{x},\underline{y})
modulo the 1-color relations of (
5.2.2
).

Given
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
, we define 1-categories
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S,\mathfrak{o})\coloneq\Hom_{\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S,\mathfrak{o})}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime})
.

Remark 5.2.6
.

The 2-category
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S,\mathfrak{o})
is universal in the sense that it is the diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category for the free Coxeter group on
S
generators.
In particular, we will later see that for a general Coxeter group
W
, its diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category is a quotient of the universal category.

The inclusion of
\{s\}\hookrightarrow S
gives rise to a locally faithful 2-functor

I_{s}:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},s,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S,\mathfrak{o}).

Similarly, the same construction and argument from Proposition
5.2.3
defines a 2-functor

\Upsilon_{S}:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

such that
\Upsilon_{S}\circ I_{s}=\Upsilon_{s}
. Unlike the one-color case,
\Upsilon_{S}
is not locally full.
In particular, it only depends on the set
S
and its action on
\mathfrak{o}
, but does not include any Coxeter theoretic information.
In other words, the universal one-color category does not include information on rank 2 and rank 3 parabolic subgroups of
W
.

The main advantage of introducing the universal category is that it contains many interesting Frobenius algebras that were not present in the one-color category.
Let
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k},s,s_{k},\ldots,s_{1})
be an endo-reduced expression for some endosimple reflection
s^{\prime}\in S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
.
Write
\underline{x}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
and let
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{x}
.
We can then give
B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
the structure of a Frobenius algebra as follows.

(5.2.3)

\mu^{\underline{w}}
\Delta^{\underline{w}}
\eta^{\underline{w}}
\epsilon^{\underline{w}}

It is easy to check from the Frobenius algebra structure on
B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and block minimality that
B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
along with the maps in (
5.2.3
) define a Frobenius algebra.
Moreover, it follows that under
\Upsilon_{S}
, this Frobenius algebra is sent to
B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong C_{t}
with its usual Frobenius algebra structure.

Proposition 5.2.7

(One-Color Endoscopy)
.

Let
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
and
\iota
be an endosimple expansion datum for
\mathcal{L}
.
There is a monoidal functor

\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}:\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S,\mathfrak{o})

defined by
\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}(B_{s^{\prime}}^{1})=B_{\iota(s^{\prime})}^{\mathcal{L}}
for
s^{\prime}\in S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
and taking the Frobenius structure maps on
B_{s^{\prime}}^{1}
to the Frobenius structure maps on
B_{\iota(s^{\prime})}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
Moreover, this functor makes the following square commute up to natural isomorphism

(5.2.4)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},S,\mathfrak{o})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/1}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Upsilon_{S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Upsilon_{S}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\textnormal{alg}}}

Proof.

The fact that
\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\diag}
is well-defined follows from the discussion on Frobenius algebra structures preceding the proposition.

It remains to check that (
5.2.4
) commutes.
After unpacking definitions, it suffices to define an isomorphism
\xi:B_{\iota(s^{\prime})}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}C_{s^{\prime}}
of Frobenius algebras in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
for each
s^{\prime}\in S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
.
Define
\xi
as the isomorphism taking the 1-tensor
u_{\iota(s^{\prime})}
to
1\otimes 1\in R\otimes_{R^{s^{\prime}}}R(1)=C_{s^{\prime}}
.
This property ensures that
\xi
is an isomorphism of coalgebras. Indeed, the coalgebra structure maps for
C_{s^{\prime}}
are the unique
R
-bimodule maps taking 1-tensors to 1-tensors.
By Proposition
4.6.4
,
D(\xi^{-1}):B_{\iota(s^{\prime})}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}C_{s^{\prime}}
is an isomorphism of algebras. It is then easy to check that
D(\xi^{-1})
also takes the
u_{\iota(s^{\prime})}
to
1\otimes 1
.
As a result, by uniqueness, we must have that
D(\xi^{-1})=\xi
. Therefore,
\xi
is an isomorphism of Frobenius algebras.
∎

5.3.
The Monodromic Dihedral Cathedral

The goal of this section is to define the diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category for Coxeter groups of type
I_{2}(m)
for
m<\infty
.
In terms of generators, this amounts to adding
2m
-valent vertices to Elias–Williamson graphs.
The relations amongst these generators will combine the one-color relations along with two new relations: two-color associativity and the Elias–Jones–Wenzl relation.
Two-color associativity is a straightforward generalization of the corresponding non-monodromic concept.
The Elias–Jones–Wenzl relation is much more subtle.
In the non-monodromic setting, the Elias–Jones–Wenzl relation is defined using Jones–Wenzl projectors for the two-colored Temperley–Lieb algebra.
Unfortunately, we do not have a good notion of a monodromic Temperley–Lieb algebra.
Instead, we will consider an endoscopic Temperley–Lieb algebra and then apply endosimple expansion.
This has the benefit of allowing us to use known results on Temperley–Lieb algebras.

Before continuing to the construction of the Jones–Wenzl projectors. We will set up some notation which will be used throughout this section.
Let
W_{m}
denote the dihedral group with simple reflections
s,t
where
m=m_{s,t}<\infty
.
Let
\mathfrak{o}
be a
W_{m}
-set. We will write
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
for the endoscopic subgroup of
W_{m}
corresponding to
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
.
Note that
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
has rank 0, 1, or 2.
When
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
is rank 2, we will write
s^{\prime},t^{\prime}
for the endosimple reflections in
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
Moreover, we will write
v=v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
for the order of
s^{\prime}t^{\prime}
which divides
m
. We then have that
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
is isomorphic as a Coxeter group to
W_{v}
.

5.3.1.
Temperley–Lieb Category

Let
A
be a
\mathbb{Z}[x,y]
-algebra.
We will review the construction of the two-colored Temperley–Lieb 2-category
2\mathcal{T}\mathcal{L}_{A}
and discuss some properties.
There is no new mathematical content here and a more detailed treatise can be found elsewhere (cf.,
[
EW16
,
EW23
,
Haz24
]
).

Definition 5.3.2
.

The
two-colored Temperley–Lieb 2-category

2\mathcal{T}\mathcal{L}_{A}
is the 2-category defined as follows.
There are two objects of
2\mathcal{T}\mathcal{L}_{A}
which are denoted by
s
and

.

(\ldots,s,t,s,t,\ldots)

For an integer

{}_{s}n
for the sequence of length
n+1
which begins with
s
, and
{}_{t}n
for the sequence of length
n+1
which begins with
t

Horizontal composition (
\star
) of 2-morphisms is defined by horizontal concatenation of crossingless matchings.

The
A
-algebra
\TL_{A}({}_{s}n)\coloneq 2\textnormal{-}\End_{2\mathcal{T}\mathcal{L}_{A}}({}_{s}n)
is called the
two-colored Temperley–Lieb algebra
.
For each
1\leq i\leq n-1
, we define a crossingless matching
e_{i}\in\TL_{A}({}_{s}n)
as follows:

\ldots
\ldots
\ldots
\ldots
i
i
e_{i}
(
i
even)
e_{i}
(
i
odd)

where the purple region is red if
n
is even and blue if
n
is odd.
It can be checked that
\TL_{A}({}_{s}n)
is the
A
-algebra with generators
e_{i}
for
1\leq i\leq n-1
, subject to the relations

\displaystyle e_{i}^{2}

\displaystyle=-x

\displaystyle\text{if }i\text{ odd},

\displaystyle e_{i}^{2}

\displaystyle=-y

\displaystyle\text{if }i\text{ even},

\displaystyle e_{i}e_{j}

\displaystyle=e_{j}e_{i}

\displaystyle\text{if }\lvert i-j\rvert>1,

\displaystyle e_{i}e_{i\pm 1}e_{i}

\displaystyle=e_{i}.

The algebra
\TL_{A}({}_{t}n)\coloneq 2\textnormal{-}\End_{2\mathcal{T}\mathcal{L}_{A}}({}_{t}n)
admits a similar presentation except for the parity conditions on
e_{i}^{2}
being switched.

Definition 5.3.3
.

Let
u\in\{s,t\}
.
An element
\JW_{A}({}_{u}n)\in\TL_{A}({}_{u}n)
is called a
two-colored Jones–Wenzl projector
if

(1)

\JW_{A}({}_{u}n)
is an idempotent,

(2)

e_{i}\JW_{A}({}_{u}n)=0
for all
1\leq i\leq n-1
,

(3)

The coefficient of 1 in
\JW_{A}({}_{u}n)
is 1.

It follows from general theory that if two-colored Jones–Wenzl projectors exist, then they are unique.

Definition 5.3.4
.

Suppose
\JW_{A}({}_{s}n)
exists.
We say that
\JW_{A}({}_{s}n)
is

if

\>\>\>\>\>\JW_{A}({}_{s}n)\>\>\>\>\>
\ldots
\ldots
\ldots
\ldots

(

\>\>\>\>\>\JW_{A}({}_{s}n)\>\>\>\>\>
\ldots
\ldots
\ldots

=

\lambda_{s,t}

for some invertible scalar

.
Likewise,

It is clear from definitions that if
\JW_{A}({}_{s}n)
is rotatable, then
\JW_{A}({}_{t}n)

In this case, it is not hard to show that

By

Historically, it has been a very troublesome question to determine when Jones–Wenzl projectors exist and when they are rotatable.
Fortunately, a complete solution to this question has been provided by Hazi.

Theorem 5.3.5

(
[
Haz24
, Theorem B]
)
.

The two-colored Jones–Wenzl projectors,
\JW_{A}({}_{s}n)
and
\JW_{A}({}_{t}n)
, exist and are rotatable if and only if
\begin{bmatrix}n+1\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{x}=\begin{bmatrix}n+1\\
k\end{bmatrix}_{y}=0
in
A
for all
1\leq k\leq n
.

Let
\mathfrak{h}
be an Abe realization for a dihedral group
W_{m}
of order
m
with simple reflections

.
Let
A=\mathbbm{k}[x,y]/(x-a_{s,t},y-a_{t,s})
. Theorem
5.3.5
implies that the two-colored Jones–Wenzl projectors exist for this
A
.
Moreover, the condition that
\mathfrak{h}
be balanced is equivalent to
\lambda_{s,t}=1
.

Lemma 5.3.8
.

Let
f:B_{{}_{u}\underline{N}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{{}_{u}\underline{N}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be an
(a,b)
-adjustable morphism and let
g:B_{{}_{u}\underline{N^{\prime}}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{{}_{u}\underline{N^{\prime\prime}}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be a
(b,c)
-adjustable morphism.
Then
g\circ f
is
(a,c)
-adjustable. Moreover,
\tau_{a}^{c}(g\circ f)=\tau_{b}^{c}(g)\circ\tau_{a}^{b}(f)
.

Proof.

Suppose
f
is truncated and
g
is truncated. It follows from definitions that
g\circ f=(\tau_{b}^{c}g\circ\tau_{a}^{b}f)\star\id
, and so
g\circ f
is
(a,c)
-truncated with
\tau_{a}^{c}(g\circ f)=\tau_{b}^{c}g\circ\tau_{a}^{b}f
.

Suppose
f
is truncated and
g
is extendable.
Since
f
is truncated, we have that
N^{\prime}-b\geq 0
. On the other hand, since

is extendable, we have that
N^{\prime}-b\leq 0
.
Therefore, we are in the cases where

which implies that

is truncated. We can then proceed as in the first case.

The remaining two cases follow from similar arguments and are omitted.
∎

Lemma 5.3.9

Monodromic Jones–Wenzl Morphisms

We define the

Lemma 5.3.12
.

The monodromic Jones–Wenzl morphisms satisfy the following properties:

(1)

is idempotent;

Let
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
. Let
\underline{w}^{\beta}
be an endo-reduced expression for
w^{\beta}
. There is an equivalence of categories

(-)\star\id_{\underline{w}^{\beta}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS,\circ}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}).

Proof.

(1):
Clearly, every morphism is contained in some block of
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
As a result, it suffices to show that every morphism
f:B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
with
b_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w})\neq b_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{y})
is zero.
We can show something stronger, namely, that no underlying monodromic Elias–Williamson graph can even exist.
This can be easily checked on the generating vertices in an Elias–Williamson graph: trivalent and univalent vertices are always in the neutral block and
2m_{s,t}
-valent vertices do not change the block by Lemma
2.1.5
.

(2):
This is obvious from the definition of blocks (Lemma
2.1.5
).

(3):
Let
u\in\{s,t\}
such that
\mathcal{L}u\neq\mathcal{L}
.
Then the block minimality relations ensure that
B_{uu}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}
via the cup and cap maps.
As a result,
(-)\star\id_{B_{u}^{\mathcal{L}}}
is an equivalence of categories with inverse
(-)\star\id_{B_{u}^{\mathcal{L}u}}
.
More generally, if
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and
\underline{w}^{\beta}
is an endo-reduced expression for
w^{\beta}
, then we can apply the above equivalences inductively to show that

(-)\star\id_{B_{\underline{w}^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}}}
is an equivalence of categories with inverse
(-)\star\id_{B_{\overline{\underline{w}}^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}
.
∎

5.3.17.
Two-Color Endoscopy

It is useful to give some extra notation to the
2m_{s,t}
-valent vertices.
Namely, suppose
2m=a+b
. We will then write

\beta({}_{s}\underline{a},{}_{t}\underline{b}):B_{{}_{s}\underline{a}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{{}_{t}\underline{b}}^{\mathcal{L}}

for the
2m_{s,t}
-valent vertex with strands
{}_{s}\underline{a}
on the bottom and
{}_{t}\underline{b}
strands on the top.
We reserve the notation
\beta_{s,t}
for the morphism
\beta({}_{s}\underline{m},{}_{t}\underline{m})
.
Similarly, we will denote variants of the above where
s
and
t
are switched everywhere.

Let
v=v_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
. Without loss of generality, we may assume that
\iota(s^{\prime})
(resp.
\iota(t^{\prime})
) starts with
s
(resp.
t
).
We wish to explain the behavior of endosimple expansion on
2v
-valent vertices.
Let
2v=a^{\prime}+b^{\prime}
. Note that
\iota({}_{s^{\prime}}\underline{2v})={}_{s}\underline{2m}
.
Let
a=\ell(\iota({}_{s}\underline{a^{\prime}}))
and
b=\ell(\iota({}_{t}\underline{b^{\prime}}))
.
It then follows that
2m=a+b
.
We can then define the endosimple expansion of a
2v
-valent vertex as follows:

(5.3.3)

\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}(\beta({}_{s^{\prime}}\underline{a}^{\prime},{}_{t^{\prime}}\underline{b}^{\prime}))\coloneq\beta({}_{s}\underline{a},{}_{t}\underline{b}).

Proposition 5.3.18

(Two-color Endoscopy)
.

The functor

\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}:\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},\{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\},1)\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},\{s,t\},\mathfrak{o})

extends to a functor

\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}:\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}},1)\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

by defining
\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}
on
2v
-valent vertices by (
5.3.3
).

Proof.

It suffices to check that
\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}
is invariant under 2-color associativity and the Elias–Jones–Wenzl relation.

(Two-color Associativity):

(Elias–Jones–Wenzl):
We will cover both variants of the Elias–Jones–Wenzl relations, so without loss of generality, we may assume that
\ell(s^{\prime})>\ell(t^{\prime})
.
We will assume that
v
is odd and that
m
is odd. The cases of
v
being odd and
m
being even is almost identical and the case of
vs
being even is similar (and in fact easier).
Let
r=\frac{1}{2}(\ell(t^{\prime})-\ell(s^{\prime}))>0
.
We can then compute directly, again omitting the face labels on the monodromic side.

\displaystyle=\tau\left(\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}(\JW_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}^{1})\right)

\displaystyle=\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}(\JW_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}^{1})\star\id_{B_{{}_{s}\underline{r}}^{\mathcal{L}}}.

The last line follows from the definition of
\tau
. Note that
\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}(\JW_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}^{1})
is extendable in this case.
By Lemma
5.3.16
, we have that
(-)\star\id_{B_{{}_{s}\underline{r}}^{\mathcal{L}}}
is an equivalence of categories.
Therefore, we conclude that
\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}(\beta_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}\circ\beta_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}})=\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\iota,\textnormal{diag}}(\JW_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}^{1})
.
∎

Claim 5.3.20
.

\Upsilon_{\Abe}:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
is well-defined.

The proof of Claim
5.3.20
will take the rest of the section.
Note that there is a special case when we know
\Upsilon_{\Abe}
is already defined. Namely, it is shown in
[
Abe21
]
that when
\mathfrak{o}=1
, then
\Upsilon_{\Abe}
is well-defined.

Step 0: Compatibility with Block Translation

We will write

\Upsilon_{\mathcal{L}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

for the restriction of
\Upsilon_{\Abe}
such that the first monodromy parameter is fixed. Let
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
. We can also write

\Upsilon_{\mathcal{L}}^{\beta}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

for the restriction of
\Upsilon_{\Abe}
to the
\beta
-block.
It is clear from its definition that
\Upsilon_{\Abe}
indeed takes objects in the
\beta
-block on the diagrammatic side to objects in the
\beta
-block on the algebraic side.

The following lemma follows readily from definitions.

Lemma 5.3.21
.

Let
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
. Let
\underline{w}^{\beta}
be an endo-reduced expression for
w^{\beta}
.
The following diagram (strictly) commutes

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS,\circ}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS,\circ}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}).}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(-)\star B_{\underline{w}^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Upsilon_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(-)\star B_{\underline{w}^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Upsilon_{\mathcal{L}}^{\beta}}

Step 1: Rotation invariance

Note that
\beta_{s,t}:B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is uniquely determined by the condition that
\beta_{s,t}(u_{{}_{s}\underline{m}})=u_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}
.
As a result, it is easy to check that
\beta_{s,t}
is invariant under rotations. Therefore,
\Upsilon_{\Abe}
is well-defined on isotopy classes of monodromic Elias–Williamson graphs.

n=2m-1
