Step 3: Elias–Jones–Wenzl

First consider the case where
\rk(W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}})<2
.
In this case,
\JW_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}=\id_{B_{{}_{s}m}^{\mathcal{L}}}
.
On the other hand, in
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
, we have that space of degree 0 endomorphisms of
B_{{}_{s}m}^{\mathcal{L}}
is a rank-1
\mathbbm{k}
-module (Theorem
4.6.2
).
Moreover,
\beta_{t,s}\circ\beta_{s,t}
and
\id
both take the 1-tensor to itself. Therefore, we must have that Jones–Wenzl relation is invariant under
\Upsilon_{\Abe}
.

We can then assume that
\rk(W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}})=2
.
Let
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
be the block containing
\JW_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
Let
\underline{w}^{\beta}
be an endo-reduced expression for
w^{\beta}
. We set

T_{\beta}^{\diag}\coloneq(-)\star B_{\underline{w}^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS,\circ}\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_{\beta}^{\alg}\coloneq(-)\star B_{\underline{w}^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS,\circ}\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}.

By block minimality, we can give a slight modification to the definition of the Jones–Wenzl morphism,

\JW_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}=T_{\beta}^{\diag}\Sigma_{\mathcal{L}}(\JW_{A}({}_{s^{\prime}}(v-1))).

We can then compute

\displaystyle\Upsilon_{\mathcal{L}}(\JW_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}})

\displaystyle=\Upsilon_{\mathcal{L}}T_{\beta}^{\diag}\Sigma_{\mathcal{L}}(\JW_{A}({}_{s^{\prime}}(v-1)))

\displaystyle=T_{\beta}^{\alg}\Upsilon_{\mathcal{L}}\Sigma_{\mathcal{L}}(\JW_{A}({}_{s^{\prime}}(v-1)))

\displaystyle=T_{\beta}^{\alg}\Upsilon_{\mathcal{L}}\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\diag}\Sigma(\JW_{A}({}_{s^{\prime}}(v-1)))

\displaystyle=T_{\beta}^{\alg}\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg}\Upsilon_{S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}}\Sigma(\JW_{A}({}_{s^{\prime}}(v-1)))

\displaystyle=T_{\beta}^{\alg}\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg}\Upsilon_{S_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}}\JW_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}^{1}

\displaystyle=T_{\beta}^{\alg}\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg}(\beta_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}\circ\beta_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}})

\displaystyle=T_{\beta}^{\alg}(\beta(\iota({}_{t^{\prime}}\underline{v}),\iota({}_{s^{\prime}}\underline{v}))\circ\beta(\iota({}_{s^{\prime}}\underline{v}),\iota({}_{t^{\prime}}\underline{v})))

\displaystyle=\beta_{t,s}\circ\beta_{s,t}.

The second equality is from Lemma
5.3.21
. The fourth equality is from Proposition
5.2.7
. The sixth equality follows from the Jones–Wenzl relation for non-monodromic Bott–Samelson bimodules (a consequence of
\Upsilon_{1}^{\circ}
being well-defined).
Finally, the last equality is an application of block minimality. This completes the proof of Claim
5.3.20
.

5.4.
Presentation of the Monodromic Hecke Category

We will now return to the general case where
(W,S)
is an arbitrary Coxeter system and
\mathfrak{o}
is a
W
-set.

We are almost ready to give the definition of the monodromic Hecke category in full generality.
Before doing so, we first need to impose a technical constraint on our Coxeter systems to ensure that the three-color relations are computable.
The constraint is essentially identical to the usual constraint that
H_{3}
does not appear as a parabolic subgroup for the non-monodromic Hecke category.

Assumption 5.4.1
.

For all type
H_{3}
standard parabolic subgroups
W_{I}
of
W
and all
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
, we have that
W_{I}\cap W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is a proper subgroup of
W_{I}
.

5.4.2.
Definition

Definition 5.4.3
.

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter system and
\mathfrak{o}
be a
W
-set such that Assumption
5.4.1
is satisfied.
Let
\mathfrak{h}
be a reflection-balanced reflection-stable Abe realization for
W
.
The
diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category
, denoted
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
, is the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear strict 2-category defined as follows.
The object set is
\mathfrak{o}
. The 1-morphisms are tensor generated by 1-morphisms
B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}:\mathcal{L}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle s}}{{\to}}\mathcal{L}s
for all
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
,
s\in S
.
A general 1-morphism is then of the form
B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}:\mathcal{L}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\underline{x}}}{{\to}}\mathcal{L}\underline{x}
for
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
.
The 2-morphism space
2\textnormal{-}\Hom_{\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
is the free
\mathbbm{k}
-module with basis
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\underline{x},\underline{y})
modulo the following relations:

(One-Color Relations)
The relations of the one-color category (
5.2.2
).

(Two-color Associativity)
The two-color associativity and Elias–Jones–Wenzl relations of (
5.3.14
).

(Zamolodchikov Equations)
There is a 3-color relation for each finitary rank-3 subset
I=\{s,t,u\}
of
S
.
The specific form depends on the type of the parabolic subgroup
W_{I}
along with its action on
\mathfrak{o}
.
By the classification of finite Coxeter groups the finite rank three parabolic can only be one of the following types:
A_{1}\times I_{2}(m)
,
A_{3}
,
B_{3}
, or
H_{3}
.

Remark 5.4.4
.

(1)

Assumption
5.4.1
is needed since the non-monodromic Hecke category still lacks a computation of the lower order terms needed for the corresponding three-color relation to hold. Further discussion on this topic can be found in
[
EW23
, §3.6]
.
Finding the
H_{3}
Zamolodchikov equation in the non-monodromic Hecke category would also complete the description in the monodromic Hecke category.

(2)

It is somewhat surprising that lower order terms appear in the Zamolodchikov equations for type
B_{3}
with an endoscopy subgroup of type
A_{3}
.
We can somewhat motivate this by the monodromic-endoscopic equivalence.
After endoscopy, the monodromic three-color relations becomes
(\leq 3)
-color relations on the endoscopic side.
The lower order terms can only appear when the endoscopic subgroup also has rank 3. This happens quite rarely.

(a)

In type
A_{1}\times I_{2}(m)
, all endoscopic subgroups are of the following types:
A_{1}\times I_{2}(v)
and
I_{2}(v)
where
0\leq v\leq m
divides (by definition, we take
I_{2}(0)=1
and
I_{2}(1)=A_{1}
).

(b)

In type
A_{3}
, all nontrivial endoscopic subgroups are of the following types:
A_{3}
,
A_{2}
,
A_{1}\times A_{1}
, and
A_{1}
.

(c)

In type
B_{3}
, all nontrivial endoscopic subgroups are of the following types:
B_{3}
,
A_{3}
,
A_{1}\times A_{1}\times A_{1}
,
A_{1}\times A_{2}
,
A_{1}\times A_{1}
,
A_{2}
,
B_{2}
, and
A_{1}
.

(d)

In type
H_{3}
, all nontrivial endoscopic subgroups are of the following types:
H_{3}
,
A_{1}\times A_{1}\times A_{1}
,
I_{2}(5)
,
A_{2}
,
A_{1}\times A_{1}
, and
A_{1}
.

One way to interpret the lack of lower terms is that in almost every case the canonical orientation of the rex graph on the monodromic side aligns with the canonical orientation of the rex graph on the endoscopic side.
There is exactly two places where this fails: (i) in type
H_{3}
when no canonical orientation exists, and (ii) in type
B_{3}
when the induced orientation on the rex graph of
A_{3}
is not the canonical one.

Remark 5.4.5
.

If
\mathfrak{o}=1
, then
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,1)
is the non-monodromic diagrammatic Hecke category of
[
EW16
]
viewed as a 2-category with one object.

Remark 5.4.6
.

It should be possible to define
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
even when
\mathfrak{h}
is not reflection-balanced.
In particular, since
\mathfrak{h}
is reflection-stable, by
[
Haz24
, Theorem B]
one can still make sense of the Jones–Wenzl projectors necessary to define the Jones–Wenzl morphisms.
When
\mathfrak{h}
is not reflection-balanced, these Jones–Wenzl morphisms fail to be rotation invariant, but instead are rotation invariant up to an invertible scalar.
To correct this, one must introduce two different
2m
-valent vertices, and modify the relations accordingly. Such a correction should be very close to the modifications done in
[
EW16
, §5.6]
.

5.4.7.
Associated 1-Categories

For two monodromy parameters
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
, we can consider the category

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\coloneq\Hom_{\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}).

Let
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
be a block and define a full subcategory
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
of
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
, called the
\beta
-block
, consisting of objects
B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
where
\underline{w}\in\Exp(W)
is an expression for an element in
\beta
.

The following is a generalization of Lemma
5.3.16
for arbitrary Coxeter systems. The proof is identical, and as such omitted.

Lemma 5.4.8
.

Let
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime},\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
.

(1)

There is a decomposition of categories

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})=\bigsqcup_{\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}).

(2)

Let
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and
\gamma\in{}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}
. Horizontal composition is compatible with block multiplication, i.e.,

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\star\>_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}^{\BS,\beta\gamma}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\subseteq\>_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}^{\BS,\beta\gamma}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}).

(3)

Let
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and let
\underline{w}^{\beta}
be an endo-reduced expression for
w^{\beta}
. There is an equivalence of categories

(-)\star\id_{B_{\underline{w}^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS,\circ}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS,\beta}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}).

5.4.9.
From Diagrammatics to Bimodules

The goal of this section is to define a 2-functor

\Upsilon_{\Abe}:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}).

On objects,
\Upsilon(\mathcal{L})=\mathcal{L}
, and on 1-morphisms
\Upsilon(B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}})=B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
for
\underline{w}\in\Exp(W)
.

\Upsilon

\displaystyle\coloneq\beta_{s,t}.

Claim 5.4.10
.

\Upsilon
is a well-defined 2-functor.

Proof.

We have already shown that
\Upsilon
is invariant under the 1-color relations in Proposition
5.2.3
and under the 2-color relations in Claim
5.3.20
.
As a result, it only remains to check that
\Upsilon
is invariant under the 3-color relations.

We compute these case-by-case for types
A_{3},B_{3}
, and
H_{3}
. There are 30 possible monodromy labeling in type
A_{3}
, 98 possible monodromy labeling in type
B_{3}
, and 164 possible monodromy labeling in type
H_{3}
.
Most of these cases, one can check by constraining Hom spaces or from existing literature that
\Upsilon
is invariant under the 3-color relations.
The one exception is when
B_{3}
has an endoscopic subgroup of type
A_{3}
. This will be checked by hand using algebraic endoscopy.

In type
A_{1}\times I_{2}(m)
, the possible endoscopic subgroups are of the form
A_{1}\times I_{2}(v)
and
I_{2}(v)
where
0\leq v\leq m
divides
m
.
When the coloring of the 3-color relation arises from an endoscopic subgroup of rank
\leq 2
, the invariance under
\Upsilon
follows from constraints on Hom spaces in low rank.
When the endoscopic subgroup is rank 3, then the 3-color relation for
A_{1}\times I_{2}(m)
maps under
\Upsilon
to the 3-color relation for
A_{1}\times I_{2}(v)
.

The complete proof is covered in Appendix
A
.
Therein, we also show how the possible monodromy parameters can be computed, some important examples, and how
\Upsilon
-invariance can be computed.
∎

5.5.
Double Leaves

We will provide a diagrammatic counterpart to the double leaves basis constructed for Bott–Samelson bimodules. In the non-monodromic setting these were first introduced in
[
EW16
]
.
Throughout we will fix an
\LL
-datum as in §
4.1.3
.

5.5.1.
Definition and the Algorithm

Let
\underline{x}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
be an expression in
W
, and let
\underline{e}
be an
\mathcal{L}
-monodromic subexpression of
\underline{x}
. For each
1\leq i\leq k
, let
x_{i}
be the element realizing
\underline{x}_{\leq i}
.
Let
w_{i}=\underline{x}_{\leq i}^{\underline{e}_{\leq i}}
.
We write
\underline{w}_{i}=\rex(w_{i})
for the reduced expression of
x_{i}
fixed by the
\LL
-datum.
The condition that
\underline{e}
be monodromic ensures that
\mathcal{L}x_{i}=\mathcal{L}w_{i}
.

The construction of the light leaves is identical to algebraic version after obvious replacements are made.
Nonetheless, for the sake of exposition, we will detail the algorithm.

We construct the light leaf
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
inductively on the length
k
of
\underline{x}
.
The base case is covered by
\LL_{\varnothing,\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}:B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}
being the identity map.
Suppose that we have already constructed a map

\LL_{i-1}^{\mathcal{L}}:=\LL_{\underline{x}_{\leq i-1},\underline{e}_{\leq i-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}:B_{\underline{x}_{\leq i-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}_{i-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}.

In a moment, we will define a map

\phi_{i}:B_{\underline{x}_{\leq i-1}s_{i}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}_{i}}^{\mathcal{L}}.

We then define

\LL_{i}^{\mathcal{L}}=\phi_{i}\circ(\LL_{i-1}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\id_{B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}w_{i-1}}}).

The definition of
\phi_{i}
depends on a decoration
\dec_{i}(\underline{w},\underline{e})
.
We will now explain
\phi_{i}
for each decoration. While the definition does not actually depend on whether
i\in K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L})
, it is still useful to show the face colorings for both cases.
The figure below describes
\phi_{i}
in all such cases. Here red is used for the simple reflection
s_{i}
. The orange corresponds to
\mathcal{L}
, the green corresponds to
\mathcal{L}w_{i-1}
, and the purple corresponds to
\mathcal{L}w_{i}
.

\alpha
\alpha
\alpha
\beta
\alpha
\beta
\alpha
\beta
\alpha
U0
U1
U1
D0
D1
D1
i\in K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L})
i\in K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L})
i\notin K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L})
i\in K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L})
i\in K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L})
i\notin K(\underline{w},\mathcal{L})

The
\alpha
indicates the rex move to
\underline{w}_{i}
and
\beta
indicates the rex move from
\underline{w}_{i-1}
to
\rex_{s}(w_{i-1})
. Both of these rex moves are uniquely determined after choosing the corresponding path in the rex graph as in §
4.1.3
.

5.5.2.
The Basis Theorem

Definition 5.5.3
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
. Let
\underline{e}\subset\underline{x}
and
\underline{f}\subset\underline{y}
be monodromic subexpressions such that
\underline{w}^{\underline{e}}=w=\underline{y}^{\underline{f}}
.
A
double leaf
is a composition of the form

\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{e},\underline{f}}^{w,\mathcal{L}}:=\overline{\LL}_{\underline{y},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}\circ\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}

where
\overline{\LL}_{\underline{y},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}:B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
denotes the horizontal reflection of
\LL_{\underline{y},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

Theorem 5.5.4
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
.
Let
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
denote the set of all
\mathcal{L}
-monodromic double leaves from
B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
to
B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
with respect to a fixed
\LL
-datum.
Then
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is a left graded
R
-module basis for
\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
.

The proof of Theorem
5.5.4
is rather involved. Showing linear independence is easy and will be covered in the following lemma. The difficult part is showing that the double leaves span the Hom space.
We have deferred the proof of this component until the next section.

Lemma 5.5.5
.

Let
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
.
Then
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is linearly independent over
R
as a subset of
\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
.

Proof.

By construction, the functor
\Upsilon:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
takes double leaves to double leaves (see Proposition
4.6.4
and Remark
4.6.5
).
The result then follows from Theorem
4.6.2
.
∎

Remark 5.5.6
.

Let
\mathfrak{o}=W
where
W
acts on
\mathfrak{o}
by right multiplication.
For all
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
, there is an equivalence of categories

\textnormal{perm}_{\mathcal{L}}^{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

obtained by the permutation of the monodromy labelings
\mathfrak{o}\to\mathfrak{o}
given by multiplication by the unique element
w
such that
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}w
.
We can then equip
\>{}_{e\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
with the structure of a monoidal category via the composition

\>{}_{e\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\times\>_{e\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{perm}_{\mathcal{L}}^{e}}}{{\cong}}\>_{e\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\times\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{e\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}).

It is easy to check from definitions, that
\>{}_{e\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
is equivalent as a monoidal category to the diagrammatic category of standard bimodules defined in
[
EW16
, §4.1]
.

Theorem
5.5.4
implies the following Hom space calculation,

\Hom_{\>{}_{e\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})\cong\begin{cases}R&\ev(\underline{x})=\ev(\underline{y}),\\
0&\textnormal{otherwise}.\end{cases}

This essentially gives a diagrammatic proof of
[
EW17
, Theorem 6.6]
.

5.5.7.
Monodromic Abe Theorem

As a consequence of the double leaves basis for the category of Bott–Samelson bimodules and the diagrammatic category, we deduce that
\Upsilon
is an equivalence of categories.
This result generalizes
[
Abe21
, Theorem 5.6]
and
[
Abe24
, Theorem 3.15]
.

Theorem 5.5.8
.

The 2-functor

\Upsilon:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

is an equivalence of 2-categories.

Proof.

It is clear that
\Upsilon
is essentially surjective.
Moreover,
\Upsilon
takes double leaves to double leaves.
The result then follows from Theorem
4.6.2
and Theorem
5.5.4
.
∎

5.6.
Diagrammatic Endoscopy

In this section, we will establish a monodromic-endoscopic equivalence for the diagrammatic Hecke categories which serves as a diagrammatic counterpart to Theorem
5.6.2
.

Let
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime},\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
,
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
, and
\gamma\in{}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}
. There is an equivalence of monoidal categories

{}^{\beta}(-):\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\circ},1)\to\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)

induced by the isomorphism of Coxeter groups
W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\circ}\to W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
defined by
w\mapsto w^{\beta}ww^{\beta,-1}
.
It follows from definitions that
{}^{\beta}({}^{\gamma}(-))\cong{}^{\beta\gamma}(-)
.

Let
\underline{x}
be an endo-reduced expression for
w^{\beta}
.
There is an equivalence of monoidal categories

{}^{\beta}(-):\>_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\oplus,\circ}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\oplus,\circ}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

defined by
M\mapsto B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\star M\star B_{\overline{\underline{x}}}^{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
. Given another endo-reduced expression
\underline{y}
for
w^{\beta}
, there is a unique isomorphism
B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
composed solely of cups, caps, and
2m
-valent vertices (with no coefficient).
This is a consequence of the 3-color relations and the Jones–Wenzl morphisms being trivial. In particular,
{}^{\beta}(-)
does not depend on the choice of endo-reduced expression up to natural isomorphism.
It then follows from this uniqueness that
{}^{\beta}({}^{\gamma}(-))\cong{}^{\beta\gamma}(-)
.

The following lemma can easily be checked from definitions.

Lemma 5.6.1
.

There are natural isomorphisms making the following diagram commute for each
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\circ},1)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\circ},1)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}^{\beta}(-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Upsilon_{\Abe}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}^{\beta}(-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Upsilon_{\Abe}}

Moreover, these natural transformations are compatible with respect to block composition.

We will construct a 2-category
\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W))
, called the
endoscopic Elias–Williamson diagrammatic 2-category
as follows.
The object set of
\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W))
is
\mathfrak{o}
.
The morphism category from
\mathcal{L}
to
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
of
\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W))
is given by
\bigoplus_{\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},\beta)
where
\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},\beta)\coloneq\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)
.
The vertical composition is induced from the composition in
\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},\beta)
. Let
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and
\gamma\in{}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}
.
We define the horizontal composition, denoted
\star
as the bifunctor

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},\beta)\times\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},\gamma)

\displaystyle=\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)\times\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\circ},1)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\id\times{}^{\beta}(-)}}{{\longrightarrow}}\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)\times\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\star}}{{\to}}\>_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},\beta\gamma).

Theorem 5.6.2

(Diagrammatic Monodromic-Endoscopic Equivalence)
.

There is an equivalence of 2-categories

\Psi^{\diag}:\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}).

Proof.

The same argument used in Theorem
3.5.10
using Lemma
5.6.1
shows that
\Upsilon_{\Abe}
gives rise to an equivalence of 2-categories

\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\mathcal{A}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W)).

The theorem then follows from the composition of 2-functors,

\mathcal{D}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\mathcal{A}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},M^{\mathfrak{o}}(W))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o}),

where the second morphism is Theorem
3.5.10
and the third morphism is Theorem
5.5.8
.
∎

Remark 5.6.3
.

There is no convenient diagrammatic description of the 2-functor in Theorem
5.6.2
.
We have constructed such a 2-functor in the dihedral case in Proposition
5.3.18
, but for a general Coxeter group, there is no obvious construction.

5.7.
Mixed Derived Categories

We will show using Theorem
5.5.4
that
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
is an object-adapted cellular category (OACC).
We can then use Appendix
B
to construct a mixed derived category for the diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category.
The study of these mixed derived categories will be a crucial component in the later proof of the monodromic Riche–Williamson theorem (see Theorem
7.8.1
).

5.7.1.
Object-Adapted Cellular Structure

In order to apply for formalism of Appendix
B
, we first must show that the diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category is an OACC.

Let
I\subseteq W
and
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
. We set

{}_{\mathcal{L}}I_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}\coloneq\{w\in I\mid\mathcal{L}w=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\}.

The Bruhat order on
W
restricts to a partial order on
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.
This induces an order topology on
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
from
W
. In particular, a subset
K\subset{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
is closed (resp. open) in
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
if and only if there exists a closed (resp. open) subset
I\subset W
such that
K={}_{\mathcal{L}}I_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.

Given
w\in W
, we write
\{\leq w\}
and
\{<w\}
for the closed subsets of
W
consisting of all elements
x\in W
such that
x\leq w
and
x<w
respectively.

Proposition 5.7.2
.

The diagrammatic monodromic Hecke category
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
is an OACC with the following data:

•

We fix a reduced expression
\underline{w}=\rex(w)
for each
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
. As a result, we can identify
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
with a subset
\Lambda
of objects in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
by
w\mapsto B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
The set
\Lambda
is a poset under the restricted Bruhat order in
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.

•

For any
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
and
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
, the sets
E(\underline{x},w)
and
\overline{E}(w,\underline{x})
are both equal to the set of
\mathcal{L}
-monodromic subexpressions of
\underline{x}
expressing
w

•

For any
w\in\Lambda
and
\underline{e}\in E(\underline{x},w)=\overline{E}(w,\underline{x})
, the maps
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
\overline{\LL}_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
are the light leaves which are taken so that
\underline{w}
is always the target (resp. domain).
We pick the
\LL
-datum such that
\LL_{\underline{w},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is the identity map when
\underline{e}
is the all 1’s subexpression.

•

The contravariant autoequivalence
\mathbb{D}(-)
is the functor which takes an Elias–Williamson graph to its horizontal reflection.

Proof.

The axioms (CC2) and (CC3) follow from definitions. Axiom (CC1) is a restatement of Theorem
5.5.4
. It remains to show that

\chi_{\leq w}\coloneq\Hom_{\leq w}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})

is a two-sided ideal.
By Proposition
4.7.11
and Theorem
5.5.8
, we have that
\chi_{\leq w}
consists of maps
f:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
such that
\left(\Upsilon(f)\right)(B_{\underline{x},Q}^{v,\mathcal{L}})=0
whenever
v\not\leq w
.
It is easy to check from the definition of morphisms in the algebraic category that these maps form a 2-sided ideal.
∎

Proposition
5.7.2
allows us to use the constructions of Appendix
B
.
We denote the mixed derived category for
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
by

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\coloneq D^{m}\left(\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\right).

These categories can be assembled into a 2-category over
\mathfrak{o}
, denoted
\>{}_{\backslash}D_{/}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

For
I\subseteq W
locally closed, we can also define

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{I/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\coloneq D^{m}_{{}_{\mathcal{L}}I_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}\left(\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\right).

5.7.3.
Generation Assumption

We will work towards showing that Assumption
B.5.3
holds for the mixed derived category of
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

Lemma 5.7.4

(
[
ARV20
, Lemma 6.1]
)
.

Let
\underline{x}
and
\underline{y}
be reduced expressions for an element
w\in W
.
Let
f:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be a rex move.
Then the cone of
f
belongs to
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{<w\}/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

Proof.

The proof can be copied almost verbatim from
[
ARV20
]
. We remark that the usage of
[
EW16
, Lemma 7.4]
and
[
EW16
, Lemma 7.5]
in
loc. cit.
should be replaced by Lemma
6.1.1
.
∎

Recall the
Hecke product
on
W
(see
[
BM15
]
).
3
3

3

This is also sometimes called in literature the Demazure product, the 0-Hecke product, or the greedy product.

Let
x\in W
,
s\in S
, define

x\star s\coloneq\begin{cases}xs&\text{if }xs>x,\\
x&\text{if }xs<x.\end{cases}

More generally, let
x,y\in W
and
y=s_{1}\ldots s_{k}
be any reduced expression for
y
.
Define the Hecke product of
x
and
y
is given by

x\star y=x\star s_{1}\star s_{2}\star\ldots\star s_{k}.

This does not depend on the choice of reduced expression for
y
and endows
W
with the structure of a monoid.
For
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
an expression, we write

\star\underline{w}\coloneq s_{1}\star\ldots\star s_{k}\in W.

Lemma 5.7.5

(
[
ARV20
, Lemma 6.2]
)
.

For any expression
\underline{w}\in\Exp(W)
, the object
B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
belongs to
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{\leq\star\underline{w}\}/\mathcal{L}\underline{w}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
Therefore, Assumption
B.5.3
holds for
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

Proof.

We argue by induction on
\ell(\underline{w})
. The claim is obvious when
\underline{w}
is reduced.
Write
\underline{w}=\underline{x}s
for some
s\in S
, and assume by induction the claim is known for all expressions of length
<\ell(\underline{w})
. In particular, the claim holds for
\underline{x}
.
We then must show that if
\underline{y}
is a reduced expression for some
y\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}\underline{w}s}
and
y\leq\star\underline{x}
, then
B_{\underline{y}s}^{\mathcal{L}}\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{\leq\star\underline{w}\}/\mathcal{L}\underline{w}}^{m,\diag}
.

If
\ell(\underline{y})<\ell(\underline{x})
, then
\ell(\underline{y}s)<\ell(\underline{w})
, so by induction
B_{\underline{y}s}^{\mathcal{L}}\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{\leq\star(\underline{y}s)\}/\mathcal{L}\underline{w}}^{m,\diag}
.
By
[
BM15
, Proposition 3.1]
, we have
\star(\underline{y}s)=y\star s\leq(\star\underline{x})\star s=\star\underline{w}
. The claim then follows.

Assume now that
\ell(\underline{y})=\ell(\underline{x})
. Then
\underline{x}
is a reduced expression, and hence,
y=\star\underline{x}
.
If
ys>y
, then
\star\underline{w}=(\star\underline{x})s
and
\underline{y}s
is a reduced expression for
\star\underline{w}
. The claim then follows from definitions.
If
ys<y
, choose a reduced expression
\underline{y}^{\prime}
for
y
ending with
s
and a rex move
\beta:B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
We can then consider the distinguished triangle

B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\beta}}{{\to}}B_{\underline{y}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to C\to,

where
C=\textnormal{cone}(f)
is in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{<y\}/\mathcal{L}y}^{m,\diag}
by Lemma
5.7.4
.
We can then apply
(-)\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
to produce a distinguished triangle

(5.7.1)

B_{\underline{y}s}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\beta\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}}}{{\to}}B_{\underline{y}^{\prime}s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to C\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to.

By induction, we have that
C\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{\leq\star w\}/\mathcal{L}\underline{w}}^{m,\diag}
.
If
\mathcal{L}ys=\mathcal{L}y
, then there is an isomorphism
B_{\underline{y}^{\prime}s}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong B_{\underline{y}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)\oplus B_{\underline{y}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}(-1)
(cf.,
[
EW16
, (5.14)]
).
Therefore,
B_{\underline{y}^{\prime}s}^{\mathcal{L}}\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{\leq y\}/\mathcal{L}\underline{w}}^{m,\diag}
.
If
\mathcal{L}ys\neq\mathcal{L}y
, then by block minimality, there is an isomorphism
B_{\underline{y}^{\prime}s}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong B_{\underline{y}^{\prime\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}
where
\underline{y}^{\prime\prime}
is the expression such that
\underline{y}^{\prime}=\underline{y}^{\prime\prime}s
.
Note
\star\underline{y}^{\prime\prime}=(\star\underline{y}^{\prime})=ys<y
.
As a result,
B_{\underline{y}^{\prime}s}^{\mathcal{L}}\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{\leq y\}/\mathcal{L}\underline{w}}^{m,\diag}
.
Therefore, (
5.7.1
) implies that
B_{\underline{y}s}^{\mathcal{L}}\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{\leq\star w\}/\mathcal{L}\underline{w}}^{m,\diag}
.
∎

5.7.6.
Convolution of Standards and Costandards

As discussed in §
B.5
, there is a theory of standard and costandard objects in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
In particular, for all
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
, there is an associated standard object and costandard object

\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\coloneq j_{{}_{\mathcal{L}}\{\leq w\}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}!}^{{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}j_{w!}^{{}_{\mathcal{L}}\{\leq w\}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}b_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\coloneq j_{{}_{\mathcal{L}}\{\leq w\}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}!}^{{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}j_{w*}^{{}_{\mathcal{L}}\{\leq w\}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}b_{w}^{\mathcal{L}},

where
b_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
is the canonical object in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{\{w\}/\mathcal{L}w}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
corresponding to
B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

Example 5.7.7
.

Let
s\in S
.

(1)

Note that
\{e\}
is closed in
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}}
. As a result, we have isomorphisms
\Delta_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\nabla_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

(2)

Assume
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
. In light of Example
B.4.5
and (
B.4.2
), the complex
\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
coincides with the complex

\ldots\to 0\to B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\epsilon^{s}}}{{\to}}B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)\to 0\to\ldots

where the nonzero terms are in degrees
0
and
1
respectively. Similarly, the complex
\nabla_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
is given by

\ldots\to 0\to B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}(-1)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eta^{s}}}{{\to}}B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to 0\to\ldots

where the nonzero terms are in degrees
-1
and
0
respectively.
We can then conclude that there are distinguished triangles

B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}\langle-1\rangle\to\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\qquad\text{and}\qquad B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\nabla_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}\langle 1\rangle\to.

(3)

Assume
\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}
. In this case,
\{s\}
is a closed subset of
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}s}
.
As a result, we have isomorphisms
\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\nabla_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

Lemma 5.7.8

(
[
ARV20
, Lemma 6.10]
)
.

Let
w\in W
and
s\in S
be such that
\mathcal{L}ws=\mathcal{L}w
and
ws>w
. Then there exist distinguished triangles

\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\langle-1\rangle\to\Delta_{ws}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\nabla_{ws}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\langle 1\rangle\to

in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}w}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
, in which the third arrows are generators of the free rank-1
\mathbbm{k}
-modules

\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}w}^{m,\diag}}(\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}},\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\langle-1\rangle[1])\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}w}^{m,\diag}}(\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\langle 1\rangle,\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}[1])

respectively.

Proposition 5.7.9

(
[
ARV20
, Proposition 6.11]
)
.

Let
w\in W
.

(1)

If
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
is a reduced expression for
w
, then we have isomorphisms

\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\Delta_{s_{1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\Delta_{s_{2}}^{\mathcal{L}s_{1}}\star\ldots\star\Delta_{s_{k}}^{\mathcal{L}s_{1}\ldots s_{k-1}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\nabla_{s_{1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\nabla_{s_{2}}^{\mathcal{L}s_{1}}\star\ldots\star\nabla_{s_{k}}^{\mathcal{L}s_{1}\ldots s_{k-1}}.

(2)

We have isomorphisms

\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\nabla_{w^{-1}}^{\mathcal{L}w}\cong B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\nabla_{w^{-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}w^{-1}}.

Proof.

We will prove the claims by induction on
\ell(w)
.
We can first prove (2) when
w=s\in S
. If
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
, then this follows from
[
AMRW17
, Lemma 4.2.4]
.
If
\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}
, then by Example
5.7.7
(3), we have that
\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\nabla_{s}^{\mathcal{L}s}\cong B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}s}
.
The claim then follows by the block minimality relation.
By induction, we then have that (2) follows from (1).

If
w
is minimal in
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
, then (1) follows from block minimality.
Write
{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{+}
for the subset of
W
containing elements
w
such that
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)>0
.
Assume the claim holds for all elements
x\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{+}
whose length is strictly smaller than that of
w
.
We will prove the first isomorphism in (1) for
w
. The second isomorphism follows from duality.
Let
(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
be a reduced expression for
w
. Set
x=s_{1}\ldots s_{k-1}
and
s=s_{k}
.
By induction, we have an isomorphism

\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\Delta_{s_{1}}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\Delta_{s_{2}}^{\mathcal{L}s_{1}}\star\ldots\star\Delta_{s_{k-1}}^{\mathcal{L}s_{1}\ldots s_{k-2}},

hence it suffices to prove that
\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}y}
. If
\mathcal{L}ys\neq\mathcal{L}y
, then this isomorphism follows from block minimality.
We can then assume that
\mathcal{L}ys=\mathcal{L}y
. By (2) for
y
, the functor

\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}\star(-):\>_{\mathcal{L}y\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}w}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}w}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

is an equivalence of triangulated categories with quasi-inverse
\nabla_{y^{-1}}^{\mathcal{L}y}
.
By applying
\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}\star(-)
and using Example
5.7.7
(2), we obtain a distinguished triangle

\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}y}\to\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}y}\to,

where the third arrow is a generator of the free rank-1
\mathbbm{k}
-module,
\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}w}^{m,\diag}}(\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}y},\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}y})
.
We can then apply Lemma
5.7.8
to deduce the isomorphism
\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}y}
as desired.
∎

5.7.10.
Right Equivariant Category

Let
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
. By Theorem
5.5.4
, we can define a category

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

obtained from
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
by applying
\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}(-)
to
\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
.
By Proposition
5.7.2
one can deduce that
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
is also an OACC with poset
{}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}W_{\mathcal{L}}
under the usual Bruhat order.
Note that the Hom spaces in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
are finitely generated free
\mathbbm{k}
-modules.
As a result, we can consider its mixed derived category

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\coloneq D^{m}\left(\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\right)

There is an “action” of
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
on
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}
. Namely, there are bifunctors

(-)\star(-):\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\times\>_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

which is suitably associative with respect to the horizontal composition in
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
This induces a bifunctor

(-)\star(-):\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\times\>_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

with similar properties.

There is an obvious functor

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{For}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})

which commutes with the recollement structure on both sides.
We abuse notation and view any object in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
as an object in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
via the functor
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{For}
.
It is easy to check that there is a natural isomorphism

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{For}(X\star Y)\cong\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{For}(X)\star Y

for all
X\in\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
and
Y\in\>_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

5.7.11.
Categorification

One application of the mixed derived category formalism is that it allows one to prove that the monodromic Hecke category categorifies the monodromic Hecke algebra without any constraint on
\mathbbm{k}
.
Without the mixed derived category, standard techniques (cf.,
[
EL16
,
EW16
]
) can be used to show this categorification result, but only when
\mathbbm{k}
is a complete local ring or a field.

Define a 2-category
\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
whose object set is
\mathfrak{o}
.
The 1-morphisms in
\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
are given by symbols
B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}(n)
where
\underline{w}\in\Exp(W)
and
n\in\mathbb{Z}
.
The 2-morphisms in
\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
from
B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}(m)
to
B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}(n)
are the 2-morphisms
B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
of degree
n-m
in
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
The horizontal and vertical compositions are those inherited from
\>{}_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
. Note that on morphism categories, using the notation of Appendix
B
,
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})=\left(\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})\right)^{\circ}
.
We will also consider the 2-category
\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
whose object set is
\mathfrak{o}
and whose morphism categories
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
are the additive hulls of
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.

Let
[\>_{\backslash}D_{/}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]_{\Delta}
denote the Grothendieck algebroid of
\>{}_{\backslash}D_{/}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
. In other words, it is the category whose object set is
\mathfrak{o}
and whose morphism spaces are given by taking the Grothendieck groups of
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
Similarly, let
[\>_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]
denote the split Grothendieck algebroid of
\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
. Explicitly,
[\>_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]_{\oplus}
is the category whose object set is
\mathfrak{o}
and whose morphism spaces are given by taking the split Grothendieck groups
[\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]_{\oplus}
.

Theorem 5.7.12
.

There exists a unique isomorphism of algebroids

\mathcal{H}^{\mon}(W,\mathfrak{o})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}[\>_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]_{\oplus}

sending
vH_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}
to
[B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)]
and
\underline{H}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
to
[B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}]
for any
s\in S
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
.

Proof.

By Lemma
B.6.1
, it suffices to prove that there exists a unique isomorphism

\mathcal{H}^{\mon}(W,\mathfrak{o})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}[\>_{\backslash}D_{/}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]_{\Delta}

sending
vH_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}
to
[B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)]
and
\underline{H}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
to
[B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}]
. Uniqueness is clear since
\mathcal{H}^{\mon}(W,\mathfrak{o})
is generated as a category by the morphisms
vH_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
\underline{H}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

We will now show that the assignment

vH_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}\mapsto[B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)],\qquad\qquad H_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\mapsto[\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}]

induces a functor
\mathcal{H}^{\mon}(W,\mathfrak{o})\to[\>_{\backslash}D_{/}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]_{\Delta}
.
By the defining relations for the monodromic Hecke algebroid it suffices to show the follow relations hold:

(5.7.2)

\displaystyle[\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}][\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}]

\displaystyle=[\Delta_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}]+[\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}(-1)]-[\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)]

\displaystyle s\in S\text{ and }\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L},

(5.7.3)

\displaystyle[\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}][\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}s}]

\displaystyle=\Delta_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}

\displaystyle s\in S\text{ and }\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L},

(5.7.4)

\displaystyle[\Delta_{xy}^{\mathcal{L}}]

\displaystyle=[\Delta_{x}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\Delta_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}]

\displaystyle x,y\in W\text{ such that }\ell(xy)=\ell(x)+\ell(y).

Here (
5.7.2
) and (
5.7.3
) follow from Example
5.7.7
along with the isomorphisms

B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\star B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}s}\cong\begin{cases}B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}(-1)\oplus B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)&\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L},\\
B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}&\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}.\end{cases}

On the other hand, (
5.7.4
) follows from Proposition
5.7.9
.
It is clear that this functor then takes
vH_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}
to
[B_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)]
and
\underline{H}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
to
[B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}]
.

It remains to check that the functor
\mathcal{H}^{\mon}(W,\mathfrak{o})\to[\>_{\backslash}D_{/}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]_{\Delta}
is an isomorphism.
By Proposition
B.6.2
, the standard objects
[\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}(m)]
for
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
and
m\in\mathbb{Z}
form a
\mathbb{Z}
-basis for
[\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]_{\Delta}
.
As a result, our functor takes a
\mathbb{Z}
-basis for
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mathcal{H}^{\mon}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(W,\mathfrak{o})
to a
\mathbb{Z}
-basis for
[\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})]_{\Delta}
.
∎

6.
Diagrammatic Double Leaves Span

In order to complete the proof of Theorem
5.5.4
, we must show that double leaves span.
The proof closely follows
[
EW16
, §7]
.
Since the proof is quite lengthy and involved, we will just outline the key statements and ideas when the arguments are virtually identical to
[
EW16
]
.

For the remainder of the section, we will work with embedded graphs rather than isotopy classes thereof.
We abuse terminology and use the term
monodromic Elias–Williamson graphs
to refer to a graph embedded without horizontal tangent lines so that no two vertices share the same
y
-coordinate.
It is convenient to assume that all monodromic Elias–Williamson graphs are embedded in the plane
\mathbb{R}\times[0,1]
such that
\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}
is the bottom of the graph and that
\mathbb{R}\times\{1\}
is the top of the graph.

6.1.
Negative-Positive Decompositions

Let
f
be a monodromic Elias–Williamson graph. We define the
height
of
f
, denoted
\textnormal{ht}(f)
as the number of generators needed to produce
f
(ignoring polynomials).
We also define the
width
of
f
at a
y
-coordinate
a\in[0,1]
(with no vertices on the line
y=a
), denoted
\text{width}_{a}(f)
, as the number of strands in
f
the line
y=a
passes through.
The
maxwidth
of
f
, denoted
\text{maxwidth}(f)
, is the maximal width attained by
f
.

Given a generator, we assign an integer called the
signed height
as follows.

(6.1.1)

+2
+1
+1
0
-1
-1
-2

More generally, the
negative height
of a graph is the number of negative generators used with multiplicities given by (
6.1.1
).
Similarly, the
positive height
is the number of positive generators used with multiplicities given by (
6.1.1
).
Note that the negative height and positive height of a map only depends on the underlying Elias–Williamson graph and not on the choice of face labelling by monodromy parameters.
Moreover, light leaves have positive height 0.

We call a graph
f:B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}

(non-)negative
(resp.
(non-)positive
) if
f
consists of solely (non-)negative (resp. (non-)positive) generators.
We say that
f
is
negative-positive
if it factors as
f=f_{2}\circ f_{1}
with
f_{2}
non-negative and
f_{1}
non-positive.
Furthermore, we call
f

strictly
negative-positive if
\text{width}_{a}(f)<\ell(\underline{w})
for some
a\in[0,1]
.

Given a morphism
f
in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W,\mathfrak{o})
, we say that
f
admits a
negative-positive decomposition
if it can be expressed as a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear combination of negative-positive graphs.
Similarly,
f
admits a
strictly
negative-positive decomposition if
f
can be expressed as a linear combination of strictly negative-positive graphs.

The following lemma is a compilation of results from
[
EW16
, §7.1]
which are generalized to the monodromic setting.

Lemma 6.1.1
.

(1)

Let
s,t\in S
with
m=m_{s,t}<\infty
. The monodromic Jones–Wenzl morphism admits a decomposition
\JW_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}=\id_{B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}}+f
where
f
has a strictly negative-positive whose terms have
\textnormal{width}_{a}\leq m-2
for
a\in(0,1)
.

(2)

Let
f:B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be a negative monodromic Elias–Williamson graph with
\underline{w}
reduced. Then
f
is in the span of maps with a bottom boundary dot.

(3)

If
\phi=fgh
for
f
non-negative,
h
non-positive, and
g
having a (strictly) negative-positive decomposition, then
\phi
has a (strictly) negative-positive decomposition.

(4)

Let
\underline{w}
and
\underline{w}^{\prime}
be rexes for
w\in W
. Let
\beta,\beta^{\prime}:B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be two rex moves. Then
\beta-\beta^{\prime}
has a strictly negative-positive decomposition.

(5)

Let
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
. Then
\id_{\underline{x}}
has a negative-positive decomposition which factors through some reduced expression
\underline{w}
for some
w
such that there exists a subsequence
\underline{e}
of
\underline{x}
with
\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=w
.

Proof.

(1):
Note that endosimple expansion takes negative (resp. positive) graphs to negative (resp. positive) graphs.
Similarly,
\tau:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS,\tau}(\mathfrak{h},\{s,t\},\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/-}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},\{s,t\},\mathfrak{o})
takes negative (resp. positive) graphs to negative (resp. positive) graphs.
Let
s^{\prime},t^{\prime}
denote the endosimple reflections in
W_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
If
g
is an Elias–Williamson graph viewed as a morphism in
\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},\{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\},1)
, then for all
a\in(0,1)
,

\displaystyle 2

\displaystyle\leq\text{maxwidth}(g)-\text{width}_{a}(g)

\displaystyle\leq\text{maxwidth}(\iota(g))-\text{width}_{a}(\iota(g))

\displaystyle=\text{maxwidth}(\tau(\iota(g)))-\text{width}_{a}(\tau(\iota(g))).

As a result, it follows from
[
EW16
, Claim 7.1]
that
\JW_{s,t}^{\mathcal{L}}=(\tau\circ\iota)(\JW_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}^{1})
has the desired properties.

(2):
The key idea is to apply the Jones–Wenzl relation which we proved in Lemma
5.3.15
. The argument then precedes as in
[
EW16
, Claim 7.2]
.

(3):
This is a restatement of
[
EW16
, Claim 7.3]
. It is obvious from definitions.

(4):
The argument is essentially the same as
[
EW16
, Lemma 7.4]
. The only substantial difference is that in the monodromic setting, one has to check that in type
B_{3}
with endoscopic type
A_{3}
, the additional terms appearing in the 3-color relations are in the lower terms ideal. This is easy to verify by hand.

(5):
One additional case is required other than those covered in
[
EW16
, Lemma 7.5]
. When
\underline{x}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k})
with
s_{i}=s_{i+1}
. We must consider both
i\in K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
and
i\notin K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
.
In the former case, the argument given in
loc. cit.
transfers. When
i\notin K(\underline{x},\mathcal{L})
, the claim follows from the block minimality relation.
∎

6.2.
Modulo Lower Terms

Let
\underline{w}
be a reduced expression for some
w\in W
.
We define an ideal under vertical composition

I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\subseteq\bigoplus_{\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)}\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}\underline{x}}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}})

consisting of
f\in\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}\underline{x}}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}})
which has a decomposition
f=f_{1}\circ f_{2}
where
f_{1}
is positive.
Lemma
6.1.1
implies that
I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is generated by all the top boundary dots.
From this description, it is obvious that when
w=w^{\beta}
for some block
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
, then
I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}=0
.

The following proposition is the monodromic analogue of
[
EW16
, Proposition 7.6]
.

Proposition 6.2.1
.

Let
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
. Fix a reduced expression
\underline{w}
for some element
w\in W
.
Choose a map
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
for each monodromic subexpression
\underline{e}
expressing
w
.
These maps form a left
R
-basis for
\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}w}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}})/I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

The proof of Proposition
6.2.1
will take substantial work.
As a corollary, we will complete the proof of Theorem
5.5.4
. The proof of Theorem
5.5.4
from the above proposition follows from the argument given in
[
EW16
, §7.3]
.
We have included it only for the sake of completeness.

Proof of Theorem
5.5.4
assuming Proposition
6.2.1
.

Fix
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
, and let
\varphi:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be a morphism.
By Lemma
5.5.5
, it suffices to show that
\varphi
is an
R
-linear combination of double leaves.

By Lemma
6.1.1
(5), we may assume, without loss of generality, that
\varphi
factors through some
B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
where
\underline{w}
is a reduced expression.
We can then write
\varphi=fg
with
g:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
f:B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.
We will prove the statement by induction on
\ell(\underline{w})
. If
\ell(\underline{w})=0
or more generally if
\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{w})=0
, then the claim follows from Proposition
6.2.1
using the observation that
I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}=0
.

By Proposition
6.2.1
, we can write
g=g_{w}+g_{l}
and
f=f_{w}+f_{l}
where
g_{w}
(resp.
f_{w}
) is an
R
-linear combination of
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
(resp.
\overline{\LL}_{\underline{y},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
) and
g_{l}\in I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
(resp.
f_{l}\in I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
).
It then suffices to prove that
\psi g_{l}
is in the span of the double leaves for any
\psi
. The argument with
f_{l}
is the same but horizontally reflected.

Now
g_{l}\in I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
so it is generated by top boundary dots, and we can further factor
g_{l}
into terms generated by a single top boundary dot. In particular,
\psi g_{l}
is of the form

\psi
??
\{
g_{l}

Let
\underline{z}
denote the expression obtained from
\underline{w}
by deleting the index with the dot above.
We then see that
\psi g_{l}
factors through
B_{\underline{z}}^{\mathcal{L}}
. By Lemma
6.1.1
(5), we can further factor
\psi g_{l}
through reduced expressions for elements
v
found in subexpressions of
\underline{z}
.
Observe that
v<w
, so we can now apply induction on
\psi g_{l}
to deduce that
\psi g_{l}
is in the span of double leaves.

\square

6.3.
The Inductive Setup

Up until now, we have fixed an
\LL
-datum required to construct a set of light leaves.
For the proof of Proposition
6.2.1
, it will be essential to let this data vary.
We will denote the set of
\LL
-data by
\Delta
.
To manage the notation, we will write
\delta\in\Delta
and denote the corresponding triple by
\delta=(\rex^{\delta},\{\rex_{s}^{\delta}\}_{s\in S},\{\Gamma_{\underline{x},\underline{y}}^{\delta}\}_{\underline{x},\underline{y}})
.
Similarly, for
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
and
\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x})
, we will write
{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
for the light leaf constructed from the choice of
\delta
.

Let
\hat{X}_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\coloneq\{{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}\mid\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x}),\delta\in\Delta\}
viewed as a subset of
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}\underline{x}}
.
There is a map
\For_{\textnormal{poly}}:{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}\underline{x}}\to{}_{\mathcal{L}}\mu\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Gr}_{\mathcal{L}\underline{x}}
given by forgetting the polynomial labels of an Elias–Williamson graph.
We denote
X_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}=\For_{\textnormal{poly}}^{-1}\hat{X}_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
, i.e., the set of all possible light leaf constructions with domain
B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
along with arbitrary polynomial decorations.

For
M\geq 0
, we consider the following two statements.

(L_{M})

Let
\delta\in\Delta
. Every map
B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
of maxwidth
\leq M
is in the left
R
-span of
\{{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}\}_{\underline{x}^{\underline{e}}=\underline{w}}
modulo
I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

(X_{M})

Every map
B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
of maxwidth
\leq M
is in the left
\mathbbm{k}
-span of
X_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
modulo
I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

It is clear that
(L_{M})
implies
(X_{M})
. The inductive argument to prove Proposition
6.2.1
then comes in two main steps: (1) prove that
(X_{M})
and
(L_{M-1})
implies
(L_{M})
, and (2) prove that
(L_{M})
implies
(X_{M+1})
.

If
M=0
, then a map has maxwidth 0 only when the underlying Elias–Williamson graph consists only of polynomial boxes.
As a result,
(L_{0})
and
(X_{0})
trivially hold.

We will now assume that
M>0
.
Assume that
\ell(\underline{w})=M
. If
\ell(\underline{x})<M
, then we can apply induction. As a result, we can also assume that
\ell(\underline{x})=M
.
It can be argued as in
[
EW16
, §7.4]
, that one can reduce to the case of a map
f:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
consisting solely of
2m
-valent vertices and polynomials.
By polynomial forcing and the Elias–Jones–Wenzl relations, we can move all polynomials to the left at the cost of potentially introducing lower terms.
It then suffices to replace
f
by a map where the polynomials are removed.
Note that for a single fixed light leaf
\LL={}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
(where
\underline{e}
is the all 1’s subexpression),
\LL
consists solely of
2m
-valent vertices.
By Lemma
6.1.1
(4), the difference of
f
and
\LL
is contained in the lower terms ideal.
In particular,
f
is in the span of
\LL
, modulo
I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
. Therefore,
(L_{M})
and likewise
(X_{M})
holds for
\underline{w}
.
As a result, we may assume that
\ell(\underline{w})<M
.

6.4.
(X_{M})
and
(L_{M-1})\implies(L_{M})

Before proceeding with the proof, we introduce the notion of light leaves with “errors”.
Let
\underline{x}\in\Exp(W)
,
\underline{e}\in\Subexp^{\mathcal{L}}(\underline{x})
, and
\delta\in\Delta
.
Given a map
E:B_{\underline{w}_{j}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}_{j}}^{\mathcal{L}}
which is strictly negative-positive, we can define a map
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{E,\mathcal{L}}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
,
called the
light leaf with error

E
, via the same algorithm as light leaves in §
5.5.1

except we replace
\phi_{i}
by a map
\phi_{i}^{\prime}
which is defined by
\phi_{i}^{\prime}=\phi_{i}
if
i\neq j
and
\phi_{j}^{\prime}=E\circ\phi_{j}
.
We denote the set of all light leaves with errors whose domain is
B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
by
\hat{X}_{\underline{x}}^{\textnormal{er},\mathcal{L}}
.

Lemma 6.4.1
.

Fix
\delta\in\Delta
.

(1)

Let
\LL\in\For_{\textnormal{poly}}^{-1}({}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}})
. Then
\LL-{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is in the span of
\hat{X}_{\underline{x}}^{\textnormal{er},\mathcal{L}}
modulo
I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}

(2)

Let
\delta^{\prime}\in\Delta
. Then
{}^{\delta^{\prime}}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}-{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is in the span of
\hat{X}_{\underline{x}}^{\textnormal{er},\mathcal{L}}
modulo
I_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

Proof.

For (1), polynomial forcing implies that the cost of sliding a polynomial across a rex move is adding at most an error term.
We can then force all polynomials to the left, modulo lower terms to show that
\LL-{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is in the lower terms ideal.

For (2), recall from Lemma
6.1.1
(4) that the difference between two rex moves is an error.
As a result, if
{}^{\delta^{\prime}}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
differ only in the choice of rex moves, then
{}^{\delta^{\prime}}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}-{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is spanned by lower terms.
If
{}^{\delta^{\prime}}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
instead differs from the choice of
\rex_{s}(w_{k})
for some
k
, we can account for the difference using rex moves as well.
Namely, we can replace the identity of
B_{\rex_{s}^{\delta}(w_{k})}^{\mathcal{L}}
appearing in a light leaf with a rex move
gf
where
g:B_{\rex_{s}^{\delta^{\prime}}(w_{k})}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\rex_{s}^{\delta}(w_{k})}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
f:B_{\rex_{s}^{\delta}(w_{k})}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\rex_{s}^{\delta^{\prime}}(w_{k})}^{\mathcal{L}}
are rex moves.
Then
f
can be absorbed into the rex move in
\phi_{k}
, and
g
can be absorbed into the rex move in
\phi_{k+1}
.
Combining both cases, we may conclude that
{}^{\delta^{\prime}}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}-{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is a linear combination of lower terms.
∎

Fix some
\delta_{0}\in\Delta
.
Let
\LL\in X_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
, so
\For_{\textnormal{poly}}(\LL)={}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
for some
\delta\in\Delta
.
By Lemma
6.4.1
, we have that the difference between
\LL
and
{}^{\delta_{0}}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is in the span of light leaves with errors.
As a result, it suffices to prove that
{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{E,\mathcal{L}}
is in the span of
\{{}^{\delta_{0}}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}\}_{\underline{f}}
modulo lower terms.

Let
\LL_{M-1}
denote the partially constructed light leaf with error map
{}^{\delta}\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{E,\mathcal{L}}
after
M-1
steps.
Now
\LL_{M-1}
has maxwidth
M-1
, so we may apply induction and replace
\LL_{M-1}
with a
\LL
map of our choosing or with a term having dots on top.

If the error occurs at the last step, then by Lemma

6.5.
(L_{M-1})\implies(X_{M})

Fix a reduced expression
\underline{w}
with
\ell(\underline{w})<M
. We will prove that
(L_{M-1})

(X_{M})
for
\underline{w}
.
Let
f:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be a diagram of maxwidth
M
(the case of maxwidth
<M
is covered by induction).

Convention 6.5.1
.

\LL
U1

\mathcal{L}
.

\underline{e}

e_{i}
over the

6.5.2.
Attaching Negative Generators

Lemma 6.5.3
.

Suppose a negative (merging) trivalent vertex is added below a light leaf. The result is a light leaf.

Proof.

Suppose that a new trivalent vertex is attached to the
k
-th strand. Then we must have that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}_{\leq k}=\mathcal{L}\underline{x}_{\leq k-1}
.
The result then follows from the same argument given in
[
EW16
, Claim 7.9]
.
∎

Lemma 6.5.4
.

Suppose a negative (bottom) dot is added below a light leaf yielding a map from
B_{\underline{x}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}
for some
\underline{x}^{\prime}\in\Exp(W)
. The result is in
X_{\underline{x}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

Proof.

Suppose that a new boundary dot colored by some
s\in S
is added after the
k
-th strand.
Then we must have that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}_{\leq k}s=\mathcal{L}\underline{x}_{\leq k}
.
The result then follows from the same argument given in
[
EW16
, Claim 7.10]
.
∎

Lemma 6.5.5

\LL
\LL

1

6.5.10.
Attaching a

-valent Vertex

The last major component we need to complete the proof of Proposition

-valent vertex below a light leaf is in the span of light leaves modulo lower terms.

Lemma 6.5.11
.

Assume
(L_{M-1})
. Let
f:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}
be in
X_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
such that
\ell(\underline{x})\leq M
.
If we add a
2m
-valent vertex below

to obtain a map from
B_{\underline{x}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}
for some
\underline{x}^{\prime}\in\Exp(W)

modulo

.

The non-monodromic variant of Lemma
6.5.11
is
[
EW16
, Claim 7.13]
.
Our proof is quite different from
[
EW16
]
. In fact, there is a subtle error in the proof provided by Elias–Williamson.
The general strategy is to reduce to the case of
W
being a dihedral group.
From here, Elias–Williamson appeal to the calculations of morphisms spaces done in
[
Eli16
]
using Soergel’s categorification theorem.
Unfortunately,
[
Eli16
]
crucially imposes additional constraints on realizations, namely that of “lesser invertibility” and “local non-degeneracy”.
These constraints are much stronger than the rather relaxed constraints on realizations imposed in
[
EW16
]
or in this work.
Our proof constitutes a corrected proof of
[
EW16
, Claim 7.13]
by taking
\mathfrak{o}=1
.

<k

Lemma 6.5.15
.

6.5.13
holds for a fixed
l\geq 0
. Let
\ell(\underline{x})=l+m
.
Then every light leaf
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
is in the span of morphisms of the form

\beta
\LL_{\underline{x}^{\prime},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}
1
1
1

modulo
I_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

Proof.

By Claim
6.5.13
, the following map

\beta
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
1
1
1

is in the span of
X_{\underline{x}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}
modulo
I_{\underline{x}^{\prime}}^{\mathcal{L}}
(where
\underline{x}^{\prime}
is the expression obtained by applying a braid relation at the end of
\underline{x}
).
We can then attach another
2m
-valent vertex under the right most
m
-strands and apply the Elias–Jones–Wenzl relation to complete the proof.
∎

Proof of Claim
6.5.13
.

By Lemma
6.5.14
, we can reduce to the case where
\underline{x}
is of the form
{}_{u}\underline{n}
and
n=l+m
.
We will then argue by induction on
l\geq 0
. To keep notation and pictures concise, we will always assume that
\underline{x}={}_{u}\underline{n}
ends in
t
.
Before proceeding with the induction, we can make a useful observation. Without loss of generality, we may assume that
\underline{e}
has no decorations of the form
U0
.
Indeed, if
\underline{e}
has a decoration of
U0
over the
2m
-valent vertex, then the Jones–Wenzl relations reduce the computation to checking whether adding a non-neutral generator below a light leaf is in the span of light leaves modulo lower terms.
These have already been shown in §
6.5.6
and §
6.5.10
.

If
l=0
, then
\underline{x}=\underline{m}_{t}
. Since we only consider
\underline{e}
with no
U0
decorations, it easily follows that
\underline{e}
must be decorated solely by
U1
’s.
In this case,
\LL_{\underline{x},\underline{e}}^{\mathcal{L}}
composed with a
2m
-valent vertex is simply a series of compositions of
2m
-valent vertices.
The base case then follows from successive applications of the Elias–Jones–Wenzl relation.

Now assume that
l>0
. Write
\underline{e}=\underline{e}_{\leq n-1}e_{n}
.
By Lemma
6.5.15
and induction, we may replace
\LL_{\underline{x}_{\leq n-1},\underline{e}_{\leq n-1}}^{\mathcal{L}}
by

(6.5.4)

\beta
\LL_{\underline{y},\underline{f}}^{\mathcal{L}}

where
\underline{f}
is a subexpression of
\underline{y}
such that
\underline{f}
is decorated by
U1
for all
1\leq i\leq l-1
.
There are 5 possible cases for the pair
(\dec_{n}(\underline{e}),\dec_{n-1}(\underline{f}))
which avoids a
U0
decoration on
\underline{e}
: (
D1
,
U1
), (
D1
,
D0
), (
D0
,
U1
), (
D0
,
D0
), and (
U1
,
U0
).
Throughout our case-by-case analysis, we will often abuse notation and write
\LL_{k}
to refer to a light leaf of maxwidth
k
.

\dec_{n}(\underline{e})=D1
and
\dec_{n-1}(\underline{f})=U1
.

Here we are using that since the domain of the light leaf on the LHS of the first
equation ends in
t
and the codomain of the rex move ends in
t
, we can pull the
trivalent vertex through the rex move and the light leaf at the cost of some lower
terms. The third equality follows from 2-color associativity. The result then
follows from induction and Lemma
6.5.3
.

\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}\underline{x}_{\leq n-1}
and write
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{x}
. Recall that using Demazure surjectivity, we have fixed
\delta=\delta_{t}\in R
such that
\partial_{t}(\delta)=1
.

The first equality follows from the splitting of

(cf.,
[

, 5.15]
).
The second and third equalities both use polynomial forcing. The first two summands of the RHS are in the span of light leaves by induction and Lemma

.
