7.7.
Verifying Relations

In order to check that
\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{O}}
is well-defined, one must check that the image of a morphism under
\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{O}}
is invariant under the defining relations in
\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{O}},W,\mathfrak{o})
.
By
[
San25
, Lemma 3.6.5]
and Theorem
5.5.4
, it suffices to check this after extending scalars to
\mathbb{K}
-coefficients.
Write
\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{K}}
for the extension of
\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{O}}
along
\mathbb{O}\to\mathbb{K}
.
By composing with
\mathbb{H}
and using Theorem
7.5.8
, we can further reduce to checking that the following diagram strictly commutes

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{K}},W,\mathfrak{o})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\>{}_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}^{\BS}(G,\mathbb{K},\mathfrak{o})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{A}_{/}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{K}},W,\mathfrak{o})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{K}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Upsilon_{\Abe}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{H}}

We can now calculate the image of the generating 2-morphisms under
\mathbb{H}
.

(1)

Polynomials:

\mathbb{H}(\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{K}}(f))
for
f\in R_{\mathbb{K}}
is given by multiplication by
f
on
R_{\mathbb{K}}
.

(2)

The upper dot:
Let
s\in S
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
such that
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
.
Any morphism of graded
R_{\mathbb{K}}
-bimodules
C_{s}\to R_{\mathbb{K}}(1)
is a scalar multiple of
\epsilon^{s}:C_{s}\to R_{\mathbb{K}}(1)
.
Recall from (
7.5.1
) that there is a unique morphism
\xi_{s}:\Theta_{\circ}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}[-1]
such that
(\epsilon_{s}[-1])\circ\xi_{s}=\epsilon_{\mathcal{L}}
.
Moreover, by Lemma
7.5.3
,
\xi_{s}
identifies with
u_{s}\in C_{s}
under the isomorphism
\mathbb{H}(\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}})\cong C_{s}
.
Similarly, by Lemma
7.5.2
,
\epsilon_{\mathcal{L}}
identifies with
1\in R
under the isomorphism
\mathbb{H}(\IC_{e}^{\mathcal{L}})\cong R
.
As a result, the relation
(\epsilon_{s}[-1])\circ\xi_{s}=\epsilon_{\mathcal{L}}
becomes
(\mathbb{H}(\epsilon_{s}))(u_{s})=1
. Hence,
\mathbb{H}(\epsilon_{s})=\epsilon^{s}
.

(3)

The lower dot:

Let
s\in S
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
such that
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
.
The map

\IC_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}[-1]=j_{e*}j_{e}^{!}\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eta_{s}}}{{\to}}\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\epsilon_{s}}}{{\to}}j_{e*}j_{e}^{*}\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}[1]\in\Hom(\IC_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}[-1],\IC_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}[1])\cong H_{T}^{2}(\pt;\mathbb{K})

is given by
\lambda\cdot\id_{\IC_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}[-1]}
for some
\lambda\in H_{T}^{2}(\pt;\mathbb{K})
.
Let
L_{s}
be the rank 1 Levi subgroup of
G
corresponding to
s
and write
j:T\hookrightarrow L_{s}
for the inclusion.
Since
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
, there is a unique multiplicative local system
\mathcal{L}^{s}
on
L_{s}
which extends
\mathcal{L}
.
There is an isomorphism of varieties
\widetilde{\mathcal{F}\ell}_{\leq s}\cong U_{s}\backslash L_{s}
where
U_{s}=U\cap L_{s}
.
Under this isomorphism, the simple perverse sheaf
\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
is canonically identified with
\mathcal{L}^{s}
.
We can then see under this isomorphism and adjunction that the natural morphism of
(T\times T,\mathcal{L}\boxtimes\mathcal{L}^{-1})
-equivariant sheaves

(7.7.1)

\mathcal{L}[-1]=j^{!}\mathcal{L}^{s}[1]\to j^{*}\mathcal{L}^{s}[1]=\mathcal{L}[1]

is given by
\lambda\cdot\id_{\mathcal{L}[-1]}
.
After applying
(-)\otimes^{L}\mathcal{L}^{-1}
to (
7.7.1
), we see that the natural morphism of
T\times T
-equivariant sheaves

\underline{\mathbb{K}}_{T}[-1]=j^{!}\underline{\mathbb{K}}_{L_{s}}[1]\to j^{*}\underline{\mathbb{K}}_{L_{s}}[1]=\underline{\mathbb{K}}_{T}[1]

is also given by
\lambda\cdot\id_{\underline{\mathbb{K}}_{T}[-1]}
. It then follows from the non-monodromic case (cf.,
[
RW18
, §10.5]
) that
\lambda=\alpha_{s}
, and as a result,
\mathbb{H}(\epsilon_{s}\circ\eta_{s})=\alpha_{s}
.
Note that
\eta^{s}
is uniquely determined by
\epsilon^{s}\circ\eta^{s}=\alpha_{s}
. As a consequence, we deduce from the upper dot computation that
\mathbb{H}(\eta_{s})=\eta^{s}
.

(4)

Cups and caps:
Let
s\in S
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
such that
\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}
. Let
\beta\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}s}
be the block containing
s
.
By Lemma
7.4.6
, there is a commutative diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Theta_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Theta_{\mathcal{L}}^{\beta}\star\Theta_{\mathcal{L}s}^{\beta^{-1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}s}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\epsilon_{\mathcal{L}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nu}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\epsilon_{\beta}\star\epsilon_{\beta^{-1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cup_{s}}

By Lemma
7.5.2
, under the canonical isomorphisms
\mathbb{H}(\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\star\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}s})\cong(R_{\mathbb{K}})_{s}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}(R_{\mathbb{K}})_{s}
and
\mathbb{H}(\mathcal{E}_{\varnothing}^{\mathcal{L}})\cong R_{\mathbb{K}}
, the above diagram translates to the condition that
\mathbb{H}(\cup_{s})(u_{(s,s)})=1
.
Therefore,
\mathbb{H}(\cup_{s})=\cup^{s}
. Since
\cap_{s}
is the inverse of
\cup_{s}
, we must also have that
\mathbb{H}(\cap_{s})=\cap^{s}
.

(5)

The trivalent vertices:
Let
s\in S
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
such that
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
. We have isomorphisms of vector spaces

\Hom(C_{s},C_{s}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}C_{s}(-1))\cong\mathbb{K}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Hom(C_{s}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}C_{s},C_{s}(-1))\cong\mathbb{K}.

These morphism spaces are generated by the maps
\nu^{s}:C_{s}\to C_{s}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}C_{s}(-1)
and
\mu^{s}:C_{s}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}C_{s}\to C_{s}(-1)
respectively. Therefore,
\mathbb{H}(\nu_{s})
(resp.
\mathbb{H}(\mu_{s})
) is a scalar multiple of
\nu^{s}
(resp.
\mu^{s}
).
Note that
\nu^{s}
(resp.
\mu^{s}
) is uniquely characterized by the identity

(\epsilon^{s}(-1)\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}\id_{C_{s}})\circ\nu^{s}=\id_{C_{s}}\qquad\text{resp.}\qquad\mu^{s}(1)\circ(\eta^{s}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}\id_{C_{s}})=\id_{C_{s}}.

Therefore,
\mathbb{H}(\nu_{s})=\nu^{s}
and
\mathbb{H}(\mu_{s})=\mu^{s}
follow from the upper and lower dot computations and the Frobenius algebra structure on
\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
.

Computing the image of the
2m_{s,t}
-valent vertices takes some work. Let
s,t\in S
be distinct simple reflections and let
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
. Denote the longest element in
\langle s,t\rangle
by
w={}_{s}m={}_{t}m
.
We will write
d=\ell_{\mathcal{L}}(w)
and denote the block in
{}_{\mathcal{L}}\underline{W}_{\mathcal{L}w}
containing
w
by
\beta
.
Recall from §
4.6
that we have morphisms

\epsilon^{{}_{u}\underline{m}}:B_{{}_{u}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to(R_{\mathbb{K}})_{w^{\beta}}(d)

for
u\in\{s,t\}
.
By Lemma
4.6.3
(2),
\beta_{s,t}
is the unique morphism of Bott–Samelson bimodules such that there is an equality of maps

(7.7.2)

\mathbb{K}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}(\epsilon^{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ\beta_{s,t})=\mathbb{K}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}\epsilon^{{}_{s}\underline{m}}:\mathbb{K}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\mathbb{K}(d).

Lemma 7.7.1
.

The constants
c_{s,t},c_{t,s}\in\mathbb{O}
defined by (
7.6.2
) satisfy

c_{s,t}c_{t,s}=1.

Proof.

It follows from the definitions of
g_{s,t}
and
g_{t,s}
that

g_{s,t}\circ g_{t,s}\circ g_{s,t}=g_{s,t}.

Applying
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{For}(\epsilon_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ(-))
both sides and using (
7.6.2
), we deduce that

c_{s,t}c_{t,s}c_{s,t}=c_{s,t}
, or alternatively that
c_{s,t}(c_{t,s}c_{s,t}-1)=0
.

It remains to prove that
c_{s,t}\neq 0
.
Since
g_{s,t}
is a generator for
\Hom(\mathcal{E}_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}},\mathcal{E}_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}})
, it suffices to show that the map

\displaystyle\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}}(G,\mathbb{O})}(\mathcal{E}_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}},\mathcal{E}_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}})

\displaystyle\to\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/{\mathcal{L}}}(G,\mathbb{O})}(\mathcal{E}_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}},\IC_{w^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}}[d])

\displaystyle f

\displaystyle\mapsto\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{For}(\epsilon_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ f)

is nonzero. It suffices to prove that this map is nonzero after applying
\mathbb{K}(-)
.

Let
f:\mathcal{E}_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\mathcal{E}_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}
. By the upper dot relation we have already verified and (
7.5.4
), we have a commutative diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom(\mathcal{E}_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}},\mathcal{E}_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom(\mathcal{E}_{\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}},\IC_{w^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}}[d])}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}w}(G,\mathbb{K})}(\mathcal{E}_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}},\IC_{w^{\beta}}^{\mathcal{L}}[d])}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom(B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom(B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}},(R_{\mathbb{K}})_{w^{\beta}}(d))}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom_{\textnormal{mod}^{\mathbb{Z}}\textnormal{-}R_{\mathbb{K}}}(\mathbb{K}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}},\mathbb{K}(d))}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{H}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\epsilon_{{{}_{t}\underline{m}}}\circ f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{H}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{For}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tilde{\mathbb{H}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\epsilon^{{{}_{t}\underline{m}}}\circ\mathbb{H}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{K}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}(-)}

By Theorem
7.5.8
and Corollary
7.5.9
, it suffices to prove that

\mathbb{K}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}(\epsilon^{{}_{s}\underline{m}}\circ\varphi)\neq 0
for some
\varphi:B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}}
, but the existence of such a morphism follows from Lemma
4.6.3
.
∎

We can now compute the image of the
2m_{s,t}
-valent vertices.

5.

2m_{s,t}
-valent vertices:
Let
m=m_{s,t}
.
By our definition for
f_{s,t}
and Lemma
7.7.1
, we have
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{For}(\epsilon_{{}_{t}\underline{m}}\circ f_{s,t})=\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{For}(\epsilon_{{}_{s}\underline{m}})
.
We can now apply
\tilde{\mathbb{H}}
and use (
7.5.4
) to deduce that

\mathbb{K}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}\tilde{\mathbb{H}}(\epsilon_{{}_{t}\underline{m}})\circ\tilde{\mathbb{H}}(f_{s,t})=\mathbb{K}\otimes_{R_{\mathbb{K}}}\tilde{\mathbb{H}}(\epsilon_{{}_{s}\underline{m}}).

Since
\tilde{\mathbb{H}}(\epsilon_{{}_{u}\underline{m}})=\epsilon^{{}_{u}\underline{m}}
for
u\in\{s,t\}
, we conclude from Lemma
4.6.3
(2) that
\mathbb{H}(f_{s,t})=\beta_{s,t}
.
By a symmetric argument, we also have that
\mathbb{H}(f_{t,s})=\beta_{t,s}

As a result, we have 2-functors

\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{O}}:\>_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{O}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}^{\BS}(G,\mathbb{O},\mathfrak{o})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{K}}:\>_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{K}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}^{\BS}(G,\mathbb{K},\mathfrak{o}).

Since all the relevant Hom spaces in are graded free
R
-modules (Theorem
5.5.4
and
[
San25
, Lemma 3.6.3]
), we can extend scalars from
\mathbb{O}
to
\mathbb{F}
to produce a 2-functor

\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}:\>_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{F}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}^{\BS}(G,\mathbb{F},\mathfrak{o}).

7.8.
Monodromic Riche–Williamson Theorem

Theorem 7.8.1
.

Let
\mathbbm{k}\in\{\mathbb{K},\mathbb{O},\mathbb{F}\}
and
\mathfrak{o}\subseteq\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k})
be a
W
-orbit. The 2-functor

\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}:\>_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}^{\BS}(G,\mathbbm{k},\mathfrak{o})

is an equivalence of 2-categories.

Remark 7.8.2
.

We expect that it should be possible to construct
\Upsilon_{\textnormal{RW}}^{\mathbbm{k}}
when
G
is a Kac–Moody group which extends the neutral block equivalence from
[
San25
, Theorem 5.3.1]
.
The main problem is that
\IC_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
for
\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}
has no canonical representative and the Whittaker model is too large to rigidify these choices.

Remark 7.8.3
.

Theorem
5.6.2
and Theorem
7.8.1
can be combined to give another proof of the monodromic-endoscopic equivalence for the geometric Hecke categories of parity sheaves (
[
San25
, Theorem 5.11.1]
).

Remark 7.8.4
.

(1)

While Theorem
7.8.1
is only stated for
\mathbbm{k}\in\{\mathbb{K},\mathbb{O},\mathbb{F}\}
, it is easy to deduce a version for
\mathbbm{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
or
\mathbbm{k}=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}
.
In these cases, the torsion constraint on
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
ensures that we can find some
\ell
-modular triple
(\mathbb{K},\mathbb{O},\mathbb{F})
such that
\mathcal{L}
(as well as any member of its
W
-orbit) descends to an
\mathbb{O}
-local system along either the morphism
\mathbb{O}\to\mathbb{K}\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
or
\mathbb{O}\to\mathbb{F}\to\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}
.
From here, one can apply extension-of-scalars to deduce the
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\ell}
- and
\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{\ell}
-variants from Theorem
7.8.1
.

(2)

Instead of taking
\mathfrak{o}
to be a
W
-orbit in
\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k})
, we could instead take
\mathfrak{o}=\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k})
. In this generality, Theorem
7.8.1
still holds.
This can be easily deduced from the decomposition of
\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k}))
and
\>{}_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}^{\BS}(G,\mathbbm{k},\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k}))
into sub-2-categories,

\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k}))\cong\bigsqcup_{W\text{-orbits }\mathfrak{o}\subseteq\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k})}\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\mathfrak{o}),

\>{}_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}^{\BS}(G,\mathbbm{k},\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k}))\cong\bigsqcup_{W\text{-orbits }\mathfrak{o}\subseteq\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k})}\>{}_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}^{\BS}(G,\mathbbm{k},\mathfrak{o}).

We will prove Theorem
7.8.1
using the same strategy invoked in
[
San25
, Theorem 5.3.1]
.
It is clear from its definition that
\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}
is a bijection on 0- and 1-morphisms.
Therefore, we only need to show that the induced functor on morphism categories

\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(G,\mathbbm{k})

is fully faithful.

Define a category
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\mathfrak{o})
obtained from
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\mathfrak{o})
by applying
\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R_{\mathbbm{k}}}(-)
to the graded Hom spaces.
This category is well-defined by Theorem
5.5.4
.
By Theorem
5.5.4
and
[
San25
, Lemma 3.6.3]
, the functor
\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}
induces a functor

\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\textnormal{Par}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(G,\mathbbm{k}).

Along the way towards proving Theorem
7.8.1
, we will prove the following result.

Proposition 7.8.5
.

Let
\mathbbm{k}\in\{\mathbb{K},\mathbb{O},\mathbb{F}\}
and
\mathfrak{o}\subseteq\Ch^{\mu}(T,\mathbbm{k})
be a
W
-orbit. For all
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
, the functor

\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\textnormal{Par}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(G,\mathbbm{k})

is an equivalence of categories.

7.8.6.
Reduction to Fields

We will prove that
\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}
and
\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}
are equivalences assuming the following special case.

Claim 7.8.7
.

\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}
is an equivalence.

We delay the proof of Claim
7.8.7
until §
7.8.8
.

Proof of Proposition
7.8.5
assuming Claim
7.8.7
.

Let
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
and
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
.
Consider the morphism of free
\mathbb{O}
-modules of finite rank

\alpha:\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{O}},W,\mathfrak{o})}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}(n))\to\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\textnormal{Par}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(G,\mathbb{O})}(\mathcal{E}_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},\mathcal{E}_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}[n])

given by
\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{O}}
.
By the Nakayama lemma,
\alpha
is an isomorphism if and only if
\mathbb{F}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\alpha
is an isomorphism.
Note that by definition,
\mathbb{F}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\alpha
is induced by
\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}
. We then have that
\mathbb{F}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\alpha
is an isomorphism by Claim
7.8.7
.
Finally, we deduce the full faithfulness of
\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{K}}
from
\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{O}}
by extension-of-scalars.

\square

Proof of Theorem
7.8.1
assuming Proposition
7.8.5
.

Let
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
and
\underline{x},\underline{y}\in\Exp(W)
such that
\mathcal{L}\underline{x}=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}\underline{y}
.
Consider the morphism of graded left
R_{\mathbbm{k}}
-modules

\beta:\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbbm{k}},W,\mathfrak{o})}^{\bullet}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})\to\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\BS}(G,\mathbbm{k})}^{\bullet}(\mathcal{E}_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},\mathcal{E}_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})

given by
\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}
.
As graded left
R_{\mathbbm{k}}
-modules, the left-hand side of
\beta
is free of finite rank by Theorem
5.5.4
and the right-hand side of
\beta
is free of finite rank by
[
San25
, Lemma 3.6.3]
.
By the graded Nakayama lemma, to show that
\beta
is an isomorphism it suffices to show that
\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R_{\mathbbm{k}}}\beta
is an isomorphism.
Note that
\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R_{\mathbbm{k}}}\beta
is the map induced from
\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbbm{k}}
.
It follows from Proposition
7.8.5
that
\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R_{\mathbbm{k}}}\beta
is an isomorphism.

\square

7.8.8.
Mixed Derived Categories

Our goal is to prove Claim
7.8.7
. This will be proved by first passing to mixed derived categories.
Let
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
.
We consider the geometrically-defined biequivariant and right equivariant mixed derived categories,

\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\geom}(G,\mathbb{F})\coloneq K^{b}\>_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(G,\mathbb{F})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\geom}(G,\mathbb{F})\coloneq K^{b}\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\textnormal{Par}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(G,\mathbb{F}).

These categories were introduced in
[
San25
, §3.9]
.
They share many similar features to the mixed derived category of §
5.7
.
In particular, there are standard objects
\underline{\Delta}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
and costandard objects
\underline{\nabla}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
defined for any
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.

The geometrically-defined biequivariant mixed derived categories can be assembled into a 2-category
\>{}_{\backslash}D_{/}^{m,\geom}(G,\mathbb{F},\mathfrak{o})
with object set
\mathfrak{o}
and morphism categories from
\mathcal{L}
to
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}
given by
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\geom}(G,\mathbb{F})
.
The 2-functor
\Upsilon_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}:\>_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{F}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\textnormal{Par}_{/}(G,\mathbb{F},\mathfrak{o})
induces a 2-functor

\underline{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}:\>_{\backslash}D_{/}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{F}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}D_{/}^{m,\geom}(G,\mathbb{F},\mathfrak{o}).

Lemma 7.8.9
.

For all
w\in W
and
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
, there are isomorphisms

\underline{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}(\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}})\cong\underline{\Delta}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\underline{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}(\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}})\cong\underline{\nabla}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}.

Proof.

We will just prove the first isomorphism. The second isomorphism follows from a similar argument.
By 2-functorality of
\underline{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}
, Proposition
5.7.9
, and
[
San25
, Proposition 3.9.6]
, it suffices to consider the case of
s\in S
.

The case when
\mathcal{L}s\neq\mathcal{L}
is obvious since
\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}=B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
\underline{\Delta}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}=\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
, so we may assume that
\mathcal{L}s=\mathcal{L}
.
In
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}D_{/\mathcal{L}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{F}},W,\mathfrak{o})
there is a distinguished triangle

(7.8.1)

\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\Delta_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)\to.

We can then apply
\underline{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}
to (
7.8.1
) to produce a distinguished triangle

(7.8.2)

\underline{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}\left(\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\right)\to\mathcal{E}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\underline{\Delta}_{e}^{\mathcal{L}}(1)\to,

where the second map is given by the unit map
\id\to j_{e*}j_{e}^{*}
in the non-mixed category.
Since
j_{x}^{*}\mathcal{E}_{x}^{\mathcal{L}}=0
for all
x\notin\{e,s\}
, the distinguished triangle (
7.8.2
) coincides with the open-closed distinguished triangle for the pair (
\widetilde{\mathcal{F}\ell}_{e},\widetilde{\mathcal{F}\ell}\setminus\widetilde{\mathcal{F}\ell}_{e}
).
As a result, we have produced an isomorphism
\underline{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}\left(\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}\right)\cong\underline{\Delta}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
as desired.
∎

Let
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}
.
The functor
\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{D}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{F}},W,\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}\textnormal{Par}_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(G,\mathbb{F})
induces a functor

\underline{\tilde{\Upsilon}}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}:\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}(\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb{F}},W)\to\>_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\geom}(G,\mathbb{F})

By Lemma
7.8.9
, we also have isomorphisms

(7.8.3)

\underline{\tilde{\Upsilon}}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}(\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}})\cong\underline{\Delta}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\underline{\tilde{\Upsilon}}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}(\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}})\cong\underline{\nabla}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}

for all
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
and
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.

Proof of Claim
7.8.7
.

It suffices to show that
\underline{\tilde{\Upsilon}}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}
is fully faithful.
Let
\mathcal{L}\in\mathfrak{o}
and
x,y\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
.
By Lemma
B.5.6
, we have that

(7.8.4)

\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\diag}}(\Delta_{x}^{\mathcal{L}},\nabla_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}(m)[n])\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb{F}&\text{if }x=y\text{ and }n=m=0,\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Similarly, by
[
San25
, Lemma 2.3.4]
, we have an isomorphism

(7.8.5)

\Hom_{\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\mathbin{\fatbslash}}D_{/\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}^{m,\geom}(\mathbb{F})}(\underline{\Delta}_{x}^{\mathcal{L}},\underline{\nabla}_{y}^{\mathcal{L}}(m)[n])\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb{F}&\text{if }x=y\text{ and }n=m=0,\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}.

In view of this, (
7.8.3
), and Beĭlinson’s lemma (
[
ABG04
, Lemma 3.9.3]
), it suffices to prove that for all
w\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}
, there exists a morphism
f:\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
such that
\underline{\tilde{\Upsilon}}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}(f):\underline{\Delta}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\underline{\nabla}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
is nonzero.

Let
\underline{w}\in\Exp(W)
be a reduced expression of
w
.
By Proposition
5.7.9
and the chain complex description of
\Delta_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
(resp.
\nabla_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
) for
s\in S
(Example
5.7.7
), the complex
\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
(resp.
\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
) is isomorphic to a complex
\mathcal{F}_{\underline{w}}^{\diag,\mathcal{L}}
(resp.
\mathcal{G}_{\underline{w}}^{\diag,\mathcal{L}}
)
such that

(\mathcal{F}_{\underline{w}}^{\diag,\mathcal{L}})^{n}=\begin{cases}B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}&n=0,\\
0&n<0,\end{cases}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(\mathcal{G}_{\underline{w}}^{\diag,\mathcal{L}})^{n}=\begin{cases}B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}&n=0,\\
0&n>0.\end{cases}

Similarly, by
[
San25
, Proposition 3.9.6]
and the chain complex description of
\underline{\Delta}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
(resp.
\underline{\nabla}_{s}^{\mathcal{L}}
) for
s\in S
(
[
San25
, (3.9.1)]
), the complex
\underline{\Delta}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
(resp.
\underline{\nabla}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
) is isomorphic to a complex
\mathcal{F}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}}
(resp.
\mathcal{G}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}}
)
such that

(\mathcal{F}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}})^{n}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{E}_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}&n=0,\\
0&n<0,\end{cases}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(\mathcal{G}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}})^{n}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{E}_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}&n=0,\\
0&n>0.\end{cases}

Consider the map
f:\Delta_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\to\nabla_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}
defined by the morphism of chain complexes

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\vdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\vdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\mathcal{F}_{\underline{w}}^{\diag,\mathcal{L}})^{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\mathcal{G}_{\underline{w}}^{\diag,\mathcal{L}})^{-1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\vdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\vdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}

Under the isomorphisms
\underline{\Delta}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\mathcal{F}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}}
and
\underline{\nabla}_{w}^{\mathcal{L}}\cong\mathcal{G}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}}
, the map
\mathcal{F}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}}\to\mathcal{G}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}}
induced by
\underline{\tilde{\Upsilon}}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}(f)
corresponds to the chain map given by

(\mathcal{F}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}})^{0}=\mathcal{E}_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\id}}{{\to}}\mathcal{E}_{\underline{w}}^{\mathcal{L}}=(\mathcal{G}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}})^{0}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(\mathcal{F}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}})^{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 0}}{{\to}}(\mathcal{G}_{\underline{w}}^{\geom,\mathcal{L}})^{n}

for all
n\neq 0
.
In particular,
\underline{\tilde{\Upsilon}}_{\RW}^{\mathbb{F}}(f)
is nonzero.

\square

Appendix A
Three-Color Relations

This appendix serves to fill in the details needed to complete the proof of Claim
5.4.10
.
The goal is to verify the three-color relations need to construct the functor

\Upsilon_{\Abe}:\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/}(W,\mathfrak{h},\mathfrak{o})\to\>_{\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\BS}(W,\mathfrak{h},\mathfrak{o}).

We will first explain the general strategy. We assume that
W
is a rank 3 finite Coxeter group.
Let
\Gamma_{L}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
\Gamma_{R}:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
denote the (linear combinations of) monodromic Elias–Williamson graphs for the left and right sides of a 3-color relation, respectively.
Note that by definition
\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{L})
and
\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{R})
both take 1-tensors to 1-tensors. As a result, if the space of degree 0 homomorphisms
\Hom_{\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\BS}}(B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}})
is a rank 1
\mathbbm{k}
-module, then we are done.
It turns out that this happens in almost every case with the following exceptions:

(Case 1)

In type
A_{3}
, when
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}=W
, the degree 0 Hom space has rank 2.

(Case 2)

In type
B_{3}
, when
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}=W
, the degree 0 Hom space has rank
\rk_{\mathbbm{k}}(\mathfrak{h})+68
.

(Case 3)

In type
B_{3}
, when
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is type
A_{3}
, the degree 0 Hom space has rank 3.

(Case 4)

In type
H_{3}
, when
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}=W
, the degree 0 Hom space has rank

\begin{bmatrix}\rk_{\mathbbm{k}}(\mathfrak{h})+3\\
4\end{bmatrix}+34\begin{bmatrix}\rk_{\mathbbm{k}}(\mathfrak{h})+2\\
3\end{bmatrix}+578\begin{bmatrix}\rk_{\mathbbm{k}}(\mathfrak{h})+1\\
2\end{bmatrix}+6644\rk_{\mathbbm{k}}(\mathfrak{h})+71160.

Cases 1 and 2 follow from the well-definedness of the Soergel functor in the non-monodromic setting. This was already proved using localization in
[
EW16
]
.
Case 4 is omitted by Assumption
5.4.1
.
As a result, the only case that requires a meaningful amount of work is Case 3.

In this section, we will first explain how we can enumerate all the possible labelings of
\Gamma_{L}
and
\Gamma_{R}
by monodromy parameters.
It is impossible to enumerate all the
W
-sets; however, we only have to restrict our attention to the small subset which may appear on a given Elias–Williamson graph.
Given a monodromic Elias–Williamson graph
\Gamma:B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathcal{L}}
, the relations in the Hecke category only depend on whether two adjacent faces are labelled the same along an edge.
As a result, we will be able to iterate over labelings of the faces of an Elias–Williamson graph where we only keep track of whether faces are equal or not.
This gives us a finite parameter space.

Next, we will use this parameter space to compute the rank of the degree 0 Hom spaces for types
A_{3},B_{3}
, and
H_{3}
using a case-by-case analysis on the parameter space and the defect formula (Corollary
4.5.3
).
Using the argument given earlier, this computation will show that
\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{L})=\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{R})
in all of these cases except when
W
is of type
B_{3}
and
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
is of type
A_{3}
.
We will then handle this case separately. We will use the algebraic monodromic-endoscopic equivalence (Proposition
3.5.7
) to handle this case.

Finally, in types
A_{1}\times I_{2}(m)
, since there are infinitely many cases, we are unable to give an exhaustion of the parameter space. Instead, we will appeal to a Coxeter theoretic argument to show using the defect formula that the degree 0 Hom spaces are rank 1.

The computations in this appendix crucially rely on computer assisted computation. The author has implemented the necessary algorithms in Python and SageMath– the code can be found here:

(A.0.1)

https://github.com/colton5007/Monodromic-Three-Color-Relations

It includes the exhaustion of the monodromy parameter spaces and the defect calculations used to compute the rank of the degree 0 Hom spaces.

A.1.
Finding Possible Cases

Definition A.1.1
.

Let
\Gamma
be an Elias–Williamson graph.
Let
\mathcal{F}
be a subset of the faces of
\Gamma
.
A
\mathcal{F}
-partial monodromy labeling
of an Elias–Williamson graph
\Gamma
is a surjective map

c:\mathcal{F}\twoheadrightarrow\{1,\ldots,n\}

for some
n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}
such that for all
F\in\mathcal{F}
and
G_{1},G_{2}\in\mathcal{F}
faces adjacent to
F
, if the edge separating
F
and
G_{1}
and the edge separating
F
and
G_{2}
are both colored by some
s\in S
, then
c(G_{1})=c(G_{2})
.

Two
\mathcal{F}
-partial monodromy labelings
c,c^{\prime}:\mathcal{F}\to\{1,\ldots,n\}
are said to be equivalent if there exists a permutation
\sigma
of
\{1,\ldots,n\}
such that
\sigma\circ c^{\prime}=c
.
We write
\lvert c\rvert=n
and say that
n
is the
number of parameters
for
c
.
If
\mathcal{F}
is the set of all faces of
\Gamma
, then we say that
c
is a
complete monodromy labeling
.

Of course, any monodromic Elias–Williamson graph automatically comes equipped with a complete monodromy labeling.
It is not always the case that a complete monodromy labeling arises via a group action
W
on
\{1,\ldots,n\}
.
Nonetheless, a complete monodromy labeling of an Elias–Williamson graph is enough to determine the monodromic subexpressions of the domain and codomain.
In particular, a complete monodromy labeling is sufficient for computing right-hand side of the defect formula (Corollary
4.5.3
) even if the left-hand side is not well-defined.

The following algorithm provides a means of computing the parameter space of complete monodromy labelings.

Algorithm A.1.2
.

Let
\Gamma
be an Elias–Williamson graph.
Let
F_{1},\ldots,F_{n}
be an enumeration of the faces of
\Gamma
. Define
\mathcal{F}_{i}=\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{i}\}
for each
1\leq i\neq n
.

(1)

There is a unique
\mathcal{F}_{1}
-partial monodromy labeling
c_{1}
taking
F_{1}
to
1
. Define
P_{1}=\{c_{1}\}
.

(2)

Recursively, assume we have defined the set
P_{i}
of
\mathcal{F}_{i}
-partial monodromy labelings.
For each
c\in P_{i}
and
1\leq j\leq\lvert c\rvert+1
, we can attempt to define a
\mathcal{F}_{i+1}
-partial monodromy labeling
c^{\prime}
by extending
c
on
\mathcal{F}_{i}
and labeling
F_{i+1}
by
j
.

We will then check that
c^{\prime}
is a valid partial monodromy labeling as follows.
We iterate through each
1\leq k\leq i+1
and each pair of adjacent faces
F,F^{\prime}
of
F_{k}
such that the edges separating
F_{k}
from
F
and
F^{\prime}
are both colored by
s
.
If
F,F^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}_{i+1}
and
c^{\prime}(F)\neq c^{\prime}(F^{\prime})
, then
c^{\prime}
is not a valid partial monodromy labeling and can be discarded from consideration. Otherwise, continue until all such
k
and pairs
(F,F^{\prime})
are checked.
If the process completes without
c^{\prime}
being rendered invalid, then
c^{\prime}
is a valid
\mathcal{F}_{i+1}
-partial monodromy labeling.

We then define a list
P_{i+1}
consisting of the
\mathcal{F}_{i+1}
-partial monodromy labelings produced as above.

(3)

After
n
iterations, the above procedure produces a set
P_{n}
consisting of complete monodromy labelings.

It is not hard to check that every complete monodromy labeling (up to equivalence) arises via Algorithm
A.1.2
.
We keep the notation from the above.
Given a complete monodromy labeling
c:\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{n}\}\twoheadrightarrow\{1,\ldots,k\}
, we can replace
c
by an equivalent complete monodromy labeling such that
c(F_{i})\leq\max_{1\leq j\leq i-1}(c(F_{j})+1)
.
Let
c_{i}
be the
\mathcal{F}_{i}
-partial monodromy labeling obtained by restricting
c
to
\mathcal{F}_{i}
.
It is clear that
\mathcal{F}_{1}\in P_{1}
. Arguing by induction, if
c_{i}\in P_{i}
, then our condition that
c(F_{i})\leq\max_{1\leq j\leq i-1}(c(F_{j})+1)
ensures that
c_{i+1}\in P_{i+1}
.

Remark A.1.3
.

Algorithm
A.1.2
is not very optimized. It is quick enough for the purposes of the present work, but grows quite quickly as the number of faces and size of
W
increases.
The algorithm’s efficiency also highly depends on choice of face enumeration. When choosing an enumeration at the
(i+1)
-st step, it is best to choose a face adjacent to the first
i
faces with maximal valence.

A.2.
Types
A_{3}
,
B_{3}
, and
H_{3}

While Algorithm
A.1.2
is sufficient for labeling one diagram, we actually need to label two diagrams simultaneously, both
\Gamma_{L}
and
\Gamma_{R}
.
To handle this, we will simply apply the algorithm to the horizontal concatenation
\Gamma_{R}^{\prime}\star\Gamma_{L}
where
\Gamma_{R}^{\prime}
is the horizontal reflection of
\Gamma_{R}
.

(1)

In type
A_{3}
, there are 30 complete monodromy labelings of
\Gamma_{L}
and
\Gamma_{R}
.

(2)

In type
B_{3}
, there are 98 complete monodromy labelings of
\Gamma_{L}
and
\Gamma_{R}
.

(3)

In type
H_{3}
, there are 164 complete monodromy labelings of
\Gamma_{L}
and
\Gamma_{R}
.

As discussed before, one can compute the graded ranks of the Hom spaces in which
\Gamma_{L}
and
\Gamma_{R}
reside using Corollary
4.5.3
and the code provided in (
A.0.1
).
All these graded ranks are 1 except in 3 cases: the non-monodromic cases in type
A_{3}
and
B_{3}
and the monodromic case in type
B_{3}
where the endoscopic group has type
A_{3}
. When the graded rank of the Hom space is 1, then the
1
-tensor argument from before is enough to show that
\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{L})=\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{R})
.
The non-monodromic cases in type
A_{3}
and
B_{3}
follow from the non-monodromic case considered in
[
EW16
]
.
As a result, we only have to check one case (type
B_{3}
with endoscopic type
A_{3}
) which is depicted below.

(A.2.1)

-\frac{1}{a_{t,s}}
+\frac{1}{a_{s,utu}}
Type
B_{3}
with Endoscopic Type
A_{3}
=

To show that
\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{L})=\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{R})
in this case, we will appeal to algebraic endoscopy. Let
w_{0}
denote the longest element of
W
.
Note that
\mathcal{L}w_{0}\neq\mathcal{L}
. Instead,
w_{0}\in{}_{\mathcal{L}}W_{\mathcal{L}w_{0}}
is in the block containing
u
.
By Proposition
3.5.7
, it suffices to show that

\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg}\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{L}\star\id_{B_{u}^{\mathcal{L}w_{0}}})=\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg}\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma_{R}\star\id_{B_{u}^{\mathcal{L}w_{0}}}).

We will compute the left-hand side and right-hand side separately.

We fix an endosimple expansion datum
\iota
as follows:
s^{\prime}=utu
,
t^{\prime}=s
, and
u^{\prime}=t
.
For each Elias–Williamson graph
\Gamma
appearing in (
A.2.1
) the strategy for computing
\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg}\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma\star\id_{B_{u}^{\mathcal{L}w_{0}}})
will be the same.
First, we will construct an Elias–Williamson graph
\Gamma^{\prime}
for the endoscopic Coxeter group
W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
.
We will then compute
\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg,-1}(\Gamma^{\prime}):M\to N
after fixing 1-tensor preserving isomorphisms
M\cong B_{\iota(\underline{x}^{\prime})}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
N\cong B_{\iota(\underline{y}^{\prime})}^{\mathcal{L}}
where
\underline{x}^{\prime}=(t^{\prime},u^{\prime},t^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},u^{\prime})
and
\underline{y}^{\prime}=(s^{\prime},t^{\prime},u^{\prime},t^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime})
.
Consider the monodromic Elias–Williamson graphs

Via
\Upsilon_{\Abe}
, these give rise to isomorphisms
\xi_{\underline{x}u,\iota(\underline{x}^{\prime})}:B_{\underline{x}u}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}B_{\iota(\underline{x}^{\prime})}^{\mathcal{L}}
and
\xi_{\underline{y}u,\iota(\underline{y}^{\prime})}:B_{\underline{y}u}^{\mathcal{L}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}B_{\iota(\underline{y}^{\prime})}^{\mathcal{L}}
in
\>{}_{\mathcal{L}\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/\mathcal{L}}^{\oplus}
.
We will then show that

\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma)=\xi_{\underline{y}u,\iota(\underline{y}^{\prime})}^{-1}\circ\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg,-1}(\Gamma^{\prime})\circ\xi_{\underline{x}u,\iota(\underline{x}^{\prime})}.

This will allow us to check the 3-color relation holds after using endoscopy to transfer the relation to a relation in
\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/1}^{\oplus}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)
.

We will use morphisms in the Elias–Williamson diagrammatic category
\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)
to denote morphisms in
\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{A}_{/1}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)
.
This is justified by
[
Abe21
, Theorem 5.6]
.

The following examples are illustrative and will be used in the proof.

A simple rank computation using Corollary
4.5.3
shows that

\rk_{\mathbbm{k}}\Hom_{\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\oplus}}(B_{(s,u,t,u,s)}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{(u,t,u,s,u,t,u)}^{\mathcal{L}})=1.

Moreover,
\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma)
and
\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg,-1}(\Gamma^{\prime})
both preserve 1-tensors. As a result, we must have that
\Upsilon_{\Abe}(\Gamma)=\Psi_{\mathcal{L}}^{\alg,-1}(\Gamma^{\prime})
.

There are two remaining monodromic Elias–Williamson graphs in (
A.2.1
) that must also be considered. The arguments are entirely similar to the two graphs considered previously and will be omitted.
We conclude that there are equalities of morphisms
B_{\underline{x}u}^{\mathcal{L}}\to B_{\underline{y}u}^{\mathcal{L}}
in

It then suffices to show the following equality holds in
\>{}_{1\backslash}\mathcal{D}_{/1}^{\BS}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ},1)
,

(A.2.2)

-\frac{1}{a_{u^{\prime},t^{\prime}}}
=
+\frac{1}{a_{t^{\prime},s^{\prime}}}

Equation (

) can be checked using the Zamolodchikov relation and the Elias–Jones–Wenzl relation for
A_{3}
.

]
.

A.3.
Type
A_{1}\times I_{2}(m)

Any reflection subgroup of a product of Coxeter groups can be written as a product of reflection subgroups of the individual factors.
As a result, the possible reflection subgroups of the Coxeter group of type
A_{1}\times I_{2}(m)
are of the following types:
A_{1}\times I_{2}(v)
and
I_{2}(v)
where
0\leq v\leq m
divides
m
(by definition, we take
I_{2}(0)=1
and
I_{2}(1)=A_{1}
).
Since
\Upsilon_{A}(\Gamma_{L})
and
\Upsilon_{A}(\Gamma_{R})
both take 1-tensor to 1-tensors, the desired relation will follow from the following lemma.

Lemma A.3.1
.

Write
S=\{s,t,u\}
where
m_{s,t}=m
,
m_{s,u}=2
, and
m_{t,u}=2
.
The
\mathbbm{k}
-module of degree 0 homomorphisms

\Hom_{\>{}_{\backslash}\!\!{}^{\circ}\mathcal{A}_{/}^{\BS}}(B_{{}_{s}\underline{m}u}^{\mathcal{L}},B_{u{}_{t}\underline{m}}^{\mathcal{L}})

is rank 1.

Proof.

Let
w_{0}
denote the maximal element in
W
.
By Corollary
4.5.3
, it suffices to show that for all proper (i.e., not all 1’s)
\mathcal{L}
-monodromic subexpressions
\underline{e}
of
{}_{s}\underline{m}u
and
\underline{f}
of
u{}_{t}\underline{m}
that

d({}_{s}\underline{m}u,\underline{e})+d(u{}_{t}\underline{m},\underline{f})>0
.
We will show something even stronger, namely, that

d({}_{s}\underline{m}u,\underline{e})>0\qquad\text{and}\qquad d(u{}_{t}\underline{m},\underline{f})>0.

We will just show the first inequality as the other follows from a similar argument.
Note that
\dec_{1}({}_{s}\underline{m}u,\underline{e})=\dec_{m+1}(u{}_{t}\underline{m},\underline{f})
and can only be equal to
U1
or
U0
.
Let
\underline{e}^{\prime}=\underline{e}_{\geq 2}
which is a subexpression of
{}_{s}\underline{m}
.
A simple computation for dihedral groups shows that
d({}_{s}\underline{m},\underline{e}^{\prime})\geq 0
with equality if and only if
\underline{e}^{\prime}
is the all 1’s expression.
We are then done unless
\underline{e}^{\prime}
is the all 1’s subexpression. Since we are assuming that
\underline{e}
is proper, this means that
e_{1}=U0
which implies that
d({}_{s}\underline{m}u,\underline{e})>0
.
∎

Appendix B
Mixed Derived Categories

Achar–Riche–Vay introduced a mixed derived category associated to the Elias–Williamson diagrammatic Hecke category
[
ARV20
]
.
Their mixed derived category was later used in
[
RV24
]
to extend the Koszul duality equivalence of
[
AMRW19
]
to arbitrary Coxeter groups.
One of the main reasons for studying the mixed derived category is that it comes equipped with a recollement formalism.
This gives rise to a theory of standard and costandard objects which generate the mixed derived category. Moreover, the Hom spaces between standards and costandards are simple to compute.

In fact, most of the constructions in
[
ARV20
]
hold in larger generality. Namely, the key properties used are about the double leaves basis.
We can then generalize their construction to produce a mixed derived category for any object-adapted cellular category.
The principal goal of this section is to develop this theory with two key examples in mind: (1) the category of monodromic Bott–Samelson bimodules and (2) the monodromic diagrammatic Hecke category.
We omit many of the proofs in this section and refer to
[
ARV20
]
for detailed arguments.

B.1.
Object-Adapted Cellular Categories

Object-adapted cellular categories were first introduced in
[
EL16
]
. A gentle treatment of the subject can be found in
[
EMTW20
]
whose terminology we closely follow.

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be a noetherian domain of finite global dimension.
Let
R
be a graded commutative ring such that
R^{0}\cong\mathbbm{k}
.

Definition B.1.1
.

An
object-adapted cellular category
6
6

6

In
[
EL16
]
, these are called strictly object-adapted cellular categories.
(abbv. OACC) is a graded
R
-linear category
\mathcal{C}
equipped with the following data:

•

There is a set
\Lambda
of objects of
\mathcal{C}
and a partial order
\leq
on
\Lambda
.

•

There is an
R
-linear contravariant involution
\mathbb{D}
on
\mathcal{C}
.

•

For each
X\in\mathcal{C}
and each
\lambda\in\Lambda
, there are two finite families

(\LL_{T})_{T\in E(X,\lambda)}\subset\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,\lambda)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(\overline{\LL}_{S})_{S\in\overline{E}(\lambda,X)}\subset\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(\lambda,X)

of homogenous morphisms, indexed by finite sets
E(X,\lambda)
and
\overline{E}(\lambda,X)
.

•

For each object
X\in\mathcal{C}
and
\lambda\in\Lambda
, there are pairwise inverse maps between the indexing sets
E(X,\lambda)
and
\overline{E}(\lambda,X)
that we denote by
\overline{\>\cdot\>}
in either direction.

This data is subject to the following requirements:

(CC1)

Define
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{S,T}^{\lambda}\coloneq\overline{LL}_{S}\circ\LL_{T}\in\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)
for
T\in E(X,\lambda)
and
S\in\overline{E}(\lambda,Y)
.
Consider the family

\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}^{\lambda}(X,Y)\coloneq\{\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{S,T}^{\lambda}\colon T\in E(X,\lambda),S\in\overline{E}(\lambda,Y)\}\subseteq\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y).

Then the family
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}(X,Y)\coloneq\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}^{\lambda}(X,Y)
is a graded
R
-basis of
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)
.

(CC2)

For all
T\in E(X,\lambda)
, we have that
\mathbb{D}(\LL_{T})=\overline{\LL}_{\overline{T}}
.

(CC3)

For each
\lambda\in\Lambda
, the sets
E(\lambda,\lambda)
and
\overline{E}(\lambda,\lambda)
are just singletons
\{*\}
and

\LL_{*}=\id_{\lambda}=\overline{\LL}_{*}.

(CC4)

For each
\lambda\in\Lambda
, the collection of morphisms

\Hom_{\leq\lambda}(X,Y)\coloneq\textnormal{span}_{R}\left(\bigcup_{\mu\leq\lambda}\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}^{\mu}(X,Y)\right)\subset\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)

forms a two-sided ideal
\mathcal{C}_{\leq\lambda}
in
\mathcal{C}
, i.e., it is stable under pre- and post-composition with arbitrary morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
.

Definition B.1.2
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an object-adapted cellular category. A map
\pi:\Ob(\mathcal{C})\to\Lambda
is called an
evaluation
if

(1)

\lambda\leq\pi(X)
whenever
E(X,\lambda)\neq\varnothing
,

(2)

\pi(\lambda)=\lambda
for all
\lambda\in\Lambda
.

An object
X\in\mathcal{C}
is said to be
reduced
with respect to
\pi
if

(1)

E(X,\pi(X))
is a singleton
\{*\}
,

(2)

the coefficient of
\id_{\pi(X)}
in
\LL_{*}\circ\overline{\LL}_{*}
is 1.

Remark B.1.3
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an object-adapted cellular category with evaluation
\pi
.

(1)

For all
\lambda\in\Lambda
, by (
), we have that
\lambda
is reduced.

(2)

If
X,Y
are reduced and
\pi(X)=\lambda=\pi(Y)
, then there is a unique map
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}^{\lambda}:X\to Y
in
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}^{\lambda}(X,Y)
.

B.2.
Homological Algebra Preliminaries

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a graded
R
-linear category.
We can define a category
\mathcal{C}^{\circ}
whose objects are symbols
X(n)
where
X\in\Ob(\mathcal{C})
and
n\in\mathbb{Z}
, and whose morphisms are defined by

\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ}}(X(n),Y(m))\coloneq\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}^{m-n}(X,Y).

We will also define a graded
R
-module

\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ}}^{\bullet}(X(n),Y(m))\coloneq\bigoplus_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ}}(X(n),Y(m+k))=\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y)(m-n).

The category
\mathcal{C}^{\circ}
admits a natural autoequivalence
(1):\mathcal{C}^{\circ}\to\mathcal{C}^{\circ}
defined by
X(n)\mapsto X(n+1)
.
For
j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, we can define
(j)
as the
j
-th power of
(1)
whose inverse is denoted by
(-j)
.
We define
\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}
as the additive hull of
\mathcal{C}^{\circ}
. It inherits a grading shift autoequivalence
(n)
for each
n\in\mathbb{Z}
from
\mathcal{C}^{\circ}
.

We can view
R
as a graded
R
-linear category itself with one object
*
. Observe that
R^{\circ}
is a monoidal category with
*(n)\otimes*(m)=*(n+m)
.
Note that the additive hull of
R^{\circ}
is equivalent to the monoidal category of finitely generated graded free
R
-modules
\Free^{\fg,\mathbb{Z}}(R)
.
Since
\mathcal{C}
is enriched over graded
R
-modules, the category
\mathcal{C}^{\circ}
(resp.
\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}
) is naturally an
R^{\circ}
-module (resp.
\Free^{\fg,\mathbb{Z}}(R)
-module).
In particular, for
X\in\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}
and
M\in\Free^{\fg,\mathbb{Z}}(R)
, we have the internal tensor object, denoted
X\underline{\otimes}_{R}M
, defined as the object representing the functor

Y\mapsto(\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(X,Y)\otimes_{R}M)^{0}.

We then deduce that there is a natural isomorphism

(B.2.1)

\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(Y,X\underline{\otimes}_{R}M)\cong\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(Y,X)\otimes_{R}M.

Now, let
X,Y\in\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}
and assume that
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}(X,Y)
is a graded free as an
R
-module.
We will define a canonical morphism

(B.2.2)

X\underline{\otimes}_{R}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(X,Y)\to Y.

If
(\varphi_{i})_{i\in I}
is a graded basis of the
R
-module
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(X,Y)
, then this choice allows us to identify
X\underline{\otimes}_{R}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(X,Y)
with
\bigoplus_{i\in I}X(-\deg(\varphi_{i}))
.
We then define (
B.2.2
) by
\bigoplus_{i\in I}\varphi_{i}(-\deg(\varphi_{i}))
.
It is not hard to check that this morphism is independent of the choice of basis. For any
Z\in\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}
, the induced morphism

\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(Z,X\underline{\otimes}_{R}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(X,Y))\to\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(Z,Y)

is identified, via (
B.2.1
), with the morphism

\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(Z,X)\otimes_{R}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(X,Y)\to\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(Z,Y)

given by morphism composition.

B.3.
Categories Attached to Locally Closed Subsets

B.3.1.
Topology on
\Lambda

Let
(\Lambda,\leq)
be a poset. We say that a subset
I\subseteq\Lambda
is
closed
if for any
\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda
with
\mu\in I
and
\lambda\leq\mu
, then
\lambda\in I
.
A subset
J\subseteq\Lambda
is called
open
if
\Lambda\setminus J
is closed. Given any subset
K\subseteq\Lambda
, we can consider its
closure

\overline{K}\coloneq\{\lambda\in\Lambda\mid\exists\mu\in K\textnormal{ such that }\lambda\leq\mu\},

which is the smallest closed set containing
K
.
Finally, we say that
K\subseteq X
is
locally closed
if
K
is open in
\overline{K}
, or equivalently if
K
is closed in
\Lambda\setminus(\overline{K}\setminus K)
.

Let
\lambda\in\Lambda
, we will write

\{\leq\lambda\}\coloneq\{\mu\in\Lambda\mid\mu\leq\lambda\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\{<\lambda\}\coloneq\{\mu\in\Lambda\mid\mu<\lambda\}.

B.3.2.
Locally Closed Subsets

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an OACC with evaluation
\pi
and fix a closed subset
I\subseteq\Lambda
.
Define a category
\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ}
as the full subcategory of
\mathcal{C}^{\circ}
whose objects are of the form
X(n)
for
n\in\mathbb{Z}
and
X
reduced in
\mathcal{C}
such that
\pi(X)\in I
.
We also write
\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\oplus,\circ}
for the additive hull of
\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ}
. Note that
\mathbb{D}
stabilizes
\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\oplus,\circ}
by (
).

Remark B.3.3
.

When
I=\Lambda
, it is generally not true that
\mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}^{\oplus,\circ}
is equivalent to the additive hull of
\mathcal{C}^{\circ}
.

Let
X,Y\in\mathcal{C}^{\circ}
, we will denote by

\mathfrak{J}_{I}(X,Y)\subseteq\Hom_{\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(X,Y)

the
R
-submodule of morphisms which factor through
\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\oplus,\circ}
.

Lemma B.3.4

(
[
ARV20
, Lemma 4.2]
)
.

Let
X,Y\in\mathcal{C}
, then

(B.3.1)

\mathfrak{J}_{I}(X,Y)=\textnormal{span}_{R}\left(\bigcup_{\lambda\in I}\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}^{\lambda}(X,Y)\right).

Proof.

It is clear from the definition that if
\lambda\in I
, then
\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{S,T}^{\lambda}\in\mathfrak{J}_{I}(X,Y)
. As a result, the right-hand side of (
B.3.1
) is contained in
\mathfrak{J}_{I}(X,Y)
.

Let
Z
be reduced with
\pi(Z)\in I
and
f:X\to Y
be a morphism in
\mathcal{C}
which factors through
\pi(Z)
.
By (
), we can replace
f
by a composition of the form

X\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{S,T}^{\lambda}}}{{\longrightarrow}}Z\to Y

for some
\lambda\in\Lambda
,
S\in E(X,\lambda)
, and
T\in E(\lambda,Z)
.
Since
\pi
is an evaluation, we must have that
\lambda\leq\pi(Z)
, and hence
\lambda\in I
. We are then done by (
).
∎

Let
I_{0}\subset\Lambda
and
I_{1}\subseteq I_{0}
be closed subsets.
We define a category

\mathcal{C}_{I_{0},I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}\coloneq\mathcal{C}_{I_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}/\!\!/\mathcal{C}_{I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus},

where the quotient appearing on the right-hand side is the “naive” quotient. I.e., its objects are the same as those in
\mathcal{C}_{I_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}
, and its morphisms are defined by

\Hom_{\mathcal{C}_{I_{0},I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}}(X,Y)=\left(\Hom_{\mathcal{C}_{I_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(X,Y)/\mathfrak{J}_{I_{1}}(X,Y)\right)^{0}

for
X,Y\in\mathcal{C}_{I_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}
.

The shift functor (1) induces an autoequivalence on
\mathcal{C}_{I_{0},I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}
. Likewise,
\mathbb{D}
on
\mathcal{C}_{I_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}
restricts to a contravariant autoequivalence of
\mathcal{C}_{I_{0},I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}
.
By Lemma
B.3.4
, we have that
\bigcup_{\lambda\in I_{0}\setminus I_{1}}\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}^{\lambda}(X,Y)
forms a graded
R
-linear basis for
\Hom_{\mathcal{C}_{I_{0},I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(X,Y)
.
It then follows (see
[
ARV20
, Lemma 4.3]
) that
\mathcal{C}_{I_{0},I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}
only depends on
I_{0}\setminus I_{1}
up to a canonical equivalence of categories.

We can then define, for any locally closed subset
I\subseteq\Lambda
, the category

\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ,\oplus}\coloneq\mathcal{C}_{I_{0},I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}

where
I_{1}\subset I_{0}
are closed subsets of
\Lambda
such that
I=I_{0}\setminus I_{1}
. Of course, when
I
itself is closed, the notation agrees with definition of the category associated to a closed subset from earlier.

B.3.5.
Case of a Singleton

We consider the special case when
I=\{\lambda\}
for some
\lambda\in\Lambda
.

Lemma B.3.6
.

Let
X\in\mathcal{C}
be reduced and
\pi(X)=\lambda
. By definition
E(X,\lambda)=\{*\}
is a singleton.
The image of the canonical map
\LL_{*}:X\to\lambda
in
\mathcal{C}_{\{\lambda\}}^{\circ,\oplus}
is an isomorphism.

Proof.

Since
X
is reduced, we must have that
\LL_{*}\circ\overline{\LL}_{\overline{*}}=\id_{\lambda}
in
\mathcal{C}_{\{\lambda\}}^{\circ,\oplus}
.
On the other hand, by Lemma
B.3.4
, we have an isomorphism
\End_{\mathcal{C}_{\{\lambda\}}^{\circ,\oplus}}(X)\cong R^{0}
.
As a result,
\id_{X}=\alpha\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{*,\overline{*}}^{\lambda}
for some
\alpha\in R^{0}
.
By applying
\LL_{*}\circ(-)
to both sides, we get that
\LL_{*}=\alpha\LL_{*}
. Therefore,
\alpha=1
.
∎

By Lemma
B.3.6
, for any reduced objects
X,Y\in\mathcal{C}
with
\pi(X)=\lambda=\pi(Y)
, there is a canonical isomorphism
X\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}Y
in
\mathcal{C}_{\{\lambda\}}^{\circ,\oplus}
.
As a result, any object in
\mathcal{C}_{\{\lambda\}}^{\circ,\oplus}
is canonically isomorphism to a direct sum of shifts of
\lambda
.
Moreover, by Lemma
B.3.4
, we know that
\End_{\mathcal{C}_{\{\lambda\}}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(\lambda)=R
.
From this, we deduce the following lemma.

Lemma B.3.7
.

There is a canonical equivalence of categories

\gamma:\mathcal{C}_{\{\lambda\}}^{\circ,\oplus}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}\Free^{\fg,\mathbb{Z}}(R)

such that
\gamma(\lambda)=R
. Moreover, under
\gamma
, the autoequivalence (1) identifies with the shift of grading autoequivalence (1) on
\Free^{\fg,\mathbb{Z}}(R)
.

B.3.8.
Open and Closed Inclusions

Let
I\subseteq\Lambda
be a locally closed subset. Write
I=I_{0}\setminus I_{1}
for some closed subsets
I_{1}\subset I_{0}\subseteq\Lambda
.
Let
J\subseteq I
be a closed subset of
I
. We can find some closed subset
J_{0}\subseteq I_{0}
such that
J=J_{0}\setminus(J_{0}\cap I_{1})
.
The natural embedding
\mathcal{C}_{J_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}_{I_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}
induces a functor

j_{J*}^{I}:\mathcal{C}_{J}^{\circ,\oplus}=\mathcal{C}_{J_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}/\!\!/\mathcal{C}_{J_{0}\cap I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}\to\mathcal{C}_{I_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}/\!\!/\mathcal{C}_{I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}=\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ,\oplus}.

It is not hard to check from Lemma
B.3.4
that
j_{J*}^{I}
functor is fully faithful and independent of the choices of
I_{0}
and
J_{0}
.
Note that
j_{J*}^{I}
commutes with
\mathbb{D}
and this construction is functorial with respect to compositions of closed inclusions in the obvious way.

Let
K\subset I
be open in
I
.
Let
J=I\setminus K
be the closed complement. We can write
J=J_{0}\setminus(J_{0}\cap I_{1})
as above. Then
K=I_{0}\setminus K_{1}
where
K_{1}=J_{0}\cup I_{1}
.
We then have a natural functor

j_{K}^{I*}:\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ,\oplus}=\mathcal{C}_{I_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}/\!\!/\mathcal{C}_{I_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}\to\mathcal{C}_{I_{0}}^{\circ,\oplus}/\!\!/\mathcal{C}_{K_{1}}^{\circ,\oplus}=\mathcal{C}_{K}^{\circ,\oplus}.

It is not hard to check from the morphism space computations earlier that
j_{K}^{I*}
is full and does not depend on the choices of
I_{0}
and
J_{0}
.
Note that
j_{K}^{I*}
commutes with
\mathbb{D}
and this construction is functorial with respect to compositions of open inclusions in the obvious way.

B.4.
Recollement

B.4.1.
Mixed Derived Category

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an OACC with evaluation
\pi
.

Definition B.4.2
.

Let
I\subseteq\Lambda
be a locally closed subset.
We define the
mixed derived category
of
\mathcal{C}
supported on
I
as the bounded homotopy category

D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\coloneq K^{b}\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ,\oplus}.

The mixed derived category admits two “shift” functors:

(1)

the internal shift inherited from
\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ,\oplus}
which is denoted by
(1)
;

(2)

the cohomological shift which is denoted by
[1]
.

We also define the
Tate twist
by
\langle 1\rangle\coloneq[1](-1)
.
The contravariant involution
\mathbb{D}
on
\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ,\oplus}
also induces a contravariant involution on
D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
which will also be denoted by
\mathbb{D}
.

If
J\subseteq I
is a closed subset and
K\subseteq I
is an open subset. The functors
j_{J*}^{I}
and
j_{K}^{I*}
induce similarly denoted functors on bounded homotopy categories

j_{J*}^{I}:D_{J}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\to D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\qquad\text{and}\qquad j_{K}^{I*}:D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\to D_{K}^{m}(\mathcal{C}).

Both
j_{J*}^{I}
and
j_{K}^{I*}
commute with
\mathbb{D}
.

B.4.3.
Recollement

Proposition B.4.4

(
[
ARV20
, Proposition 5.6]
)
.

Let
I\subseteq\Lambda
be a locally closed subset, and
J\subset I
be a finite closed subset.
Then the functor
j_{I\setminus J}^{I*}:D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\to D_{I\setminus J}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
admits a left adjoint
j_{I\setminus J!}^{I}
and a right adjoint
j_{I\setminus J*}^{I}
.
Similarly, the functor
j_{J*}^{I}:D_{J}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\to D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
admits a left adjoint
j_{J}^{I*}
and a right adjoint
j_{J}^{I!}
.
Together, these functors constitute a recollement diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{D_{J}^{m}(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{D_{I\setminus J}^{m}(\mathcal{C}).}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j_{J*}^{I}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j_{I\setminus J}^{I*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j_{J}^{I*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j_{J}^{I!}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j_{I\setminus J!}^{I}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j_{I\setminus J*}^{I}}

We will not provide a proof of Proposition
B.4.4
instead referring to
[
ARV20
]
.
The argument provided in
loc. cit.
is rather technical; however, it translates using the facts provided in the previous subsections.

Example B.4.5
.

It is enlightening to see how
j_{I\setminus\{\lambda\}*}^{I}
is defined on objects when
I
is locally closed and
\lambda\in I
is minimal (see
[
ARV20
, §5.2]
).
Let
X\in\mathcal{C}
be reduced such that
\pi(X)\in I\setminus\{\lambda\}
. The underlying complex of
j_{I\setminus\{\lambda\}*}^{I}X
is given by

\ldots\to 0\to\lambda\underline{\otimes}_{R}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(\lambda,X)\to X\to 0\to\ldots,

where
X
is in cohomological degree
0
. The only nontrivial differential is given by the canonical morphism from (
B.2.2
),

\lambda\underline{\otimes}_{R}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(\lambda,X)\to X.

Moreover, there is a canonical distinguished triangle

(B.4.1)

X\to j_{I\setminus\{\lambda\}*}^{I}X\to\lambda\underline{\otimes}_{R}\Hom_{\mathcal{C}_{I}^{\circ,\oplus}}^{\bullet}(\lambda,X)[1]\to

in
D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
.

B.4.6.
Pushforward and Pullback under Locally Closed Inclusions

Let
J\subseteq I\subseteq\Lambda
be finite locally closed subsets.
We can write
J=J_{0}\setminus J_{1}
for some closed subsets
J_{1}\subset J_{0}\subset I
.
We define the pushforward and pullback functors

\displaystyle j_{J*}^{I}

\displaystyle\coloneq j_{J_{0}*}^{I}\circ j_{J*}^{J_{0}}:D_{J}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\to D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C}),

\displaystyle j_{J!}^{I}

\displaystyle\coloneq j_{J_{0}!}^{I}\circ j_{J!}^{J_{0}}:D_{J}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\to D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C}),

\displaystyle j_{J}^{I*}

\displaystyle\coloneq j_{J}^{I\setminus J_{1}*}\circ j_{I\setminus J_{1}}^{I*}:D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\to D_{J}^{m}(\mathcal{C}),

\displaystyle j_{J}^{I!}

\displaystyle\coloneq j_{J}^{I\setminus J_{1}!}\circ j_{I\setminus J_{1}}^{I!}:D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\to D_{J}^{m}(\mathcal{C}).

It follows from
[
ARV20
, Lemma 5.10]
that these functors are naturally independent of the choices of
J_{0}
and
J_{1}
.
Moreover,
\left(j_{J!}^{I},j_{J}^{I!}\right)
and
\left(j_{J}^{I*},j_{J*}^{I}\right)
are adjoint pairs of functors.
We also have canonical isomorphisms

(B.4.2)

\mathbb{D}\circ j_{J*}^{I}\cong j_{J!}^{I}\circ\mathbb{D}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{D}\circ j_{J}^{I!}\cong j_{J}^{I*}\circ\mathbb{D}.

By Proposition
B.4.4
, the adjunction morphisms

j_{J}^{I*}\circ j_{J*}^{I}\to\id\qquad\text{and}\qquad\id\to j_{J}^{I!}\circ j_{J!}^{I}

are isomorphisms. Finally, we note that when
J\subset I
is closed, the
*
-pushforward and
!
-pushforward coincide.
Similarly, when
J\subseteq I
is open, the
*
-pullback and
!
-pullback coincide.

The four functors are also functorial with respect to compositions of locally closed subsets.

Lemma B.4.7
.

Let
I\subseteq\Lambda
be a finite locally closed subset, and let
J\subset I
and
K\subset J
be locally closed subsets.
Then there exist canonical isomorphisms

\displaystyle j_{J*}^{I}\circ j_{K*}^{J}

\displaystyle\cong j_{K*}^{I},

\displaystyle j_{J!}^{I}\circ j_{K!}^{J}

\displaystyle\cong j_{K!}^{I},

\displaystyle j_{K}^{J*}\circ j_{J}^{I*}

\displaystyle\cong j_{K}^{I*},

\displaystyle j_{K}^{J!}\circ j_{J}^{I!}

\displaystyle\cong j_{K}^{I!}.

Let
I\subseteq\Lambda
be a finite locally closed subset.
If
\lambda\in I
, then we will simplify the notation for the pullbacks and pushforwards corresponding to the inclusion
\{\lambda\}\subset I
by replacing
\{\lambda\}
with
\lambda
.

B.5.
Standards and Costandards

B.5.1.
Generation

Definition B.5.2
.

The
mixed derived category
of
\mathcal{C}
is the bounded homotopy category

D^{m}(\mathcal{C})\coloneq K^{b}\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}.

As in Remark
B.3.3
,
\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}
is not generally equivalent to
\mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}^{\circ,\oplus}
.
The situation is somewhat rectified after passing to mixed derived categories provided the following generation assumption holds.

Assumption B.5.3
.

Every object
X\in\mathcal{C}
when viewed as an object in
D^{m}(\mathcal{C})
is isomorphic to an object in
D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
for some finite locally closed subset
I\subseteq\Lambda
.

Whenever Assumption
B.5.3
holds, the canonical embedding

D_{\Lambda}^{m}(\mathcal{C})\hookrightarrow D^{m}(\mathcal{C})

is an equivalence of categories. Indeed, the assumption implies that
D^{m}(\mathcal{C})
is generated as a triangulated category by reduced objects in
\mathcal{C}
. Therefore, the embedding is essentially surjective.

Remark B.5.4
.

Assumption
B.5.3
is fairly mild. For example, this is known to hold whenever
\mathbbm{k}
is a complete local ring or a field by
[
EL16
, Proposition 2.24]
.
Additionally, it holds without any restriction on
\mathbbm{k}
when
\mathcal{C}
is the Hecke category of a Coxeter group
[
ARV20
, Lemma 6.2]
; although, their proof crucially uses properties of the Hecke category which are not featured in a general OACC.
It would be interesting to reinterpret Assumption
B.5.3
as a condition on the cellular structure.
This could lead to interesting generalizations of categorification results that historically have been beholden to constraints on
\mathbbm{k}
(see Proposition
B.6.2
).

B.5.5.
Definitions of Standards and Costandards

Let
I\subseteq\Lambda
be a finite locally closed subset.
For each
\lambda\in I\subseteq\Lambda
, we define the
standard
and
costandard
objects in
D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
respectively by

\Delta_{\lambda}^{I}\coloneq j_{\lambda!}^{I}\lambda\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nabla_{\lambda}^{I}\coloneq j_{\lambda*}^{I}\lambda.

When
I=\Lambda
, we will sometimes omit the superscript in the notation.

The following lemmas are simple consequences of recollement (Proposition
B.4.4
), Lemma
B.3.7
, and other basic properties of pushforwards/pullbacks along locally closed subsets.

Lemma B.5.6

(
[
ARV20
, Lemma 6.6]
)
.

Let
I\subseteq\Lambda
be a finite locally closed subset. Let
\lambda,\mu\in I
.
Then we have

\Hom_{D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})}(\Delta_{\lambda}^{I},\nabla_{\mu}^{I}\langle n\rangle[m])\cong\begin{cases}R^{m}&\text{if }\lambda=\mu\text{ and }m=-n,\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Lemma B.5.7

(
[
ARV20
, Lemma 6.8]
)
.

Let
I\subseteq\Lambda
be a finite locally closed subset, and let
J\subset I
be a locally closed subset.
Then for any
\lambda\in J
, we have

j_{J!}^{I}\Delta_{\lambda}^{J}\cong\Delta_{\lambda}^{I}\qquad\text{and}\qquad j_{J*}^{I}\nabla_{\lambda}^{J}\cong\nabla_{\lambda}^{I}.

Likewise for any
\mu\in I
, we have

j_{J}^{I*}\Delta_{\mu}^{I}\cong\begin{cases}\Delta_{\mu}^{J}&\text{if }\mu\in J,\\
0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\qquad\text{and}\qquad j_{J}^{I!}\nabla_{\mu}^{I}\cong\begin{cases}\nabla_{\mu}^{J}&\text{if }\mu\in J,\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Suppose
I\subseteq\Lambda
is locally closed (but possible infinite).
Let
\lambda\in I
. We can pick
J\subseteq\Lambda
finite and closed such that
\lambda\in J
.
We can define
\Delta_{\lambda}^{I}
and
\nabla_{\lambda}^{I}
by

\Delta_{\lambda}^{I}\coloneq j_{J!}^{I}\Delta_{\lambda}^{J}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nabla_{\lambda}^{I}\coloneq j_{J!}^{I}\nabla_{\lambda}^{J}.

These objects are independent of the choice of
J
.

Lemma B.5.8

(
[
ARV20
, Lemma 6.9]
)
.

For any locally closed subset
I\subseteq\Lambda
, the category
D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
is generated, as a triangulated category, by objects of the form
\Delta_{\lambda}^{I}(m)
for
\lambda\in I
and
m\in\mathbb{Z}
.
Alternatively,
D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
is also generated by objects of the form
\nabla_{\lambda}^{I}(m)
for
\lambda\in I
and
m\in\mathbb{Z}
.

B.6.
Grothendieck Groups

We
\mathcal{A}
is an essentially small triangulated category (resp. additive category), we denote by
[\mathcal{A}]_{\Delta}
(resp.
[\mathcal{A}]_{\oplus}
), the Grothendieck group of
\mathcal{A}
(resp. the split Grothendieck group of
\mathcal{A}
).

Lemma B.6.1

(
[
Ros15
, Theorem 1.1]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an essentially small additive category. The natural group homomorphism

[\mathcal{A}]_{\oplus}\to[K^{b}\mathcal{A}]_{\Delta}

is an isomorphism.

Proposition B.6.2
.

Assume that
\mathcal{C}
is an OACC with evaluation
\pi
satisfying Assumption
B.5.3
.

(1)

There exists an isomorphism of
\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}]
-modules

\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}][\Lambda]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}[D^{m}(\mathcal{C})]_{\Delta}

sending
v^{n}\lambda
to
\Delta_{\lambda}(n)
for all
\lambda\in\Lambda
and
n\in\mathbb{Z}
.

(2)

There exists an isomorphism of
\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}]
-modules

\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}][\Lambda]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}[\mathcal{C}^{\circ,\oplus}]_{\oplus}.

Proof.

The proof is essentially the same as
[
ARV20
, Theorem 6.13]
.

By Lemma
B.6.1
, the second isomorphism will follow from the first isomorphism.
By Assumption
B.5.3
, we have that
[D^{m}(\mathcal{C})]_{\Delta}\cong[D_{\Lambda}^{m}(\mathcal{C})]_{\Delta}
.
We can construct a
\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}]
-module homomorphism

\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}][\Lambda]\to[D_{\Lambda}^{m}(\mathcal{C})]_{\Delta}

by
v^{n}\lambda\mapsto[\Delta_{\lambda}(n)]
for
\lambda\in\Lambda
and
n\in\mathbb{Z}
.
By Lemma
B.5.8
, the elements
\{[\Delta_{\lambda}(n)]\}_{\lambda\in\Lambda,n\in\mathbb{Z}}
form a
\mathbb{Z}
-spanning set of
[D_{\Lambda}^{m}(\mathcal{C})]_{\Delta}
.
In order to prove this spanning set is linearly independent over
\mathbb{Z}
, we will argue by contradiction. Suppose there is a relation

\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\in K_{1}\\
m\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}c_{\lambda,m}[\Delta_{\lambda}(m)]=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\in K_{2}\\
n\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}c_{\mu,n}[\Delta_{\mu}(n)]

for some disjoint finite subsets
K_{1},K_{2}\subset\Lambda
and integers
c_{\lambda,n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
such that (1)
K_{1}\neq\varnothing
, (2)
c_{\lambda,m}\neq 0
for some
\lambda\in K_{1}
and
m\in\mathbb{Z}
, and (3)
c_{\lambda,m}
and
c_{\mu,n}
are only nonzero for finitely many
m
and
n
’s.
We can then define

X_{1}=\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\in K_{1}\\
m\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}\left(\Delta_{\lambda}(m)\right)^{\oplus c_{\lambda,m}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad X_{2}=\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\in K_{2}\\
n\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}\left(\Delta_{\mu}(n)\right)^{\oplus c_{\mu,n}}.

By
[
Tho97
, Lemma 2.6]
, there exists objects
Y,Y^{\prime},Y^{\prime\prime}\in D_{\Lambda}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
and distinguished triangles

Y\oplus X_{1}\to Y^{\prime}\to Y^{\prime\prime}\to\qquad\text{and}\qquad Y\oplus X_{2}\to Y^{\prime}\to Y^{\prime\prime}\to.

We can find a finite closed subset
I\subseteq\Lambda
such that all the above objects belong to
D_{I}^{m}(\mathcal{C})
.
Choose
\lambda\in K_{1}
such that
c_{\lambda,m}\neq 0
for at least one
m
. By Lemma
B.5.7
, we obtain distinguished triangles

j_{\lambda}^{I*}Y\oplus j_{\lambda}^{I*}X_{1}\to j_{\lambda}^{I*}Y^{\prime}\to j_{\lambda}^{I*}Y^{\prime\prime}\to,\qquad\qquad j_{\lambda}^{I*}Y\to j_{\lambda}^{I*}Y^{\prime}\to j_{\lambda}^{I*}Y^{\prime\prime}\to.

Therefore,
[j_{\lambda}^{I*}X_{1}]=0
in
[D_{\{\lambda\}}^{m}(\mathcal{C})]_{\Delta}
.
However, by Lemma
B.3.7
and Lemma
B.6.1
, there is an isomorphism of
\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}]
-modules,

\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm}]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}[D_{\{\lambda\}}^{m}(\mathcal{C})]_{\Delta}

defined by
v^{n}\mapsto\lambda(n)
for
n\in\mathbb{Z}
. Under this equivalence, we see that
c_{\lambda,m}=0
for all
m
which is a contradiction.
∎
